claim: "We have an 80 percent graduation rate in high school after spending more per student than any country in the world other than Liechtenstein, I think, or Luxembourg and a couple other small countries."
rationale: The U.S. public high-school adjusted cohort graduation rate in recent years has been in the mid-80s percent, not 80%, and depends on the specific metric used. Also, while the U.S. is among the higher spenders per pupil, OECD and international data show several countries (e.g., Luxembourg, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and some Nordic countries) spend as much or more per student, so the claim that the U.S. spends more than every country except a couple of very small ones is inaccurate.

claim: "More black babies are aborted in NYC than born."
rationale: Available NYC vital statistics and public-health summaries indicate that, in recent years, the number of live births to Black mothers in New York City has generally exceeded the number of abortions recorded for Black residents. The claim is ambiguous about year and how 'black babies' are counted and appears to conflate different datasets and definitions.

claim: Says the Dickey Amendment "prevents the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from even researching the relationship between gun violence and public health. ... The government can’t study gun violence but is spending $400,000 analyzing the effects of Swedish massages on rabbits."
rationale: The Dickey Amendment language bars CDC funds from being used to "advocate or promote gun control," but it does not explicitly prohibit the CDC or other government agencies from studying gun violence; however, the amendment and subsequent appropriations language produced a chilling effect that sharply reduced federally funded firearm research for years. The separate claim about a $400,000 grant for "Swedish massages on rabbits" is a misleading characterization of isolated or misdescribed research grants rather than evidence that the government can study nothing but frivolous animal massages.

claim: "If the Republicans were the majority, (Rep. Barton) would have actually the gavel and the chairmanship."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify: it does not specify which Rep. Barton, which committee, or which Congress. Committee chairmanships depend on the majority party but are assigned by the majority caucus and influenced by seniority, ethics, and leadership decisions, so one cannot definitively state Barton "would have actually the gavel" without that context.

claim: Says unlike Tim Kaine, who "invested" in education, Indiana Gov. Mike Pence "slashed education funding."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad characterization. As governor Pence presided over noteworthy cuts to higher-education operating support and funding shifts that critics called deep, but K–12 funding in Indiana was not universally slashed and in some budget years state K–12 appropriations rose; calling his administration as a whole to have "slashed education funding" is misleading. By contrast, Tim Kaine as Virginia governor increased K–12 and higher-education support in his budgets.

claim: "There comes a point in the last year of the president, especially in their second term, where you stop nominating" both Supreme Court justices and Court of Appeals judges.
rationale: There is no formal rule that presidents must stop nominating Supreme Court or Court of Appeals judges in the last year of a term; the Constitution gives the president the nomination power at all times. In practice the Senate may refuse to consider or confirm nominees in an election year (as in 2016) or may move quickly to confirm them (as in 2020), so whether nominations continue is a political choice, not a fixed cutoff.

claim: Says Ted Cruz said, "When gays stayed hidden we had no mass shootings; we had no public nudity. Society was polite. Now anything and everything goes and I blame them."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or mainstream reporting that Senator Ted Cruz ever made this exact statement. While Cruz has criticized LGBT policies in the past, this highly inflammatory quotation appears to be fabricated or misattributed and would have been widely reported if authentic.

claim: "Lindsey Graham threatens to convert to Democrat if Republicans don’t Dump Trump."
rationale: There is no credible public record or major news reporting that Senator Lindsey Graham threatened to convert to the Democratic Party if Republicans did not 'dump' Donald Trump. While Graham has at times criticized Trump, he has remained a Republican and has not announced an intention to switch parties.

claim: Says Ted Cruz said: "While there may have been an age difference, Josh Duggar’s transgressions are far less an affront to God than what gays do to each other."
rationale: There is no reliable record or reputable news source attributing this exact statement to Ted Cruz. While Cruz has publicly opposed same-sex marriage and spoken about sexual morality, major media coverage of Josh Duggar's scandal does not show Cruz saying Duggar's abuses were "far less an affront to God" than consensual gay relationships; the quote appears to be a misattribution circulating on social media.

claim: Says U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement "will be at every polling station" on Nov. 3, 2020.
rationale: There is no evidence that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement planned to or announced it would be physically present 'at every polling station' on Nov. 3, 2020. Election administration is handled by state and local officials, and ICE/DHS publicly denied plans to deploy immigration agents to polling places; multiple fact-checkers debunked similar claims.

claim: Says Mitt Romney was clear that he "would not provide government assistance to the U.S. auto companies, even if they went through bankruptcy."
rationale: During the 2008–2009 campaign period Romney publicly opposed government bailouts of the U.S. auto industry and explicitly said he would not provide government assistance to the automakers even if they went through bankruptcy. His comments were widely reported and cited as a clear statement of his position at the time.

claim: "Obama secretly gave citizenship to 2,500 Iranians as part of nuke deal."
rationale: Multiple independent fact-checks found no evidence that President Obama secretly granted U.S. citizenship to 2,500 Iranians as part of the Iran nuclear deal. U.S. naturalization requires individual applications, residency and background checks and cannot be secretly conferred en masse as part of an international agreement.

claim: "Actually, on some procedures, you're more likely to die if you're on Medicaid than if you're uninsured."
rationale: Peer-reviewed observational studies have reported that for certain surgical procedures and acute care contexts, adjusted mortality rates can be higher for patients on Medicaid than for uninsured patients. This pattern is not universal and likely reflects differences in case mix, access to higher-quality hospitals, and residual confounding rather than a simple causal effect of insurance status.

claim: Says he didn't cancel a political rally because after Sept. 11, "the New York Stock Exchange was open the following day."
rationale: This is false — the New York Stock Exchange did not reopen the day after the September 11, 2001 attacks. U.S. financial markets were closed for several trading days and the NYSE reopened on Monday, September 17, 2001, not the following day.

claim: A video shows "the COVID-19 vaccine when it hits your blood."
rationale: A consumer video cannot plausibly show the COVID-19 vaccine 'when it hits your blood' — vaccines are given intramuscularly, the material is not visually observable entering bloodstream in such footage, and viral clips are typically animations or misattributed microscopy. Additionally, mRNA vaccines largely remain near the injection site and in draining lymph nodes rather than instantly dispersing through the blood.
cited_knowledge: General medical knowledge of intramuscular vaccine administration and pharmacokinetics of COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, plus documented patterns of animations/mislabelled microscope footage circulating online.
safety_notes: I cannot inspect the specific video; it may be an animation, conceptual illustration, or unrelated microscopy, so the claim is unverified and misleading without provenance.

claim: Wisconsin’s middle class is the "most diminished" in the United States.
rationale: The claim is too sweeping and depends entirely on how "most diminished" is defined (share of households in the middle-income band, median real income, mobility, or change over a specific period). While some studies have found significant erosion of Wisconsin's middle-income share in certain years, other states show equal or larger declines depending on the metric and timeframe, and there is no authoritative consensus that Wisconsin is definitively the single most diminished state.

claim: "Maxine Waters Is Getting Criminally Charged!"
rationale: There is no publicly available, verifiable record (indictment, complaint, or DOJ announcement) showing that Rep. Maxine Waters has been criminally charged. The claim appears to be a sensational assertion without corroboration from major news outlets or official sources.

claim: "(Pete) Sessions has held at least two fundraisers at adult-themed clubs and made no apologies."
rationale: I could not find verifiable, credible reporting that Congressman Pete Sessions held at least two fundraisers at adult-themed (e.g., strip) clubs and refused to apologize; media coverage and public records do not corroborate that specific multi-event claim and it may conflate or misattribute isolated incidents. Because independent sources do not substantiate the assertion, the claim is unproven.

claim: Says the Security Against Foreign Enemies Act of 2015 would not "pause" the resettlement of Syrian refugees in the United States.
rationale: The Security Against Foreign Enemies Act of 2015 imposed interagency certification and information-sharing requirements that had to be met before Syrian refugees could be admitted. Although the bill did not use the word "pause," its conditions would have prevented new resettlements from proceeding until the required certifications and vetting procedures were completed, effectively halting admissions.

claim: Says Marco Rubio tweeted a verse from the New Testament to shame "his own constituents for flocking to Trump rally."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence in Rubio’s public tweet history or reputable news accounts up to mid‑2024 that he posted a New Testament verse explicitly to shame his own constituents for attending a Trump rally. While Rubio has occasionally quoted scripture on social media, the specific claim that he tweeted a New Testament verse with the stated purpose appears to be a misattribution or out‑of‑context interpretation rather than a documented action.

claim: Says the National Labor Relations Board told Boeing that it couldn’t build a factory in South Carolina because South Carolina is a right-to-work state.
rationale: The NLRB did not tell Boeing it could not build a factory in South Carolina because the state is right-to-work. The agency or its General Counsel alleged Boeing unlawfully shifted work to South Carolina for anti-union reasons in a complaint, but the NLRB does not have authority to ban a company from locating a plant simply because a state is right-to-work. News coverage and the NLRB actions concerned alleged labor-law violations, not a categorical prohibition based on state right-to-work status.

claim: Trump supporters are heading to the border as the migrant caravan approaches.
rationale: The claim is a broad, time-unspecified assertion that cannot be verified as a general fact. While media reporting has documented some pro-Trump groups and individual activists mobilizing to U.S. border areas in response to particular migrant caravans, there is no evidence that “Trump supporters” as a whole are heading to the border now; without specifics the statement is misleading.

claim: "We're the only system of federalism in the world."
rationale: The claim is false: many countries operate federal systems that divide power between a central government and constituent states or provinces. Examples include Germany, Canada, Australia, India, Brazil, Switzerland, Mexico, and others, so no single country is uniquely the only federal system.

claim: The Banking Committee voted a 1,336-page bill "out of committee in 21 minutes with no amendments, with the understanding that before the bill came to the floor, we would reach this bipartisan agreement."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim as stated and it appears implausible: Senate/House banking committees typically allow time for review and amendments, and moving a 1,336‑page bill out in 21 minutes with no amendments would be unusual. Without a cited date, committee name, or bill number this reads like a mischaracterization or missing-context quote rather than a documented committee action.

claim: "Our economy created over 6.5 million new jobs just last year, more jobs in one year than ever before in the history of the United States of America."
rationale: Official U.S. payroll data for the most recent full year (2021) show roughly a 6.4 million increase in nonfarm payroll employment, not "over 6.5 million." It is true that the roughly 6.4 million gain was the largest annual increase on record in the BLS payroll series, but the numeric claim is inaccurate/overstated.
cited_knowledge: Bureau of Labor Statistics monthly payroll (establishment) data for 2021 showing about a 6.4 million net increase and the note that this was the largest over-the-year rise in the historical series; different surveys can produce slightly different counts.
safety_notes: Claim depends on which survey (establishment vs household) and the exact 12-month window; rounding or different data vintages can change the stated total.

claim: Under his leadership, more people in Wisconsin "have access to health care."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who “he” is, the timeframe, or how “access to health care” is being measured. Whether more people gained access depends on specific policies, enrollment data, and definitions (insurance coverage, Medicaid expansion, provider availability), so the statement cannot be confirmed without that context.

claim: "Gina Haspel, CIA head is dead!"
rationale: There have been no credible reports or official announcements indicating that Gina Haspel has died. She served as CIA director from 2018–2021 and was reported alive through my latest reliable updates; I have no confirmed information of her death.

claim: "I never was in favor of shutting down the government. … (I) voted to fund the government fully."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it lacks the identity of the speaker and specific votes or dates. Determining whether someone 'never' favored a shutdown and voted to fund the government fully requires checking that person's public statements and official roll-call votes; without that evidence the assertion is unsubstantiated. Given the missing context and the plausibility that a politician could both vote to fund at times and previously support shutdown tactics, the claim is treated as false until sourcing is provided.

claim: "This kind of snowstorm happens every 10 or 15 years."
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated because it gives no location, time period, or precise definition of 'this kind' of snowstorm. Frequency of severe snowstorms varies widely by region, storm type, and climate variability—some events might have ~10–15-year return periods while others do not. Without specific data or a clear metric, the universal statement is not supportable.

claim: "Here's a man who brags about how he made the city safe. It was the Biden crime bill that became the Clinton crime bill that allowed him to do that."
rationale: The statement refers to the 1994 Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act, which Joe Biden helped author and shepherd through the Senate while Bill Clinton, as president, championed and signed it into law. It is commonly described as both a 'Biden crime bill' (given Biden's legislative role) and a 'Clinton crime bill' (because Clinton promoted and signed the legislation).

claim: Barack Obama is the "first president to file lawsuits against the states he swore an oath to protect."
rationale: The federal government (through the Department of Justice acting under the president) has long initiated lawsuits against states, well before Barack Obama’s administration. Examples include DOJ civil‑rights suits in the 1950s–1960s and much earlier federal suits over boundaries and federal law, so Obama was not the first president under whose administration the federal government sued states.

claim: "We’ve got 600-plus police and fire pensions Downstate that are on the cusp of insolvency because they don’t have the revenues that they need to be able to keep those pensions going."
rationale: State-level reporting and policy analyses show Illinois has well over 600 local police and fire pension funds outside Chicago, and many of those funds are heavily underfunded and face insolvency risk because their local revenue streams (small municipal tax bases, pension levies, and limited state support) are insufficient to meet obligations. Descriptions that these 600+ downstate funds are on the cusp of insolvency are consistent with actuarial and budget analyses warning of imminent funding shortfalls for numerous small pension funds.

claim: "More suicide deaths than coronavirus death past two months."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify because it gives no country or exact two-month period. COVID-19 and suicide death counts vary widely by jurisdiction and time; in many places COVID deaths have exceeded suicides, while in some short windows or regions suicides may outnumber COVID deaths. Without a specified location and dates the statement cannot be supported and is therefore judged false as presented.

claim: Gas prices during the Obama-Biden administration were $5.49 a gallon.
rationale: The U.S. national average retail gasoline price did not reach $5.49 per gallon at any point during the Obama–Biden administration (2009–2017); national averages peaked well below $5 (generally under $4). While some local retail stations in high-cost states (e.g., California or Hawaii) occasionally sold gasoline above $5 per gallon, that was not the nationwide price during that administration.

claim: Says President Obama has "doubled" the deficit.
rationale: The claim is misleading. The annual federal deficit surged in 2009 amid the financial crisis but fell in subsequent years and was smaller by the end of Obama's second term than the 2009 peak; the national debt increased substantially during his presidency but did not literally 'double' during his tenure.

claim: Says Scott Walker "said that forcing women facing abortion to get invasive ultrasounds was 'just a cool thing.'"
rationale: News coverage shows Scott Walker praised ultrasound imaging as "a pretty cool thing" while discussing ultrasound technology during debates over abortion-related requirements, but he did not explicitly say that forcing women to undergo invasive ultrasounds was "just a cool thing." The claim misstates and conflates his comment about the technology with an endorsement of coercive medical procedures.

claim: "We now consume at the federal level 25 percent of the gross domestic product. Historically we were at 20 percent. So we've taken 5 percent away from the private sector."
rationale: The statement conflates an imprecise change in the federal share of GDP with a direct 5 percentage-point transfer 'away from the private sector.' Federal share and the private sector share are measured in different ways and depend on definitions (federal spending vs. total government consumption vs. revenues) and time period. Even if the federal share of GDP rose by about five points, that does not automatically mean the private sector lost an equal amount because GDP growth, borrowing, transfers, and tax incidence complicate where resources come from and go.

claim: "A year ago we had the lowest unemployment in history without using taxpayers money."
rationale: The statement is unverified and implausible because it gives no country or exact date and asserts a historical low was achieved 'without using taxpayers money.' Unemployment records are country- and measure-specific, and macroeconomic outcomes are typically influenced by government or central bank actions that are directly or indirectly funded by taxpayers, so the blanket claim cannot be supported as written.

claim: "Across the country, more than half of the U.S. attorney seats remain without a prosecutor chosen by Obama."
rationale: The claim gives no date and is not verifiable as stated. There are 93 U.S. attorney offices and while many can be vacant early in a new administration, vacancies fluctuate and presidents typically fill most posts over time, so a blanket statement that "more than half" remain without an Obama appointee is unsupported without a specific timeframe or evidence.

claim: "We have completely turned our economy around."
rationale: The claim is a vague, absolute statement and cannot be verified as true without specifying which country, time period, and what metrics constitute 'completely turned...around.' Economic performance is multidimensional (growth, unemployment, inflation, wages, debt) and typically shows mixed results rather than a single definitive turnaround. Political statements using 'completely' are often exaggerations and require concrete, measurable evidence to be supported.

claim: The federal government "now tells us which light bulbs to buy."
rationale: The federal government has enacted energy-efficiency standards (notably the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 and subsequent DOE rules) that effectively ban the manufacture and sale of many traditional incandescent 'general purpose' bulbs. While the rules do not tell consumers a specific brand or model to buy, they limit which types of bulbs manufacturers can sell, thereby constraining consumer choices.

claim: "Historically," Senate ratification of arms control treaties "has been bipartisan."
rationale: Most major arms control treaties that the U.S. Senate has ratified (for example the NPT, ABM/SALT-era accords, START and New START, and the Chemical Weapons Convention) received substantial bipartisan support. While there have been notable exceptions and contentious votes (for example the Senate rejected the CTBT in 1999 and some proposed accords were never submitted), the historical pattern for treaties that were accepted has generally involved cross‑party coalitions.

claim: "Look at what’s happening last night in Sweden. Sweden, who would believe this? Sweden. They took in large numbers. They’re having problems like they never thought possible."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific recent crisis in Sweden ('last night') caused by taking in large numbers of migrants; there was no corroborated major incident on that timeline. While Sweden has accepted many refugees and faces integration and localized crime challenges, the claim that they experienced an unexpected nationwide calamity 'last night' is inaccurate and misleading.

claim: A "majority in every state favors path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants."
rationale: While national polls routinely find a majority of Americans support a pathway to citizenship for undocumented immigrants, there is significant state-by-state variation and no evidence that every single state contains a majority in favor. State-level and subnational polls sometimes show lower support or plurality/opposition in some states, and results depend on question wording and timing.

claim: Veterans should vote Republican "because the damn Democrats blocked the VA Healthcare bill again."
rationale: The claim asserts as fact that “the Democrats blocked the VA Healthcare bill again,” but it gives no date, bill identifier, or legislative context and therefore cannot be verified as a general truth. Whether a specific VA-related bill was blocked (and by whom) depends on the particular bill, chamber, vote counts, and procedural rules; historical voting on VA bills has not consistently been a single-party action. Without specific details, the blanket assertion is unsupported and misleading.

claim: Property taxes "are now 18% higher than when (Mark Sharpe) first took office."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it lacks key details (which jurisdiction, which "property taxes" metric, and the date Mark Sharpe took office). Property-tax changes vary by locality and can be reported as rate changes, average bills, or revenue and may be affected by reassessments and inflation. Without those specifics and supporting local tax records, the 18% figure cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Three of five detainees swapped (for Bowe Bergdahl) are now ISIS leaders."
rationale: The five men exchanged for Bowe Bergdahl in 2014 were senior Taliban detainees (e.g., Mullah Mohammad Fazl, Khairullah Khairkhwa, Norullah Nori, Mohammad Nabi Omari, and Abdul Haq Wasiq). There is no reliable evidence that three of them became leaders of ISIS; reporting instead documents some returning to insurgent activity or remaining aligned with the Taliban, not serving as ISIS leaders.

claim: After laying off 30,000 people, Carly Fiorina said that in retrospect, "I would have done them all faster."
rationale: There is no reliable record that Fiorina uttered that exact line; the quote is a widely circulated paraphrase/mischaracterization. Contemporary reporting and later fact-checking show she was criticized for layoffs and made comments about tough decisions, but she did not plainly say, as stated, 'I would have done them all faster.'

claim: Says Steph Curry decided to split with Nike because the company wouldn’t allow him to write Bible scriptures in his shoes.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Steph Curry 'split' with Nike for refusing Bible scriptures on his shoes. Public accounts show Curry's prominent deal has been with Under Armour after Nike did not offer him a major rookie endorsement, and no reputable reporting documents Nike blocking scripture inscriptions as the cause for any split.

claim: "I was speaking out on pension reform almost 17 years ago."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable because it lacks a speaker identity and a reference date; 'almost 17 years ago' is relative to when the statement was made. Without specific evidence (dated speeches, media reports, or records showing the person publicly advocated pension reform at that time) the claim cannot be confirmed. Given this missing context, I treat it as not proven.

claim: The Baucus health care bill would require taxes on medical devices such as X-ray machines, female condoms, HIV tests and surgical needles.
rationale: The Baucus Senate Finance Committee health reform proposals included an excise/assessment on medical devices to help pay for coverage expansions. The tax was broad in scope and was widely described as applying to items such as diagnostic equipment, condoms and other disposable medical supplies, test kits and needles as examples of taxable devices.

claim: "Obamacare isn't helping anyone."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act expanded insurance coverage to millions, reduced the uninsured rate, established protections for people with pre-existing conditions, and provided subsidies and Medicaid expansion in many states; while it has shortcomings and some people face higher costs or limited choices, it is incorrect to say it helps no one.

claim: The Biden administration "gifted the Taliban with $80 billion-plus" in military-grade weapons but now "wants your 9mm pistols."
rationale: The claim conflates several different facts and is inaccurate. U.S. military equipment left behind in Afghanistan was estimated by the DoD at roughly $7 billion in usable gear, not an $80+ billion deliberate "gift" to the Taliban, and the U.S. did not transfer $80B in weapons; the larger $80B figure is sometimes a mistaken reference to long-term spending or frozen Afghan central-bank assets. There is also no federal program to seize common privately owned 9mm pistols; current proposals focus on specific regulatory changes (e.g., on ghost guns or certain braces), not a blanket confiscation of 9mm handguns.

claim: Rob Cornilles is a Tea Party candidate.
rationale: There is no widely known or documented public record identifying Rob Cornilles specifically as a 'Tea Party' candidate. Without a clear jurisdiction, election year, or cited endorsement from Tea Party organizations, the label appears unsubstantiated. Because multiple people can share the name and political labels are context-dependent, the claim cannot be verified as stated.

claim: Obama said he would "stand with the Muslims should the political winds shift in an ugly direction."
rationale: Barack Obama did say the line about standing with Muslims if the political winds shifted in an ugly direction; it was part of a broader statement he made during his campaign-era remarks about defending civil liberties and minority rights. The sentence has been widely quoted and attributed to him in contemporary news coverage.

claim: Quotes show Democrats supported riots "when BLM was BURNING down cities and killing people in the streets!"
rationale: This is an overbroad and misleading claim. While a small number of individual Democrats made controversial remarks that critics said encouraged confrontation, the vast majority of Democratic leaders publicly condemned violent rioting and called for peaceful protest and reform. Characterizing Black Lives Matter as broadly "burning down cities and killing people" is also inaccurate: most BLM protests were peaceful and incidents of arson or fatalities during unrest were limited and often involved a mix of actors.

claim: Says a mall Santa beat up a child molester.
rationale: The claim is unverified and lacks specific details (time, place, names) needed for confirmation. Claims that 'a mall Santa beat up a child molester' have circulated as viral anecdotes and memes without corroboration from reputable news outlets or official statements, so it should be treated as false until reliable evidence is provided.

claim: The Affordable Care Act alters the "sensible doctor-patient-relationship-centered health care program ... we see today."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act changed insurance rules, coverage expansion, and payment incentives, but it did not explicitly abolish or replace the traditional doctor–patient relationship. While some ACA provisions (e.g., new payment models, quality metrics, and delivery reforms) can indirectly affect how care is organized, the law does not formally eliminate or replace the clinician–patient relationship itself.

claim: In Virginia, "people are going and getting marriage licenses who are 12 and 13, and 14 and 15 years old."
rationale: The claim that 12- and 13-year-olds (and routinely 14- and 15-year-olds) are simply 'going and getting' marriage licenses in Virginia is not accurate. State law imposes parental-consent and/or judicial-approval requirements for minors, and routine issuance of licenses to children that young would not occur; marriages of very young teens would be exceptional and require court orders. Available reporting and legal reforms indicate such extremely young legal marriages are not commonplace in Virginia.

claim: When Terry McAuliffe was governor, "Unemployment went down in every single county, including rural Virginia by nearly 50%.
rationale: While Virginia's overall unemployment rate fell during Terry McAuliffe's 2014–2018 term, the claim that unemployment went down in "every single county" and that rural Virginia fell "by nearly 50%" is inaccurate. County-level labor statistics show variation and at least some localities did not experience declines, and the "nearly 50%" figure depends on how "rural" is defined and which start/end months are selected.

claim: Says Joe Biden called ANTIFA "courageous Americans."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Joe Biden saying the specific phrase 'courageous Americans' in reference to Antifa; media fact-checks have found this wording is a misquote or taken out of context from other remarks about protesters or criticism of violence. Biden has repeatedly condemned political violence and called for peaceful protest rather than praising extremist groups. The claim appears to be a rhetorical distortion spread on social media.

claim: Says Paul Manafort "played a very limited role" in the Trump presidential campaign.
rationale: Paul Manafort served as Donald Trump's campaign chairman and senior adviser in 2016 and oversaw strategy and delegate operations; he led the campaign for several months and continued advising after stepping down. Given his formal title, responsibilities, and the attention paid to his actions in investigations, describing his role as 'very limited' is inaccurate.

claim: "Paul Broun Jr. sides with sexual deviants to support sale of 'crush videos.' "
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Rep. Paul Broun (or anyone named Paul Broun Jr.) publicly “sided with sexual deviants” or advocated legalizing or supporting the sale of so‑called crush videos. Federal legislation specifically targeting crush videos passed with broad bipartisan support after court rulings, and Broun is not documented as having sponsored or led efforts to permit their sale. The claim mixes inflammatory language with an assertion for which I find no corroborating record.

claim: No one showed up for this Joe Biden and Kamala Harris joint campaign event in Arizona.
rationale: An absolute claim that 'no one showed up' to a joint Biden–Harris campaign event is implausible and not supported without specific evidence. Presidential campaign events routinely include campaign staff, security, press, volunteers and at least some attendees, and an entirely empty turnout for such high-profile figures would have been widely reported.

claim: Rhode Island "charter schools are nationally recognized as outperforming their counterparts across the country."
rationale: There is no broad, uncontested national recognition that Rhode Island charter schools uniformly outperform counterparts across the country. Research on charter school performance (e.g., CREDO and other national analyses) shows wide variation by state, district, and individual school, and Rhode Island has not been identified as consistently outperforming national peers in a way that supports this sweeping claim.

claim: Says television host Steve Harvey authored a pro-Trump rant about raccoons and exterminators.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Steve Harvey authored a pro‑Trump rant involving raccoons and exterminators; the purported piece appears to be a fabricated or satirical social‑media post misattributed to him. Major news outlets and fact‑checking organizations did not corroborate such a column and Harvey has not been documented publishing that content.

claim: "324,000 pregnant people experience domestic violence during their pregnancy."
rationale: The claim presents a precise count without specifying a country or timeframe, and I cannot verify a widely accepted statistic of exactly 324,000 pregnant people experiencing domestic violence. Prevalence estimates for intimate partner violence during pregnancy vary by survey, year, and jurisdiction and are usually reported as rates or ranges rather than a single global count. Without a cited source and context, the specific figure is not reliably supported.

claim: "Babysitter on crystal meth eats 3-month-old baby."
rationale: There are no credible news reports or official records corroborating an incident in which a babysitter on crystal meth ate a 3-month-old baby; an event of this nature would be widely and repeatedly reported by reputable outlets. The claim is sensational, lacks any identifying details (date, location, names), and cannot be verified from reliable sources.

claim: "#GradInsurance debacle is a DIRECT result of #ObamaCare. #MIZZOU has to break the law to do the right thing."
rationale: The claim asserts a direct causal link between the Affordable Care Act and an unspecified "GradInsurance debacle" at Mizzou and further claims the university must break the law to resolve it. There is no clear public evidence that the ACA directly created such a debacle or that it legally compels the University of Missouri to violate laws; administrative insurance disputes are typically the result of institutional decisions, insurer actions, or state regulations rather than a single federal law forcing illegal action.

claim: Says "there have been some job gains in the McMansion State since Mr. Christie took office, but they have lagged gains both in the nation as a whole and in New York and Connecticut, the obvious points of comparison."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous because it does not specify the exact time window “since Mr. Christie took office.” Employment gains vary by chosen start/end dates; New Jersey’s job growth under Christie sometimes lagged the national rate and New York, but not consistently across his entire tenure and sometimes outperformed Connecticut depending on the period. Without a specified timeframe the blanket comparative claim cannot be verified as generally true.

claim: Under my platform, "I will make no changes to the current (Medicare) system for current retirees and anyone approaching retirement."
rationale: This is a forward-looking political promise that cannot be verified as an absolute fact. Elected officials cannot unilaterally guarantee no future changes to Medicare because Congress, future administrations, budgetary pressures, and courts can alter the program; historically, campaign promises about preserving entitlement rules have sometimes been changed. Without a specific, legally binding mechanism tied to the claim, it is not reliably true.

claim: Says Sen. Sherrod Brown voted to keep "an extreme, job-killing Internal Revenue Service paperwork mandate."
rationale: There is no clear record that Sen. Sherrod Brown voted to retain an "extreme" $600 IRS paperwork mandate as described. The contested 1099-K reporting proposal was changed in response to pushback, and public records and statements show Democrats (including Brown) supported revisions to protect small businesses; political ads have conflated or mischaracterized different votes and proposals.

claim: "More people, almost twice as many, pay the penalty or take the waiver than signed up for (Obamacare)."
rationale: This is not supported by available data: ACA marketplace enrollments were in the millions (often 10+ million in a given open‑enrollment period), while the number of people who paid the individual mandate penalty or received exemptions was substantially lower and never nearly double marketplace sign‑ups. The claim conflates distinct counts (enrollments vs. penalty filers/exemptions) and misstates their relative sizes.

claim: "$21T in Pentagon accounting errors. Medicare for All costs ~$32T. That means 66% of Medicare for All could have been funded already by the Pentagon."
rationale: The arithmetic (21/32 ≈ 66%) is correct, but the premise is misleading: the often-cited $21 trillion refers to cumulative accounting adjustments and unsupported journal entries in Pentagon records over many years, not actual missing or recoverable cash that could be reallocated. Additionally, the ~$32 trillion figure for "Medicare for All" depends on the timeframe, scope, and assumptions (gross vs. net costs and savings), so you cannot directly equate the two numbers as available funding.

claim: A mansion in photo is Joe Biden’s house.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because no photo, metadata, or reliable source is provided; images of houses are frequently misattributed online. Without provenance or a reverse-image match to a documented Biden residence, the assertion that the pictured mansion is Joe Biden’s house is unsubstantiated.

claim: Jeff Mann has an ethics complaint against him alleging he used county workers for campaign work, which is an indictable offense.
rationale: I cannot verify a specific, credible report that a person named Jeff Mann has an ethics complaint alleging he used county workers for campaign work; no widely reported or documented complaint matching that description is known to me. Additionally, whether such conduct is an indictable offense depends on the jurisdiction and specific statutes, so the blanket statement that it 'is an indictable offense' is not universally correct.

claim: Says as Assembly Speaker he is a "constitutional officer" of Wisconsin.
rationale: The Speaker of the Wisconsin Assembly is an officer of that legislative chamber chosen by its members, but is not ordinarily classified as a statewide "constitutional officer" like the governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, or treasurer. While the state constitution authorizes each house to select its own officers, the term "constitutional officer" in Wisconsin practice is used for offices established as statewide executive offices by the constitution rather than internal legislative posts.

claim: Says the U.S. Constitution "doesn’t say anything about (redistricting) being fair. … it’s set up to be partisan."
rationale: The U.S. Constitution does not contain language requiring redistricting to be 'fair' or nonpartisan; it vests authority over congressional elections and districting largely with state legislatures (and Congress) rather than prescribing fairness standards. That structure allows partisan actors to draw districts in ways that advantage their party, though judicial rulings and statutes (e.g., equal-population requirements and bans on racial discrimination) impose some limits.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Paul Ryan’s budget proposal "eliminates Medicare" in 10 years.
rationale: Paul Ryan’s budget proposals did not literally repeal or eliminate the Medicare program within ten years; they proposed converting Medicare’s guaranteed-benefit structure into a premium-support (voucher-style) system for future beneficiaries beginning about a decade out. Critics described that change as effectively ending traditional Medicare, but the proposals changed benefit structure and federal financing rather than outright abolishing Medicare immediately.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We need to repeal Daylight Savings Time as a primary measure to decrease the rate of climate change. Less hours of sun shine equal less heat hitting Earth’s surface."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made this statement, and the claim rests on a misunderstanding: repealing Daylight Saving Time only shifts clock hours and does not reduce the total amount of sunlight or primary global heat input. Climate scientists do not identify ending DST as a primary measure to decrease the rate of climate change.

claim: Gina Raimondo "paid 70 million in taxpayer dollars to millionaire hedge fund managers."
rationale: The claim is misleading. As Rhode Island general treasurer, Raimondo shifted pension assets to external managers and the pension system did pay tens of millions in fees to private equity/hedge fund managers, but those fees were paid from pension assets (not a direct line-item payment from the state budget) and framing it as her personally 'paying $70 million in taxpayer dollars to millionaire hedge fund managers' omits key context and attribution. The characterization about who was paid and how the funds are classified is therefore inaccurate.

claim: "Just on Jan. 1 of this year, there were 40,000 new laws put on the books in one day."
rationale: There is no evidence that 40,000 distinct new laws took effect nationwide on a single day. Federal Congress passes only a few hundred public laws per year, and even when aggregating state legislatures and local ordinances it is implausible to reach 40,000 discrete new statutes becoming effective on one date; claims like this usually conflate different categories (statutes, administrative rules, or policy changes) or misuse counting methods.

claim: A video shows Kim Jong Un calling Joe Biden a "thug," a "coward," and "mentally unstable" in a speech.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Kim Jong Un delivered a speech calling Joe Biden a 'thug,' 'coward,' and 'mentally unstable.' North Korean official statements rarely use such casual, direct name-calling of a named foreign head of state in the manner described, and viral clips making such claims have been debunked or shown to be edited or manipulated.

claim: Says Tom Barrett "has directed that tens of millions of City of Milwaukee tax dollars be used for the construction of a downtown trolley at the expense of: health and public safety; repair and replacement of public infrastructure; public education; and, job creation and economic development."
rationale: The claim overstates responsibility and causation. While Mayor Tom Barrett supported Milwaukee’s downtown streetcar (The Hop), the project was funded by a mix of federal, state, county, private and city sources rather than solely by 'tens of millions' extracted unilaterally by Barrett from city tax revenues, and there is no clear evidence that its funding directly forced cuts to health, public safety, infrastructure repair, education, or economic development budgets as claimed.

claim: Ron Klein "sponsored an amendment that specifically allows price gouging."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Rep. Ron Klein authored or sponsored an amendment that explicitly 'allows price gouging.' Reports that make that claim appear to mischaracterize or omit context about the actual amendment language, which did not contain a provision authorizing price gouging.

claim: Insulin prices have "gone THRU THE ROOF for patients/taxpayers bc of manufacturer, health plan & PBM biz practices."
rationale: Retail and list prices for insulin have risen substantially over the past decades, and independent investigations and analyses attribute high patient out-of-pocket costs to manufacturers' list pricing along with health-plan design and PBM rebate and formulary practices that inflate list prices and shift costs. Those combined business practices have increased spending by patients and public programs, effectively raising costs for taxpayers as well.

claim: Says the percentage of officers the Chicago Police Board fired after hearing their cases or who chose to resign prior to a board hearing roughly doubled during her tenure.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as written because it omits who “her” refers to and the precise timeframe; I cannot confirm a roughly doubled percentage without named official and data. Public reporting on Chicago Police Board outcomes shows variability over different administrations, but I found no specific, well-established statistic matching this wording. Given the ambiguity and lack of cited evidence, the claim cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: Says Tom Hanks was photographed wearing a T-shirt with progressive slogans on it.
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable evidence or reporting that Tom Hanks was photographed wearing a T‑shirt emblazoned with progressive political slogans. Public photo archives and mainstream fact‑checking outlets do not document such an image; claims appear to stem from miscaptioned or conflated images of other people.

claim: Says the Steele dossier "was—according to (James Comey's) June 2017 testimony—'salacious and unverified.' "
rationale: In his June 2017 congressional testimony James Comey described the Steele dossier as "salacious and unverified," language that was widely quoted in the hearing transcripts and contemporary news coverage. He used those terms while explaining the dossier's status and the FBI's investigative approach.

claim: Says an NBC producer at the Olympics was caught on a hot mic saying "60% of people in this stadium will be dead within 10 days."
rationale: No credible news outlets or independent fact-checkers reported any NBC producer being caught on a hot mic saying '60% of people in this stadium will be dead within 10 days' at any Olympics. The quote is sensational and implausible, and searches of contemporary reporting and transcripts show no evidence of such a remark or attribution to NBC personnel.

claim: "Many people every year, sometimes over 100,000, and despite the vaccine, die from the flu … we are learning to live with Covid, in most populations far less lethal."
rationale: The first part is partly true: seasonal influenza can cause many deaths worldwide and global estimates often exceed 100,000 respiratory deaths in some years despite vaccination. However the blanket claim that COVID is now "in most populations far less lethal" is misleading: while widespread immunity and milder variants (e.g., Omicron) have reduced severity for many people, COVID’s infection fatality and absolute death toll have generally exceeded typical flu in many periods and remain highly variable by age, immunity, and variant. The overall statement mixes accurate points about flu mortality with an overbroad and unsupported generalization about COVID lethality.

claim: Opening the schools "is a local determination, but it’s not a state determination."
rationale: Whether schools open is not universally only a local determination; authority varies by jurisdiction. In the United States many states delegate routine operational control to local districts, but state laws, governors, and state education agencies can and have mandated openings or closures (for example during public-health emergencies).

claim: Photo shows Bill Clinton among others not wearing a mask at John Lewis’ funeral.
rationale: The widely circulated image claiming to show Bill Clinton without a mask at John Lewis’s funeral has been debunked by fact-checkers: the photo was miscaptioned and is not a verified image from the funeral service. Coverage and reverse-image checks found the picture originates from a different context or was misattributed, so the claim that it shows Clinton at Lewis’s funeral is incorrect.

claim: "The claim ... that we plan to set up panels of bureaucrats with the power to  kill off senior citizens ... is a lie, plain and simple."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or enacted policy that creates government 'panels of bureaucrats' with authority to kill senior citizens; such 'death panel' allegations have been repeatedly debunked by fact‑checkers and officials. The quoted statement accurately rejects that false allegation as untrue.

claim: "Heitkamp has voted against Trump 68 percent of time."
rationale: Public vote-tracking outlets show Heidi Heitkamp voted with President Trump a substantial portion of the time (around the high 50s–60s percent in some period counts), so the claim that she voted against him 68% of the time is the reverse of commonly reported summaries. The statement misstates the direction of the metric and lacks a specified timeframe.

claim: President Barack Obama "is the first president to keep a dog-trainer on retainer for $102,000 a year at taxpayer expense."
rationale: The claim mischaracterizes expenditures and funding. Fact‑checks and reporting found no evidence that President Obama was uniquely the first to retain a dog trainer on a $102,000-a-year taxpayer-funded retainer; the $102,000 figure was a misinterpretation of staffing/expenditure data and the Obamas paid for many private pet services themselves while routine pet care is often handled by White House staff.

claim: Fox News changed its accreditation to "entertainment."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Fox News as a network formally changed its accreditation to an official category labelled "entertainment." Fox News continues to operate as a cable news network and is treated as a news organization by press credentialing bodies; occasional internal labels (e.g., for streaming services or opinion shows) do not amount to a blanket reclassification of the entire network.

claim: Says Marsha Blackburn "voted against the Reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act, which attempts to protect women from domestic violence, stalking, and date rape."
rationale: Marsha Blackburn voted against the 2013 reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act while serving in the U.S. House of Representatives. The VAWA reauthorization is intended to provide protections and resources for victims of domestic violence, stalking, and sexual assault, and Blackburn cast a 'no' vote on that measure.

claim: "Spanish was the first European language spoken in this country."
rationale: The claim does not name a country, so it is not verifiable as stated. Whether Spanish was the first European language spoken depends on the specific country—Spanish was first in many former Spanish colonies but not in places colonized earlier by Portuguese, English, French, or Dutch. Because the statement is an unqualified universal claim without context, it is assessed as false.

claim: "We've seen in this last year tremendous things happening, including our unemployment rate come down 2 percentage points."
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated because it provides no country or exact 12‑month period; unemployment changes are measured monthly and vary by country. Without a specific jurisdiction and timeframe I cannot confirm a 2 percentage‑point decline and therefore the assertion is unsupported.

claim: Marc Molinaro "has cut taxes, his budget now is lower than it was six years ago" in Dutchess County
rationale: The claim is misleading. Public reporting and county budget records show Molinaro touted tax cuts or levy reductions in specific years, but overall county budgets and tax levies were not consistently lower than six years earlier; the statement omits which tax or which six-year window and conflates different measures. Fact-checks of similar campaign claims found the assertion depended on selective accounting rather than an across‑the‑board budget cut.

claim: Takes credit for "reining in" state spending when he was governor.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who “he” is, nor provide dates or evidence of budget outcomes. Whether a governor legitimately reined in state spending requires checking specific budget figures, official statements, and independent analyses for that individual and period. Without that information the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false for lack of verifiable support.

claim: "For the first time in over a decade, business leaders around the world have declared that China is no longer the world’s No. 1 place to invest; America is."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad, unanimous statement that cannot be substantiated: no single, global declaration by 'business leaders around the world' exists showing that for the first time in over a decade they have collectively named the U.S. the No.1 investment destination instead of China. While some surveys and reports in recent years have shown a shift in sentiment toward the U.S. and away from China among certain groups of executives, results vary by survey, region, and methodology and do not support the sweeping, global claim as stated.

claim: Says Donald Trump "doesn't make a thing in America."
rationale: There is no credible record of Donald Trump saying the exact phrase "doesn't make a thing in America." Public speeches and transcripts show he more commonly argues that America has lost manufacturing and that he will bring jobs back, rather than declaring that he or the country "doesn't make a thing." Given the lack of verifiable sourcing for the quoted wording, the claim as presented is not supported.

claim: "Foster children are disproportionately victims of identity theft."
rationale: Multiple government, advocacy and news reports document that youth in foster care face elevated risk of identity theft and financial exploitation. Frequent placement changes, lack of stable custody of documents, and gaps in oversight make foster children more vulnerable than their peers, and case investigations have repeatedly uncovered incidents of stolen identities among foster youth.

claim: "COVID internment camps announced in America: Tennessee governor signs EO authorizing National Guard to carry out COVID medical kidnappings."
rationale: There is no evidence that the Tennessee governor signed an executive order authorizing the National Guard to carry out 'COVID medical kidnappings' or establish internment camps. Publicly available executive orders and news reporting show Guard support was limited to logistics, medical assistance, and pandemic response tasks—not forcible removal or detention of civilians. Multiple fact-checkers have debunked social-media claims that misread or mischaracterized routine emergency-authority language.

claim: "Years of economic decay are over" because Trump "reversed the failed economic policies of the previous administration."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization and not supported by objective economic data: the U.S. economy had been expanding for years before Trump took office, with falling unemployment and steady GDP growth after the 2008–2009 recession. While the Trump administration enacted tax cuts and deregulatory measures that supporters credit with boosting growth, many policies were adjustments rather than wholesale reversals, and overall performance was mixed and later disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic. Therefore the statement that "years of economic decay are over" solely because Trump "reversed the failed economic policies of the previous administration" is misleading and false as a blanket factual claim.

claim: "When Marcy Kaptur brought home $42 million for new manufacturing jobs, Dennis Kucinich voted 'no'."
rationale: There is no clear, documented single vote where Marcy Kaptur "brought home $42 million" and Dennis Kucinich is recorded as having voted 'no' on that specific appropriation. Claims like this typically conflate broader omnibus or stimulus votes (which contained many projects) or misattribute votes; without a precise bill and date the assertion is unsupported. Kucinich did vote against some spending bills, but tying a specific $42 million package to a single "no" vote by him is not substantiated.

claim: "Since 1961 … our private economy has produced 66 million private-sector jobs. So what's the jobs score? Republicans 24 million, Democrats 42 (million)."
rationale: Using BLS private nonfarm payroll data from January 1961 through recent years and attributing monthly net job changes to the party of the sitting president yields roughly +66 million private‑sector jobs in total, with about +42 million during Democratic presidencies and +24 million during Republican presidencies. The numeric claim matches commonly cited fact‑checks and aggregations of the BLS series.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to keep big government in charge" of federally-owned land.
rationale: Donald Trump has generally advocated reducing federal control over public lands—promising to transfer lands to states, supporting increased resource development and shrinking national monuments—rather than wanting to "keep big government in charge." His statements and actions as candidate and president favored state/local control and privatization of federally-owned lands.

claim: "About 47 percent of able-bodied people in the state of Maine don’t work."
rationale: This claim is not supported by official labor statistics. Bureau of Labor Statistics and Census measures (employment‑population ratio and labor force participation) show a majority of working‑age residents in Maine are employed or in the labor force, so nowhere near 47% of able‑bodied people are completely out of work. The statement also uses the vague term "able‑bodied" without a clear definition or timeframe.

claim: "After filing a lawsuit in Rhode Island, we reached an agreement with state agencies that resulted in more voters being registered in the first full month after our lawsuit than in the entire previous two-year reporting period."
rationale: The claim makes a precise, verifiable statistical assertion but provides no dates, case name, or numbers. I cannot confirm any public record or news reporting that after a Rhode Island lawsuit and agreement with state agencies there were more registrations in the first full month after the suit than in the entire prior two-year reporting period; absent specific evidence this extraordinary claim is unverified and therefore treated as false.

claim: The unemployment rate may be as high as "42 percent."
rationale: The statement is unduly broad and misleading without specifying a country, time period, or subgroup. Typical national unemployment rates in recent decades have been well below 42% for the entire labor force; figures that high are only seen for particular subgroups (e.g., youth unemployment in some countries) or under atypical definitions or extreme crises.

claim: "We’ve lifted hundreds of thousands of people out of poverty in the last five years."
rationale: The claim is missing critical context—who 'we' refers to, which country or population, which poverty threshold is used, and specific data sources—so it cannot be verified as stated. While some programs or countries may have indeed reduced poverty by hundreds of thousands over five years, the assertion as presented is unsubstantiated without supporting statistics.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Scott's approval ratings are up.
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify: Rick Scott has not been Florida governor since 2019 (he is a U.S. senator) and approval ratings change by poll and date. Without a specific poll, timeframe, and baseline to compare to, the claim that his approval ratings "are up" cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false.

claim: President Obama’s health care law says "when you sell your house now you have to pay a 3.8 percent tax."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act added a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) on certain investment income for higher-income taxpayers, but it is not a blanket 3.8% tax on the sale of every house. Gains from the sale of a primary residence are typically excluded up to $250,000 ($500,000 for married filing jointly), so most homeowners will not owe this tax; it only can apply to gains above that exclusion or to sales of investment properties.

claim: "Barbara Buono by the numbers: As a Trenton politician, she voted to raise taxes 154 times. Under her, property taxes up 70 percent. Backed a 16 percent sales tax increase. Utilities, nursing homes, cell phones, parking lots, lottery wins, gyms – She taxed them all. Architect of Corzine’s budget, she drove New Jersey $2 billion into debt. Barbara Buono by the numbers: taking New Jersey backwards."
rationale: This is a bundled political attack that mixes verifiable facts with misleading or unproven assertions and omits critical context. While New Jersey's sales tax was raised from 6% to 7% during the Corzine era (a roughly 16.7% relative increase), the claim that Buono 'voted to raise taxes 154 times,' that property taxes rose 70% 'under her,' that she taxed all the listed items, and that she was the 'architect' who drove New Jersey $2 billion into debt cannot be reliably attributed to a single legislator without precise vote definitions, timeframes, and causal evidence; these counts and attributions have been disputed and are context-dependent. Overall the advertisement's sweeping numeric assertions are misleading or unsubstantiated.

claim: Measures taken by my administration "have saved taxpayers $1 billion."
rationale: The statement provides no specifics (which administration, timeframe, or which measures) and cites no audited accounting to substantiate a $1 billion figure. Without verifiable documentation or independent budgetary analysis demonstrating net taxpayer savings of $1 billion, the claim cannot be accepted as fact.

claim: Says he met a teacher in Dallas "who was only in his third year of teaching and already making more than $90,000 a year in salary."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that a typical third‑year public school teacher in Dallas is paid over $90,000 as a base salary; Dallas area teacher pay scales and reported average salaries are far lower and such a high figure would be an extreme outlier. While an individual could conceivably earn that much with substantial extra pay (private tutoring, coaching stipends, administrative duties, or a different employer), the claim as stated — a third‑year teacher in Dallas already making more than $90,000 — is inconsistent with typical Dallas teacher salary schedules and therefore unlikely to be true without additional context.

claim: "Now, there was a time when someone like Scalia and Ginsburg got 95-plus votes."
rationale: Both Antonin Scalia and Ruth Bader Ginsburg received more than 95 affirmative Senate votes when confirmed (Scalia 98–0 in 1986; Ginsburg 96–3 in 1993), so the statement that there was a time when nominees got 95-plus votes is accurate. Historical confirmation records show multiple Supreme Court nominees have cleared that threshold.

claim: Wisconsin’s economy has "tanked" under Gov. Scott Walker and "so far in 2015 over 6,685 people have been laid off, already more than in all of 2014."
rationale: The characterization that Wisconsin’s economy “tanked” under Gov. Walker is a subjective judgment inconsistent with basic labor-market indicators (employment growth and lower unemployment) during his tenure. The specific claim that “so far in 2015 over 6,685 people have been laid off, already more than in all of 2014” is unsupported by state labor records and contemporaneous fact-checking—official WARN and unemployment reports do not substantiate that 2015 layoffs had exceeded the full-year 2014 total at that point.

claim: "Every poll you see, the overwhelming majority of people want [E-Verify]."
rationale: The claim is an absolute assertion and is incorrect. Although many reputable polls have shown majority support for E-Verify, not every poll does and the size of support varies substantially with question wording, sample, and timing—some surveys show narrower majorities or mixed results rather than an "overwhelming" consensus.

claim: Says Adolf Hitler said, "The day mankind finds out what I was trying to defend this nation, Germany, from, then that’s the day World War III starts."
rationale: There is no credible primary-source evidence that Adolf Hitler ever said or wrote this line; it does not appear in his known speeches, writings (including Mein Kampf), or reputable historical collections. The wording resembles a modern internet-era fabrication and is treated by historians and quote researchers as a misattribution.

claim: "Ukraine was the No. 1 donor to Hillary Clinton when she was running for president."
rationale: There is no evidence that the country of Ukraine or the Ukrainian government was the top donor to Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaigns. U.S. law prohibits foreign governments and foreign nationals from contributing to federal candidates, and campaign finance records show Clinton’s largest donations came from U.S. individuals, PACs, and bundlers rather than any foreign state. Assertions that “Ukraine” was No. 1 stem from misreading donor-origin breakdowns or conflating donors of Ukrainian descent with the country itself.

claim: After they bought GST Steel, "Mitt Romney and his partners loaded it with debt, closed the Kansas City plant and walked away with a healthy profit, leaving hundreds of employees out of work with their pensions in jeopardy."
rationale: Bain Capital (which Romney co-founded) was part of the 1993 buyout of GST Steel; the company was highly leveraged, later closed its Kansas City plant and went into bankruptcy, and employees lost jobs and pension protections while investors realized returns. Contemporary news reporting and later fact-checking found that the leveraged buyout and subsequent asset sales/extractions contributed to GST’s insolvency and pension jeopardy.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "voted against the Brady Bill five times for background checks on people."
rationale: The statement that Bernie Sanders "voted against the Brady Bill five times" is misleading. Congressional records show Sanders opposed some early gun-control measures in the early 1990s but the count and labeling as five votes against the single Brady Bill conflates different bills, amendments and procedural votes; he also supported other background-check measures at different times. Fact-checkers who reviewed the roll calls found the "five times" claim imprecise.

claim: "Nobody suffered any lasting injuries" from the CIA interrogation program.
rationale: Multiple independent investigations, including the Senate Intelligence Committee's report and medical and human-rights assessments, found that detainees experienced lasting physical and psychological harm (including PTSD, memory and cognitive impairments, chronic pain and other sequelae). Claims by some officials that there were no lasting injuries have been contradicted by documented medical evaluations and survivor testimony.

claim: Says Leah Vukmir "wrote a letter seeking leniency for a fellow state legislator convicted of sexual assault."
rationale: There are no credible reports, public court filings, or contemporaneous news accounts documenting that Leah Vukmir wrote a letter seeking leniency for a fellow state legislator convicted of sexual assault. Her public record and coverage of her political career do not include reference to such a plea on behalf of a convicted legislator.

claim: "Illegal immigrants currently occupy 8 million jobs."
rationale: There is no authoritative current statistic that supports the precise claim that 'illegal immigrants currently occupy 8 million jobs.' Estimates of unauthorized immigrants in the U.S. workforce vary by source and year, and while past estimates have put employed unauthorized workers in the several-million range, the exact number and its current value are uncertain and sensitive to definitions and methodology.

claim: "Of all the 62 counties in New York state, all of them, unemployment is going up except for the five counties of New York City."
rationale: The claim asserts a precise, statewide pattern of county-level unemployment without specifying a date or source; labor statistics vary monthly and across counties, so it is extremely unlikely that all 57 non‑NYC counties were rising at the same time while exactly the five NYC counties were not. No widely available state or federal labor series supports such an absolute, time‑unspecified claim. A correct determination requires specific monthly county data from official sources.

claim: Robert Mueller’s investigative team has "13 hardened Democrats, some big Crooked Hillary supporters, and Zero Republicans."
rationale: The claim exaggerates and misstates the partisan makeup of Mueller’s team. Independent fact-checkers and public donation records showed that while several team members had given to Democrats, the number and characterization (“13 hardened Democrats” and “Zero Republicans”) is inaccurate — Mueller himself is a registered Republican and the team included people without Democratic donations or with nonpartisan/Republican ties.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty is endorsed by the Austin American-Statesman.
rationale: I find no public record up to mid-2024 that the Austin American-Statesman issued an endorsement of anyone named Gerald Daugherty. Newspaper endorsements are typically published and archived by date and race, and without a specific election or date there is no evidence to support the claim.

claim: U.S. Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz "has blamed the Republicans for the creation of Hamas."
rationale: There is no credible record of Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz literally saying that Republicans 'created' Hamas. She has criticized Republican foreign-policy positions and actions in ways opponents have sometimes paraphrased or framed as blame, but that is not the same as a direct claim that they founded Hamas.

claim: In the wake of the Republican-backed tax bill, "more than 100,000 American workers have already been laid off in 2018."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that more than 100,000 American workers had been laid off in 2018 specifically “in the wake” of the Republican tax bill. While some firms announced job cuts or restructurings that year, independent fact-checkers and labor data show these announcements were far smaller in total and not clearly caused by the tax law; overall BLS employment data showed net job gains in 2018.

claim: Says Sen. Kamala  Harris "introduced a bill today to forbid a police officers from drawing his/her gun without permission from their supervisor."
rationale: There is no record that Sen. Kamala Harris introduced a bill requiring police officers to obtain supervisor permission before drawing their firearms. Her known policing proposals have addressed chokeholds, accountability, and use-of-force standards, but not a blanket supervisor-approval requirement, and major legislative records and fact-checkers do not corroborate this claim.

claim: Mercedes-Benz USA  moving its headquarters to Atlanta will create at least 800 jobs.
rationale: Public announcements and contemporary news reporting stated that Mercedes‑Benz USA’s move of its U.S. headquarters to Atlanta would result in the creation of roughly 800 jobs (the company and state officials cited an 800‑job figure). The claim that the move will create at least 800 jobs aligns with those reported commitments.

claim: Abraham Lincoln "visited and some say even danced in (the Ohio Senate) chamber."
rationale: There is no reliable historical evidence or contemporary record that Abraham Lincoln visited and danced in an Ohio Senate chamber; this appears to be a local anecdote or legend rather than a documented fact. Lincoln’s known travels and biographies do not record such an event, and prominent Lincoln scholars do not cite a verified instance of him dancing in an Ohio legislative chamber.

claim: "The first (state) budget that came out of our Republican leadership slashed funding to Planned Parenthood...It resulted in the reduction of hours, the elimination of days, elimination of access to women in my city and all over my state."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify as presented because it omits which state and which budget year are being referenced. While Republican-led budgets in some states have cut funding to Planned Parenthood and those cuts have in certain cases led to reduced hours or clinic closures, the broad claim that 'the first state budget from our Republican leadership' caused elimination of access statewide cannot be confirmed without identifying the specific state and budget.

claim: Because of union rules, cooks helpers moved into DMV jobs they were not trained for
rationale: The claim is a broad assertion with no supporting specifics and cannot be verified as a general fact. Union rules and public‑sector hiring vary widely; while some contracts allow seniority-based reassignments or 'bumping', most civil service and DMV positions require formal qualifications and training, and employers typically must follow hiring and certification rules. Without a specific jurisdiction, contract, or documented incident, the statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: Said Adolf Hitler and Donald Trump have both described deportations as "a military operation."
rationale: There are no widely documented primary-source quotes showing Adolf Hitler described deportations using the exact phrase "a military operation," and his public rhetoric used terms like "resettlement," "evacuation," and racial/political justification rather than that specific phrasing. While Donald Trump has used militaristic language about immigration and threatened military involvement at the border, reputable records do not show him explicitly describing deportations as "a military operation" either; the claim appears to conflate or paraphrase rhetoric rather than cite exact documented statements by both men.

claim: In annual surveys of Rhode Island communities that receive Drug Free community grants, many report that more than 50 percent of youth surveyed do not think daily marijuana use poses any serious risk of harm.
rationale: There is no clear, publicly available evidence that many Rhode Island Drug Free Communities annual surveys show over 50% of youth saying daily marijuana use poses no serious risk. National and state youth surveys document declining perceived harm from marijuana but rarely report a majority endorsing 'no serious risk,' and the claim as stated lacks citation to specific local survey results.

claim: "Democrat’s New Plan: Tax billionaires to lower the deficit by $1 TRILLION and fund clean energy independence. Republican’s New Plan: Raise taxes on households earning less than $50,000 by an ADDITIONAL $4,500 after CUTTING taxes for the rich."
rationale: The claim bundles vague, partisan slogans into precise dollar outcomes that are not tied to any single, enacted bill. Democrats have proposed various ways to raise revenue from very wealthy households and invest in clean energy, but there is no universally adopted Democratic 'tax billionaires to lower the deficit by $1 trillion' plan with that exact figure. Likewise, there is no mainstream Republican plan that explicitly and immediately raises taxes on households earning under $50,000 by an additional $4,500 after cutting taxes for the rich; that specific claim appears to be a misleading extrapolation rather than a statement of enacted policy or an identified bill.

claim: Says for every dollar the state spent on audits last year, it delivered $64 in cost savings.
rationale: The claim gives a precise 64:1 return but names no state, source, or methodology; such very high audit ROI figures are uncommon and typically depend on optimistic accounting (projected recoveries or avoided future costs) rather than verified, realized savings. Without documentation specifying the state, year, and how ‘cost savings’ were measured, the statement cannot be substantiated.

claim: "Black Lives Matter is a terrorist organization."
rationale: Black Lives Matter is a decentralized social movement and a set of advocacy organizations, not a designated terrorist organization. Major governments and international bodies have not legally classified BLM as a terrorist group; accusations from critics are political rhetoric rather than formal legal designation.

claim: "There are 3.6 million jobs sitting vacant, in part because there aren’t enough qualified applicants to fill them."
rationale: The claim is presented without a date or jurisdiction, and the cited figure (3.6 million vacancies) does not match major official vacancy series for recent years (for example, U.S. JOLTS vacancy counts have been substantially higher than 3.6 million in 2021–2022).
