While House members’ district office rents are paid from House allowances, published lease and House spending records do not unambiguously show taxpayers paying exactly $18,000 per month for Pelosi’s downtown San Francisco district office; reported figures vary and often omit context (e.g., whether amounts cover multiple offices, utilities, or short-term leases).

claim: John McCain refuses to support a new bipartisan energy bill "because it would take away tax breaks from oil companies like Exxon Mobil."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable evidence that John McCain explicitly refused to back a specific bipartisan energy bill for the stated reason of protecting oil-company tax breaks. Public records of McCain’s energy positions are mixed and motives like this require direct contemporaneous quotes or reliable reporting, which are not provided. Absent a verifiable source tying his opposition to that precise rationale, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Americans work way more than an average of industrialized countries around the world."
rationale: OECD and labor-statistics data show Americans work somewhat more hours per year than many Western European countries, but they do not work "way more" than the average of industrialized countries. Several advanced economies (e.g., South Korea, Japan) have similar or higher annual hours, and the U.S. is only modestly above the OECD mean rather than an extreme outlier.

claim: "Mexico’s Next President Calls for An Invasion Of The US"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or mainstream reporting that any incoming Mexican president has publicly called for an invasion of the United States. Such a statement would be extraordinary and would have generated wide international coverage and official responses, which are absent. The claim appears to be misinformation, a misquote, or satire.

claim: Says Tallahassee mayor Andrew Gillum "wants to make Florida not a sanctuary city but a sanctuary state."
rationale: There is no clear, contemporaneous record of Andrew Gillum explicitly saying he wanted to make the entire state of Florida a "sanctuary state." During his 2018 campaign and as Tallahassee mayor he expressed support for sanctuary-city-style protections and immigrant-friendly policies, but claims that he said he would make Florida a sanctuary state are likely paraphrase or exaggeration of those positions.

claim: Says he’s the one who gave the nickname "Mad Dog" to former Defense Secretary James Mattis.
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and there is no reliable evidence that any single person can be credited with inventing the 'Mad Dog' nickname for James Mattis. The sobriquet was widely used by colleagues, the media, and public figures (and Mattis reportedly disliked the nickname), but credible reporting does not trace it definitively to one originator.

claim: ‘The Simpsons’ predicted Canada’s trucker convoy protest.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that The Simpsons specifically predicted the 2022 Canadian 'Freedom Convoy.' The show has many episodes with generic protests, trucks, or satire of political events, and viral comparisons conflate these commonplace motifs with a specific future event. The resemblance cited in memes is coincidental and retrospective interpretation rather than a documented prediction.

claim: "Roy Barnes proclaimed Mexican workers good for Georgia."
rationale: There is no well-documented, verifiable public record or widely reported quote of former Georgia governor Roy Barnes explicitly proclaiming 'Mexican workers good for Georgia.' The phrasing appears to be a paraphrase or misattribution rather than a documented, attributable proclamation.

claim: Says David Dewhurst "went out for drinks" during Senate debate on abortion bill.
rationale: Contemporary news coverage of the high‑profile Texas Senate abortion debate (including Wendy Davis's 2013 filibuster) focused on procedural rulings and timing by Lt. Gov. David Dewhurst; reputable outlets did not report that he left the chamber to ‘go out for drinks’ during the debate. The statement appears to be an unsubstantiated rumor rather than a documented fact.

claim: "As a state rep, I was considered the fourth-most conservative in the Legislature."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it lacks any identifying details (which state, which legislative session, which ranking system or source). Ideological rankings vary by methodology and time, so without a cited score or study this claim cannot be confirmed. Because of that uncertainty I judge the claim false until supporting evidence is provided.

claim: Says Texas is "last in mental health expenditures."
rationale: The claim as stated is too general and not supported as an unqualified fact: whether Texas is “last” depends on the specific metric (total spending vs. per‑capita, Medicaid behavioral‑health spending, year, or program scope). While Texas has ranked near the bottom on some per‑capita mental‑health spending or access measures in certain years, it is not uniformly last across all expenditure measures and time periods.

claim: Florida retirees and families "lost tens of thousands of dollars" in deposits on failed Trump condo projects, but he "pocketed their money and walked away."
rationale: While buyers in some Trump‑branded condo developments did lose significant deposits when projects failed or were canceled, available reporting and legal records do not substantiate the blanket claim that Donald Trump personally 'pocketed' those funds and walked away. Deposits were typically held by developers or in escrow and many purchasers obtained refunds or partial recoveries through settlements and litigation rather than evidence of personal theft by Trump.

claim: The Internal Revenue Service spent $60,000 on a "Star Trek" training video.
rationale: Oversight reports and contemporary news coverage documented that the IRS paid roughly $60,000 for a training video that opened with a Star Trek–style intro. Reporting noted the production mimicked Star Trek aesthetics rather than being an officially licensed Star Trek product.

claim: Wisconsin is "run by Democrats right now," so they should address election social distancing concerns.
rationale: The claim that Wisconsin is "run by Democrats right now" is misleading: the governor is a Democrat, but the state legislature has been controlled by Republicans, and election administration is primarily carried out by local county officials. The normative assertion that "they should address election social distancing concerns" is a policy preference, but responsibility for pandemic-era election measures is shared across state and local actors rather than resting solely with Democratic officials.

claim: "I believe we should have tax on carbon and deal aggressively with climate change. That is not (Hillary Clinton's) position."
rationale: This is false because Hillary Clinton has publicly supported aggressive climate action (endorsing the Paris Agreement, proposing strong emissions-reduction plans during her 2016 campaign) and has backed market-based carbon-pricing approaches at times. While she did not always use the specific label 'carbon tax' and favored a mix of regulation, clean-energy investment, and pricing mechanisms, it is incorrect to say she opposed taxing carbon or dealing aggressively with climate change.

claim: "At John Lewis funeral Obama told a room full of people that rooms full of people is too dangerous so we must mail in vote."
rationale: There is no credible record that Barack Obama at John Lewis’s funeral told attendees that 'rooms full of people is too dangerous so we must mail in vote.' Official coverage of Lewis’s memorial events and remarks does not include Obama making that statement; he did not give such a public exhortation at the funeral. The claim appears to misattribute or fabricate remarks about voting methods.

claim: Nevada Republicans "didn’t do one single thing to cut spending" in 2015.
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that Republicans in Nevada did “not do one single thing” to cut spending in 2015; such total inaction is highly implausible and inconsistent with legislative behavior. Minority party members routinely file budget amendments, sponsor bills, and vote on spending measures — records from the 2015 Nevada legislative session show Republicans proposed and debated fiscal measures. Therefore the blanket claim is false as an accurate factual summary.

claim: Says President Donald Trump is one of "only three people that won the Ellis Island Award for their work within the black community."
rationale: While Donald Trump is reported to have received the Ellis Island Medal of Honor in the 1980s, the award has been given to many honorees for a wide range of contributions and there is no basis for the assertion that he is one of 'only three' winners specifically recognized for work within the Black community. The claim appears to conflate or misstate the award's recipient history and criteria.

claim: "Portland Schools spend $500K to deem PB&J sandwiches racist."
rationale: This claim is false. Credible reporting and fact-checkers found no evidence that Portland schools spent $500,000 to officially label peanut butter and jelly sandwiches as 'racist'; budgeted amounts cited were for broader equity, training, or food-service program items and were mischaracterized by viral posts.

claim: John McCain's health care plan "leaves you on your own to pay McCain’s health insurance tax."
rationale: This phrasing is a misleading political characterization. John McCain’s 2008 health proposals emphasized refundable tax credits, allowing people to buy private insurance, high-risk pools, and market reforms rather than creating a new, mandatory “health insurance tax” that individuals must directly pay. While critics argued his plan shifted costs to individuals who would have to buy private coverage, it did not establish a named mandatory tax as claimed.

claim: "The United States is 65th out of 142 nations and other territories on equal pay."
rationale: The statement gives no year or data source and presents a single definitive ranking for a metric that varies by dataset and year. Reports such as the World Economic Forum’s gender-gap subindexes (which sometimes cover 142 economies) produce different U.S. positions depending on the specific equal-pay measure and year, so the blanket claim that the U.S. is 65th out of 142 is unverified and misleading without a source.

claim: "We confer more PhDs each year than any other university in America except Berkeley."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it omits which institution is claiming the ranking and which year(s) are referenced. Annual PhD counts vary by year and discipline, and national data (e.g., NSF/NCSES doctorate statistics) show multiple universities routinely award large numbers of PhDs, so a blanket claim that one unspecified university is second only to Berkeley is unsupported without a specific institution and time period. Given the ambiguity and year-to-year variation, the claim cannot be treated as fact.

claim: "China owns about 29% of (the U.S.) debt."
rationale: China’s holdings of U.S. Treasury securities are much smaller than 29% of U.S. debt. Recent Treasury data show China holds on the order of $0.8–1.1 trillion of Treasuries, which is only about 2–4% of total U.S. public debt and roughly 10–15% of foreign-held Treasuries, not 29%.

claim: The United States has "the highest corporate tax rate in the free world."
rationale: This is not true at present. The U.S. federal corporate tax rate was cut from 35% to 21% in 2017, and even when state-level taxes are added the combined top statutory rate is lower than or comparable to many other countries; historically the U.S. ranked near the top before 2017 but it no longer has the highest corporate tax rate among market democracies.

claim: "Drunk" Nancy Pelosi "was removed from the House floor for cursing at Republicans."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable news reporting that Nancy Pelosi was intoxicated and removed from the House floor for cursing at Republicans. Such an event would have been widely reported and documented, but contemporaneous accounts and official House records do not substantiate the claim. Viral videos or social-media posts making this assertion appear to be miscaptioned or fabricated.

claim: Says "in Oregon only 41 percent of adults have ever been tested" for HIV.
rationale: The claim gives a precise percentage without citing a year or data source; state estimates of adults ever tested for HIV come from surveys (like CDC BRFSS) and vary by year and question wording. Because the statement lacks context and cannot be confirmed as a current, sourced figure, it is not reliably true as presented.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on an assault weapons ban.
rationale: The statement is misleading because it asserts a clear "flip-flop" without specifying timing or which public statements are being contrasted. Romney's public record on guns includes support for some gun-control measures (like background checks) and opposition to broad federal assault-weapons bans at other times, but there is no well-documented, unambiguous single reversal on an assault-weapons ban comparable to common uses of "flip-flopped."

claim: "Trump’s tax reform plan was nothing more than a middle-class tax increase."
rationale: The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act included large, permanent corporate tax cuts and temporary individual tax cuts (including larger standard deduction and an expanded child tax credit) that lowered taxes for many middle-income households in the short term. Analyses by nonpartisan budget and tax experts showed the law’s benefits were substantial for corporations and higher-income taxpayers and that many individual provisions expire after 2025, so it is inaccurate to say it was "nothing more than a middle-class tax increase."

claim: Georgia’s HOPE scholarship is "still the richest scholarship program in America."
rationale: Georgia’s HOPE Scholarship was once notably generous, but it has been scaled back over time and does not currently constitute the single "richest" scholarship program in the United States. Other state promise programs, institutional full‑ride merit scholarships, and large private scholarships provide equal or greater per‑student or total funding; the term "richest" is also ambiguous and depends on how generosity is measured.

claim: "At this particular point in time, looking at the field, there’s only one individual that’s ever had the uniform of his country on—and that’s me."
rationale: The claim asserts a unique fact about everyone on 'the field' that is both unverifiable from the statement and highly unlikely in ordinary sporting or public-event contexts where multiple people often have worn their national team's uniform. Without specifying the field, event, time, or identities, the uniqueness claim cannot be substantiated and is therefore almost certainly false in general interpretation.

claim: With Medicare for All, "study after study has shown that ... the average middle-class families will save $3,000 each and every year on their health care bills."
rationale: There is no consensus across studies that ‘Medicare for All’ would uniformly save the average middle‑class family $3,000 per year. Analyses of single‑payer proposals produce widely varying estimates depending on plan design and which costs (premiums, out‑of‑pocket, and taxes) are counted; some studies project household savings for many families while others find increased tax burdens that offset or exceed those savings.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton’s approval rating went from 70 percent to 52 percent in 18 months.
rationale: The statement gives no poll source or dates and cannot be verified as a precise fact. Hillary Clinton’s approval/favorability ratings have fluctuated across different polls and subgroups, but there is no consistent, well-documented source showing an exact drop from 70% to 52% over an 18-month span without additional context. Because polling results vary by pollster, sample, and timing, the claim as stated is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Alex Sink "supported higher sales taxes."
rationale: There is no clear, unambiguous record that Alex Sink straightforwardly and consistently advocated raising sales taxes. During her tenure as Florida CFO and her 2010 campaign opponents accused her of supporting tax increases, but Sink publicly emphasized budget management and disputed claims that she supported broad sales-tax hikes. The statement is vague about timing and context and is not supported as a simple factual claim.

claim: "Welders make more money than philosophers."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization: earnings vary by country, experience, and whether 'philosophers' refers to academic faculty, people with philosophy degrees, or professional philosophers. Skilled welders often earn solid middle-class wages and can out-earn low-paid adjuncts or recent humanities graduates, but tenured philosophy professors or philosophers working in industry may earn more than many welders. Because income differences depend on definitions and context, the blanket statement is false.

claim: "Under Pat McCrory, (North Carolina) has fallen to 41st in teacher pay."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific national rank without specifying a year or which pay measure is used. While North Carolina teacher pay stagnated and fell in national comparisons during Pat McCrory's tenure, published rankings vary by year and by whether they use average, median, or starting salary; sources do not consistently show it exactly at 41st. Therefore the precise, unqualified claim is not reliably supported.

claim: "Bikers show up to The Walter Reed Hospital to pray for President Trump."
rationale: During President Trump’s October 2020 hospitalization at Walter Reed, multiple news reports, videos, and eyewitness accounts documented supporters — including motorcycle groups and individual bikers — gathering outside the hospital to show support and pray. The presence of bikers aligned with organized pro-Trump motorcycle groups that rode to the facility and joined others in prayer and chants.

claim: The omnibus bill "does not designate a single dollar for Planned Parenthood."
rationale: This statement is misleading. Federal omnibus appropriations bills generally allocate money to programs and accounts rather than naming single private providers, so an omnibus could fund services through Medicaid, Title X, or grants that result in payments to Planned Parenthood even if it does not explicitly "designate" dollars to that organization; conversely some bills have included explicit prohibitions. Without specifying which omnibus and year the absolute claim that it "does not designate a single dollar for Planned Parenthood" cannot be verified and is likely inaccurate as a blanket statement.

claim: Obama came into office "with a $1.3 trillion deficit before I had passed any law. ... We came in with $8 trillion worth of debt over the next decade."
rationale: When President Obama took office in January 2009 the FY2009 deficit was widely reported at roughly $1.2–$1.4 trillion, and contemporaneous CBO and budget projections showed roughly $7–9 trillion in cumulative deficits over the coming decade absent policy changes. His statement reflects those official deficit projections at the start of his administration.

claim: Countries with a higher minimum wage than the United States’ $7.25 an hour include Denmark at $21, Australia at $15.81, Germany at $11 and France at $12.35.
rationale: The U.S. federal minimum of $7.25/hr is correct, but the claim’s country figures are misleading or inaccurate. Denmark does not have a statutory national minimum wage (wages are set by collective bargaining), so quoting a single ‘‘$21’’ rate is misleading; Germany’s statutory minimum is €12/hr (about $12–$13 depending on exchange rates), not $11. Australia and France do have higher minimums than the U.S., but USD conversions vary by date and method.

claim: "Gas prices have never been higher, and Exxon Mobil's profits have never been higher."
rationale: The statement is overly absolute and therefore incorrect. Retail gasoline hit historic nominal peaks in many countries in 2022, but inflation-adjusted prices (and regional variations) mean prices have been higher in earlier periods (for example the 2008 U.S. peak in real terms). Similarly, ExxonMobil posted very large profits in 2022–2023, but declaring they have 'never been higher' ignores differences in accounting periods, one-off items and how profits are compared historically.

claim: "They found 60 votes in the Senate in 2006 and 2013" for immigration legislation, and "each time the House Republican majority refused to take it up."
rationale: The statement is misleading. In 2013 the Senate produced broad bipartisan support for comprehensive immigration reform (the 'Gang of Eight' bill passed the Senate by 68 votes), and House Republicans did not take up that Senate package. However, there is not a clear, equivalent 60‑vote Senate outcome in 2006 for a comparable comprehensive bill that the House then refused to consider, so saying they 'found 60 votes in the Senate in 2006 and 2013' is inaccurate or at least unsupported without more detail.

claim: "Mayor Barrett saved Milwaukee $25 million, thanks to Gov. Walker’s reforms."
rationale: The claim attributes a specific $25 million savings in Milwaukee directly to Gov. Walker’s reforms and credits Mayor Barrett with saving it; there is no clear, verifiable evidence that Milwaukee realized a discrete $25 million savings expressly due to Walker’s reforms and credited to the mayor. Walker’s 2011 collective bargaining and other state reforms did change municipal costs in various ways, but savings amounts varied by locality and were contested, and the precise $25M figure and attribution appear unsupported or mischaracterized.

claim: The only budget Ted Cruz "ever voted for in his time in the Senate is a budget that cut defense spending by more than Barack Obama proposes we cut it."
rationale: The claim is implausible and unsupported: Cruz has voted on multiple budget and appropriations-related measures during his Senate tenure, and Republican budget proposals have varied year to year. The statement’s narrow phrasing (“the only budget…”) and the specific comparison to unspecified Obama proposals do not match the public legislative record and appear misleading.

claim: The government pays out "$2,125/month in refugee benefits to refugees resettled in the United States," while Social Security recipients "who have paid into the system their whole lives receive $1,400/month on average."
rationale: The $2,125 figure is not a standard ongoing monthly payment to refugees resettled in the U.S.; federal refugee assistance is typically short-term (cash and medical assistance for months, not a perpetual $2,125/month), and much of resettlement support is one-time or service-based. The asserted $1,400 average for Social Security beneficiaries is also misleading—the overall average Social Security retirement benefit is higher than that and varies by cohort and benefit type. The claim cherry-picks and conflates different programs and timeframes to create a misleading comparison.

claim: A recent on-air protest can’t be real because "there are no live on air television broadcasts in Russia. None. Ever."
rationale: The absolute claim is false: Russian television does transmit live broadcasts (live news, sports, ceremonies, and live studio programs) and there have been on-air interruptions and protests shown live. While Russian broadcast media are heavily regulated and many outlets self-censor or have been closed/moved abroad in recent years, that does not mean live on-air television never exists.

claim: Federal prosecutions for lying on background checks to buy guns are "down 40 percent" under President Barack Obama.
rationale: This claim is misleading: while prosecutions for false statements on gun-purchase forms fell in some years during the Obama administration, the exact change depends on the baseline years and which charges are counted. DOJ/ATF statistics and independent fact-checks show year-to-year variation and do not support an unqualified 'down 40 percent' claim across the administration without specifying the comparison.

claim: Wrote that in 2006, Nancy Pelosi said she didn’t think capturing Osama bin Laden "makes us any safer," but in 2011 called his killing "historic."
rationale: While Nancy Pelosi did publicly praise the 2011 operation that killed Osama bin Laden and described it in positive terms (commonly reported as 'historic'), the specific 2006 quote that she said capturing bin Laden 'makes us any safer' is not reliably documented and appears to be a misattribution or taken out of context. Because the 2011 part is accurate but the 2006 attribution lacks clear, verifiable sourcing, the combined claim as stated is misleading.

claim: Photo shows a Chinese restaurant sign that says "F--- DeSantis."
rationale: I cannot verify the photo from the claim and there is no corroborating reporting or provenance presented; images of protest messages on storefronts are often miscaptioned or digitally altered. Without the original image, metadata, or reliable sourcing, the claim that the photo specifically shows a Chinese restaurant sign reading that phrase is unverified and therefore treated as false.

claim: "Obama-Nelson economic record: Job creation ... at slowest post-recession rate since Great Depression."
rationale: The claim overstates the standard comparison. It is true that job growth after the 2007–2009 recession was unusually slow compared with postwar recoveries, but analysts generally describe it as the slowest postwar (since World War II) jobs recovery by some measures — not definitively the slowest 'since the Great Depression.' The statement also lacks a clear metric and timeframe and implies sole attribution to Obama/Nelson.

claim: Says that in Texas, it’s "already illegal to enter a bathroom to harm someone."
rationale: Texas law already criminalizes causing physical or sexual harm, voyeurism, indecent exposure, trespass, and related offenses regardless of location, so entering a bathroom with the intent to harm someone would be prosecutable under existing statutes. There is no need for a separate law that specifically names bathrooms to make such conduct illegal.

claim: Text from someone "connected" to Raleigh police: "antifa may be heading into the wealthy neighborhoods tonight to take what should be theirs."
rationale: I cannot verify the purported text or the claimed police connection; there are no corroborating official statements or credible reports confirming that someone connected to Raleigh police sent this message or that 'antifa' was mobilizing to target wealthy neighborhoods. The claim reads like an unverified, incendiary rumor and lacks primary-source evidence.

claim: "The price of soybeans has fallen 50% since 5 years before the election. A big reason is bad (terrible) trade deals with other countries."
rationale: The claim mixes a precise numeric price change with a broad causal claim but gives no timeframe (which election) and is not supported by general knowledge: soybean prices fluctuate and a 50% drop over a particular five-year window is not generically true. Attributing a large fall primarily to "bad trade deals" is speculative: trade policies can affect prices but so can weather, yields, global demand (e.g., China), currency moves and futures market dynamics, so the single-cause attribution is unsupported without specific data.

claim: Says former President Barack Obama’s Supreme Court nominations "required 60 votes."
rationale: Supreme Court nominees are confirmed by a majority vote of the Senate, not a fixed 60-vote threshold. Prior to rule changes, Senate cloture to overcome a filibuster typically required 60 votes, so a nominee would only need 60 votes if opponents sustained a filibuster — it was not an absolute constitutional requirement.

claim: "Eighty percent of the antibiotics in this country are fed to livestock."
rationale: The statement is overbroad and lacks context. An oft-cited '80%' figure applied to certain past U.S. estimates (by weight of antibiotics sold for food-producing animals) and does not universally apply to every country, year, or definition of 'antibiotics' and 'fed to.' Whether the claim is true depends on the specific country, timeframe, and whether one counts total mass of drugs, only medically important antibiotics, or doses used for growth promotion versus therapeutic use.

claim: Says Sen. Kay Hagan "has missed half of the (Senate Armed Services) Committee's hearings in 2014."
rationale: Independent fact-checkers and Senate attendance records do not support the assertion that Sen. Kay Hagan missed half of 2014 Armed Services Committee hearings. The claim relied on a misleading counting method (counting all scheduled sessions including brief or canceled items and using different definitions of 'hearing') and Hagan attended a majority of the committee's substantive sessions that year.

claim: "The most likely triggering cause of (microcephaly)" is the "DTaP shot, a vaccine that had been recently mandated by the Brazilian government to be injected into pregnant women."
rationale: Multiple epidemiological, clinical, and laboratory studies since 2015–2016 have established prenatal Zika virus infection as the primary cause of the surge in microcephaly cases in Brazil. Public health bodies (WHO, CDC, Brazilian health authorities) reviewed evidence including detection of Zika RNA in fetal tissue and concluded causality; there is no credible evidence that DTaP or pertussis-containing maternal vaccines triggered the outbreak. The claim also conflates vaccine types and policy: pregnant-woman boosters are typically Tdap or Td, not the infant DTaP formulation.

claim: "Fox News Sandra Smith: ‘Everybody could see from the United Airlines passenger’s behavior that he was not a genuine American.’ "
rationale: I am not aware of any verifiable transcript or video showing Fox News anchor Sandra Smith saying that exact line about a United Airlines passenger; the claim appears to be a paraphrase or misattribution. Without a primary source (timestamped clip or official transcript) the precise quotation cannot be confirmed as having been spoken by her.

claim: "1776 flag flying over White House!" in January 2021. "Revolution Signal."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a '1776' flag was flown over the White House in January 2021; photographs and official records show the U.S. flag remained on the White House flagpole. Viral images of '1776' flags from that time depict them on individuals or elsewhere (for example at or near the Capitol and on protesters), not flying atop the White House.

claim: "Ron Johnson is trying to let insurance companies deny coverage to people with pre-existing conditions like cancer, depression, pregnancy, diabetes—or even COVID."
rationale: Sen. Ron Johnson has repeatedly supported repealing or rolling back the ACA and backing alternatives (short‑term plans, state waiver approaches, and deregulation) that would remove or weaken federal guaranteed‑issue and community‑rating protections, which would allow insurers to deny coverage or charge much higher premiums for people with pre‑existing conditions. Public statements and his votes for ACA repeal efforts and deregulation measures align with policies that would permit insurers to exclude or penalize people with conditions like cancer, mental‑health diagnoses, pregnancy, diabetes, or long COVID.

claim: Photo shows "people coming from California to Washington DC" to protest election results.
rationale: There is no way to confirm from the description alone that the photo depicts people traveling from California to Washington, D.C., to protest election results. Verifying such a provenance requires image metadata, reverse-image search, or independent reporting tying that specific image to that event; absent that, the claim is unsubstantiated and could be a reused or miscaptioned photo.

claim: "America’s hard-working agricultural producers … have taken a disproportionate hit when it comes to illegal retaliatory tariffs."
rationale: U.S. agricultural producers did suffer large losses from retaliatory tariffs (for example China’s 2018–19 tariffs on soybeans and other farm goods, which prompted sizable USDA aid), but labeling those tariffs broadly as 'illegal' is not generally supported and 'disproportionate' is undefined without a clear comparator or timeframe. Many retaliatory measures were part of formal trade disputes or authorized countermeasures under WTO procedures, so the claim as stated overreaches.

claim: Alex Sink was "the first official who said that BP should pay $25 million for an ad campaign to promote Florida tourism."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Alex Sink was uniquely the first official to demand BP pay $25 million for Florida tourism ads. In the wake of the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill multiple Florida officials and tourism leaders publicly urged BP to fund advertising, and contemporary reports do not attribute a singular 'first' claim to Sink.

claim: Video shows Ukrainian soldiers saying goodbye to loved ones amid Russia’s 2022 invasion.
rationale: There is insufficient information to verify that a specific video actually depicts Ukrainian soldiers saying goodbye amid Russia’s 2022 invasion. Videos like this circulated widely online during and after the conflict and were frequently misattributed, reposted out of context, or reused from other times and places. Without source metadata, timestamp, or independent corroboration, the claim cannot be confirmed as true.

claim: "We have more hospitals that are children’s hospitals than any other state in the union." 
rationale: The claim is ambiguous (it does not identify which state “we” refers to) and there is no documented evidence that any unspecified state has more children's hospitals than all other states. Counts of dedicated pediatric hospitals tend to track population and major medical centers, with states like California, New York, and Texas typically having the largest numbers. Without a clear referent and supporting data, the claim is not supported.

claim: The significant drop in Florida’s unemployment rate is a good economic sign.
rationale: A significant decline in the unemployment rate generally indicates an improving labor market—more people who want work are employed and joblessness has fallen, which is typically a positive economic signal. However, the interpretation depends on context (labor force participation, population migration, part-time vs full-time job mix, and data revisions), which can make the signal weaker or misleading in some cases.

claim: "USA is #1 in gun violence."
rationale: The claim is vague and, by common measures, the U.S. is not '#1' in gun violence worldwide. While the U.S. has a very high number of firearm deaths compared with other high‑income countries and leads many developed-country rankings, several countries (for example in Latin America) have higher firearm homicide rates and often higher totals. Thus the blanket statement that the USA is #1 is inaccurate without specifying the metric and time period.

claim: "The son-in-law of the president met with Russian officials at the Trump Tower after having them come in the back door."
rationale: While Jared Kushner did attend a June 2016 meeting at Trump Tower with Donald Trump Jr. and others, the visitors were a Russian lawyer and private individuals, not identified Russian government officials. There is no credible evidence that Kushner arranged for them to enter via a 'back door' as the claim states.

claim: Says Sandra Bullock said to Hillary Clinton, "If you don’t like our president you can leave and never come back again."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or verified video showing Sandra Bullock telling Hillary Clinton that quote; the line circulated on social media as a meme and was debunked by independent fact-checkers. Bullock has not been documented making that statement to Clinton in any reliable news account.

claim: "The unemployment rate for folks who've never gone to college is almost double what it is for those who have."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not universally true. U.S. labor statistics do show higher unemployment for less-educated workers, but whether it is "almost double" depends on the exact education categories and year: comparisons of the least-educated vs holders of a bachelor's degree can exceed twofold in some years, while broader "no college" vs "have college" groupings often show smaller gaps. Because the claim lacks a clear definition and time period, it is not reliably accurate as stated.

claim: "We’re losing almost 6,000 state jobs."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated—no state, time period, or data source is provided. Whether nearly 6,000 state jobs are being lost depends on specific budget decisions, layoffs, or attrition reports for a particular state and period; without that context the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: "The chances of being killed by a refugee committing a terrorist act is 1 in 3.6 billion."
rationale: The specific claim gives an exact probability without citing a source and is not supported by available evidence. Risk estimates for deaths from terrorist acts by refugees vary widely by country, timeframe, and definition of 'refugee' and no credible study establishes the precise figure 1 in 3.6 billion. While empirical analyses show the risk is very low in many contexts, the asserted exact probability is unverified and misleading.

claim: Says Texas "high school graduation rates are at all-time highs."
rationale: The statement is overly broad and therefore misleading. While Texas reported record-high graduation rates for certain recent cohorts (early 2020s) using specific metrics, graduation rates vary by year, student subgroup, and the metric used, so a blanket claim that they are 'at all-time highs' without a timeframe or metric is not reliably true.

claim: Obama "voted for ... $3-million for an overhead projector at a planetarium in Chicago."
rationale: This claim misstates and exaggerates the record. As an Illinois state senator Obama voted for a large capital projects bill that included money for many local projects, but there is no evidence he voted for a standalone $3 million appropriation specifically for an "overhead projector" at a Chicago planetarium; fact‑checking organizations have debunked the specific wording as misleading. The appropriation was part of broader funding for facility projects, not a single-line purchase of an overhead projector.

claim: Says police unions have it "written into a contract that (officers) are not going to be accountable" for misconduct.
rationale: The claim as stated is an overgeneralization. While many police union contracts include procedural protections (limits on investigatory access, timelines for discipline, arbitration, and privacy protections) that can make disciplining officers harder, contracts do not typically contain blanket language saying officers "are not going to be accountable" for misconduct. The practical effect of some provisions can impede accountability in certain cases, but this varies greatly by jurisdiction and contract.

claim: The CDC "adjusted the US Covid deaths from 153,504 to 9,210."
rationale: The CDC did not reduce the total U.S. COVID-19 death toll from 153,504 to 9,210. That smaller figure arose from misreading a specific CDC table/category (for example, deaths listing COVID-19 as the sole cause or a limited subset/timeframe), while the overall reported COVID-19 death counts remained far higher and were not revised down to 9,210.

claim: Bill McCollum "backed Jim Greer's effort to hide financial irregularities."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bill McCollum supported or helped Jim Greer hide financial irregularities. Jim Greer was indicted and later convicted for financial misconduct involving the Florida GOP, but public reports and court records do not implicate McCollum in backing efforts to conceal those irregularities, and McCollum was not charged.
cited_knowledge: Contemporary news reporting and court records about Jim Greer's indictment and conviction for misappropriation and falsifying financial statements, and the absence of allegations or charges tying Bill McCollum to concealing those actions.
safety_notes: Political actors made competing accusations during that period, so ambiguous partisan claims exist; a specific source or allegation would be needed to evaluate any particular allegation further.

claim: "Every day over 450,000 Americans sit in jail not because they've been convicted of anything, but because they are too poor to pay bail & don't have high powered attorneys."
rationale: It is true that on any given day hundreds of thousands of people (roughly 450,000–480,000 in recent years) are held in jails pretrial and therefore are not convicted, but it is incorrect to say they are all there solely because they are too poor to pay bail and lack high-powered attorneys. Research shows a large share of pretrial detainees cannot afford bail, but others are held because judges deny release for public-safety reasons, because of holds or technical detainers, or other case-specific reasons; many do have appointed counsel, though resources and quality vary.

claim: On Sandra Day O'Connor: "I think one reason she was a good judge is she had no judicial experience" before she joined the Supreme Court.
rationale: Sandra Day O'Connor did have judicial experience before joining the U.S. Supreme Court: she was appointed to the Arizona Court of Appeals in 1979 and served there until her 1981 Supreme Court nomination. Therefore the assertion that she had no judicial experience prior to the Court is incorrect as stated.

claim: U.S. Senate candidate Michelle Nunn "earned as much as $300,000 running a nonprofit that had laid off 90 workers."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and nonprofit filings show Michelle Nunn’s reported compensation as CEO of Points of Light/HandsOn Network was roughly $250,000–$300,000 in the years around 2011–2012. Around the same period, HandsOn Network cut about 90 positions after a merger and financial restructuring, so the claim’s two factual components are accurate though presented without context.

claim: Since 2009, the Ohio Republican Party has made more contacts with voters — nearly 6.6 million — than any other GOP state organization in the nation.
rationale: There is no independent, authoritative national comparison or audit publicly available that verifies the Ohio Republican Party has made nearly 6.6 million voter contacts since 2009 and that this exceeds every other state GOP. "Contacts" is undefined and states report such metrics differently, so the claim appears to be a self-reported, promotional figure rather than a verifiable national record. Without third‑party verification the assertion cannot be accepted as fact.

claim: "Spending on welfare, on prisons, and education, all of those have dropped by hundreds of millions of dollars" because of Arizona’s immigration laws that drove out undocumented immigrants.
rationale: The claim is an unsubstantiated broad causal assertion. While Arizona’s 2010-era immigration enforcement measures (e.g., SB 1070) may have influenced migration patterns modestly, there is no solid evidence that spending on welfare, prisons, and education all fell by “hundreds of millions” as a direct result; research finds mixed and much smaller fiscal effects and many public programs (especially K–12 education) are funded by residency and legal requirements rather than immigration status.

claim: "No Bridge to Nowhere could occur."
rationale: The statement that “No Bridge to Nowhere could occur” denies the possibility of poorly justified or underused bridge projects, but such outcomes have happened historically. Well-known examples include proposed or built bridges widely labeled “bridges to nowhere” (e.g., the Gravina Island/Alaska proposal) and other infrastructure projects that proceeded despite limited demand. Therefore it is false that such occurrences are impossible.

claim: "Julia Roberts claims ‘Michelle Obama isn’t fit to clean Melania’s toilet’ "
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Julia Roberts ever said ‘Michelle Obama isn’t fit to clean Melania’s toilet.’ The quote appears to be a viral, misattributed or fabricated social-media claim and has not been corroborated by reputable news outlets or Roberts’ public statements.

claim: Suggests Amber Heard snorted cocaine while on the stand in court.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Amber Heard snorted cocaine while testifying; independent news fact-checks and reviews of the trial footage found no proof of drug use and no official reports or charges followed such claims. Viral posts appear to be misinterpretations of video clips or speculation rather than demonstrated forensic evidence.

claim: Oregon Rep. Tina Kotek, D-Portland, has "never held a job nor run a business"
rationale: Tina Kotek has held multiple paid positions and elected offices: she has been an elected state representative (and served as Speaker of the Oregon House) and worked in staff and nonprofit roles prior to and during her legislative career. Therefore the assertion that she has “never held a job” is incorrect.

claim: A photo of a homeless camp on old railroad tracks is present-day Los Angeles.
rationale: This claim is not verifiable without the actual image's metadata, geolocation, or reliable sourcing. Homeless encampments on disused railroad tracks occur in many cities and images are often misattributed, so treating the assertion as false is prudent until corroborated.

claim: In Congress, "on the Democratic side of the room, you’ve got men and women of all different races; on the other side, you’ve got a bunch of white men in dark suits, all over 55 or so."
rationale: The statement is a broad, exaggerated generalization. While the Democratic caucuses in Congress are indeed more racially and gender diverse and the Republican caucuses are majority white, male, and older on average, it is inaccurate to claim the Republican side is exclusively "a bunch of white men in dark suits, all over 55" because there are Republican women, nonwhite Republicans, and members under 55.

claim: Says that singer Dolly Parton said, "Trump in one year is already better than 16 years of Bush, Obama put together."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or primary-source evidence that Dolly Parton ever said this line praising Trump; the quote appears to be a social-media misattribution. Parton has generally avoided public political endorsements and reliable outlets do not attribute this statement to her.

claim: "In 2014 ... in McDowell County, W.Va., one of the poorest counties in the nation, life expectancy for men was 64 years. In Fairfax County, Va., a wealthy county, just 350 miles away, life expectancy was nearly 82 years, an 18 year differential. The life expectancy gap for women in the two counties was 12 years."
rationale: Published county-level life expectancy estimates for the mid-2010s show McDowell County, WV had male life expectancy around 64 years while Fairfax County, VA was near 82 years, yielding roughly an 18-year difference; female life expectancy differences between the two counties are reported around 12 years. These specific figures were widely reported using CDC/IHME and other county life-expectancy datasets for that period.

claim: "Austin is the largest city in the U.S. or Texas with no geographic representation" on its city council.
rationale: Austin currently elects its city council members from 10 single-member geographic districts (with the mayor elected at-large), so it does have geographic representation on its council. The city moved from an all at-large system to district-based council seats following a voter-approved change in 2012 implemented for subsequent elections.

claim: "We’re spending tremendous amounts of money to educate our kids. In the world, we're No. 1 per pupil by a factor of four."
rationale: The United States does spend a lot per student and ranks near the top in many international datasets, but authoritative sources (OECD, World Bank, NCES) do not show U.S. per-pupil K–12 spending being four times higher than other countries or the global average. Several countries spend similar or greater amounts per pupil once comparable definitions and purchasing-power adjustments are applied.

claim: "Here's the fact: The No. 1 source of income into Mexico are Mexicans working here and sending the money back."
rationale: Remittances from Mexicans working abroad are a major and growing source of foreign currency for Mexico and in recent years have even exceeded oil revenues, but they are not the country’s top source of income overall. Mexico’s exports of goods and services (particularly manufactured exports to the United States) are substantially larger than remittance inflows and remain the leading source of national income from abroad.

claim: "We have more women in the workforce than ever before."
rationale: The claim is too vague — it gives no time period or geography. While absolute numbers of women working globally are higher than in past centuries due to population growth and expanding opportunities, labor-force participation rates have plateaued or fallen in some countries (e.g., the U.S. participation rate peaked around 1999–2000). Without a clear reference (global vs. country, absolute numbers vs. participation rate, and what historical baseline), the statement cannot be verified as universally true.

claim: Says that Minnesota Democratic congressional candidate Dean Phillips doesn’t offer health insurance for his employees.
rationale: Contemporaneous news reporting and statements from Dean Phillips and his campaign indicate his businesses have offered health insurance to employees; the recurring attack appears to conflate full-time and part-time workers or specific subsidiaries. As an absolute statement that he doesn’t offer health insurance to his employees, the claim is inaccurate or misleading.

claim: "3.8% of Wisconsin’s coronavirus funding has been spent."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false because it gives a single precise percentage without a date or defined funding pool. Pandemic relief funding in Wisconsin came from multiple sources (CARES Act, federal/local grants, FEMA, etc.) and spending rates varied by program and reporting date; publicly available state reports show different percentages at different times. Without a specific timeframe and source, the 3.8% figure cannot be confirmed.

claim: "I'm also the only lieutenant governor to not take a security detail."
rationale: The claim gives no jurisdiction or timeframe and is implausible as stated: there are dozens of lieutenant governors in the U.S. (and comparable officials in other countries) and security-detail practices vary by state and era. Multiple state-level officials have publicly declined or foregone security details for cost or personal reasons, so it is extremely unlikely any one person is uniquely the only lieutenant governor to do so.

claim: Says Miami Congressman Carlos "Curbelo supports drilling offshore" and "repeatedly voted against President Obama's ability to fight pollution and combat climate change."
rationale: This statement is misleading. Carlos Curbelo publicly opposed new offshore drilling off Florida’s coast and supported coastal protections and bipartisan climate initiatives, so the blanket claim that he "supports drilling offshore" is inaccurate; while he did vote with Republicans on some Obama-era measures, portraying him as having "repeatedly voted against President Obama's ability to fight pollution and combat climate change" without naming specific votes overstates and mischaracterizes his mixed record.

claim: Says 12 restaurants and food companies are "supporting Trump’s re-election."
rationale: The claim that exactly 12 restaurants and food companies are "supporting Trump’s re-election" cannot be verified as presented because no specific list, timeframe, or definition of "support" is given. Public records (PAC filings, corporate statements, individual executive donations) would be required to substantiate such a count, and companies frequently differ in whether they endorse candidates, give via PACs, or have executives make personal donations.

claim: "Across the board, violent crime in jurisdictions that recognize the Right to Carry is lower than in areas that prevent it."
rationale: The claim is a universal statement but empirical research is mixed: some studies report declines in certain violent crimes after right-to-carry laws, others find increases or no significant effect. Methodological differences, varying law types, and local confounders mean there is no clear, across-the-board reduction in violent crime attributable solely to recognizing the right to carry.

claim: Wayne Powell has a "stated position of having no objection to taking `In God We Trust" off of U.S. currency."
rationale: I find no verifiable public record or reliable reporting up to mid-2024 that documents a person named Wayne Powell explicitly stating he has no objection to removing 'In God We Trust' from U.S. currency. The name is common and the claim appears unverified and possibly a misattribution without a primary source quotation or reliable citation.

claim: Says Donald Trump warned outgoing Ghana President against last-minute job appointments.
rationale: There is no credible record or widely reported instance up to mid‑2024 of former President Donald Trump publicly warning an outgoing Ghanaian president about making last‑minute job appointments. Such a statement would likely have been reported by major international media and documented in Trump's public statements, but no such coverage is known.

claim: People carrying guns can’t wear face masks to protect against the coronavirus because it’s a "class 4 felony."
rationale: The claim is false. There is no blanket law making it a "class 4 felony" for someone carrying a gun to wear a face mask for health protection; anti-mask or disguise statutes generally target concealing identity while committing crimes, not routine public-health face coverings worn by lawful carriers. Criminal classifications like "class 4 felony" are jurisdiction-specific, so the claim is an incorrect universal statement.

claim: A video shows Joe Biden lost and confused on stage.
rationale: I cannot verify the referenced video or its context from this claim alone, and a short clip can be edited, miscaptioned, or taken out of context. Even if Joe Biden pauses, looks for a prompt, or appears momentarily unsure, that does not prove he was definitively 'lost and confused' on stage without unedited footage and corroborating evidence. A reliable determination requires the original video, event details, and independent reporting.

claim: President Barack Obama "has doubled the size of government since he took office."
rationale: The claim is false as stated: common measures of government size such as the federal civilian workforce and annual federal outlays did not double during President Obama’s tenure. The civilian federal workforce was roughly flat or slightly smaller and annual outlays rose but by much less than twofold. The one metric that did roughly double was the total federal debt, which may be the source of the claim but is not the same as 'size of government.'

claim: "Not a single Republican candidate, announced or potential, is clearly and consistently supporting a path to citizenship. Not one."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that no Republican candidate (announced or potential) clearly and consistently supports a path to citizenship; that is false because several prominent Republicans have publicly supported some form of a path to citizenship at times. For example, Marco Rubio was a principal co‑author of the 2013 'Gang of Eight' immigration bill which included a pathway to citizenship, and other Republicans (including some governors and former presidential candidates) have backed paths for Dreamers or broader legalization in various periods. Positions do vary and some politicians have shifted, so blanket absolutes about every announced or potential candidate are unreliable.

claim: "Republicans in the General Assembly cut teacher pay so much when they took over in 2011 that even with recent pay raises, we are still below pre-Recession pay levels."
rationale: The claim is a broad, causal assertion about “Republicans in the General Assembly” and the current salary level versus pre‑Recession pay but provides no state or inflation adjustment. Teacher pay trends after the 2008–09 recession varied widely by state: some states that switched to Republican legislative control did reduce education spending or limit raises, and some have not fully recovered to pre‑recession inflation‑adjusted pay, but this is not a universal or provable national fact without state‑specific data.

claim: The Obama administration "was successful in rushing a massive spending bill through Congress in just two days — after which it sat on the president's desk for three days, while he was away on vacation."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable record that a major Obama-era spending bill was passed by Congress in exactly two days and then sat unsigned on the president’s desk for three days while he was on vacation. Major bills such as the 2009 Recovery Act and later omnibus appropriations had longer legislative timelines and public signing events; contemporary news and congressional records do not corroborate the precise two-day passage/three-day desk-delay narrative.

claim: The majority of revenue generated by a proposed Kenosha casino would be sent to the Seminole tribe in Florida.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a majority of revenue from a proposed Kenosha casino would be transferred to the Seminole Tribe of Florida. Tribal casinos are normally owned and operated by the tribe on whose land the facility sits, and outside operators or managers typically receive limited management fees rather than a majority share of gross revenue. A Florida tribe receiving most revenue from a Wisconsin casino would be highly unusual and would require a specific contractual arrangement not publicly documented.

claim: "Military arrests Adam Schiff."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official records indicating that Rep. Adam Schiff has been arrested by the military. Such an action would be extraordinary and legally constrained in the United States, and contemporary news sources up through mid-2024 show no evidence of it.

claim: Chris Christie "cut equal pay for women, calling it 'senseless bureaucracy.' "
rationale: There is no clear, reliable evidence that Chris Christie formally 'cut equal pay for women' as a legal entitlement or used the quoted phrase 'senseless bureaucracy' in that context. Reporting about Christie shows he opposed or vetoed certain regulations and budget items at times, but the specific claim conflates actions and an attributed quote that do not appear in public records or reputable news accounts.

claim: The WIC program "is an incredibly cost effective program, serving nearly 10 million Americans each year and costing less than $100 per person. In my district, more than 18 percent of residents suffer from food insecurity and depend on WIC to make ends meet."
rationale: The claim mixes metrics and understates costs. WIC’s average monthly participation is roughly 6–7 million people, and the unduplicated number served over a full year can approach—but is not reliably—'nearly 10 million' depending on counting method. However, program spending implies a per-person cost well above $100 on an annual basis (the claim gives no time frame, and <$100 would only be plausible as a short-term monthly or narrowly defined cost). The district-specific statement that 'more than 18 percent of residents ... depend on WIC' is unverifiable without the district name and seems implausibly high for an entire population share.

claim: "As the election tracker FiveThirtyEight has reported, whoever wins Pennsylvania will be our next President."
rationale: FiveThirtyEight produces probabilistic forecasts and does not state as a general rule that winning a single state (Pennsylvania) guarantees the presidency. Whether winning Pennsylvania decides the presidency depends on the electoral math in a given election, and historically the winner of Pennsylvania has not always become president (for example, Al Gore won Pennsylvania in 2000 but did not become president).

claim: Says of flood of non-Mexicans being apprehended at the border: "These are people that are coming from states like Syria that have substantial connections back to terrorist regimes and terrorist operations."
rationale: Available border enforcement statistics show most non-Mexican apprehensions are from Western Hemisphere countries (e.g., Central America, Venezuela, Cuba, Haiti), not large inflows from Syria. Instances of migrants from Syria or with proven links to terrorist organizations at the U.S. border are extremely rare and do not support the claim of a 'flood' with 'substantial connections' to terrorist regimes.

claim: Says Kentucky Attorney General Daniel Cameron "married his mentor Mitch McConnell's granddaughter."
rationale: Public reporting and official records identify Daniel Cameron's spouse and show he is not married to a member of Mitch McConnell's family. Multiple fact-checks and contemporary news accounts that profile Cameron and McConnell list no familial marriage between them.

claim: "We cut taxes for 95 percent of working families."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify and cannot be confirmed as a general fact without specifying which tax law, year, country, or definition of "working families." Different tax changes benefit different shares of households depending on whether one measures filers, families, or 'working' status, and whether effects are measured in the short term or long term. Independent analyses of major U.S. tax laws have produced widely varying estimates, so the blanket claim that 95% of working families received tax cuts is not reliably supported as stated.

claim: U.S. Rep. Matt "Cartwright proposes to defund the Wilkes-Barre police."
rationale: There is no record that U.S. Rep. Matt Cartwright has proposed defunding the Wilkes-Barre police. Public statements and reporting about Cartwright show he has supported policing reforms and public safety funding but has not advocated eliminating or defunding the Wilkes-Barre police department.

claim: Says Ben Carson said "illegal immigrants caught voting should be stripped of their citizenship."
rationale: There is no credible record of Ben Carson saying the quoted line; fact-checkers and news archives do not support that he made this exact claim. In addition, the statement is legally incoherent because someone who is an "illegal immigrant" is not a citizen and therefore cannot be "stripped of their citizenship."

claim: That Donald Trump said in 1998 if he were to run for president he would run as a Republican because "They’re the dumbest group of voters in the country. They believe anything on Fox News. I could lie and they’d still eat it up. I bet my numbers would be terrific."
rationale: The widely circulated 1998 quote cannot be reliably sourced to a contemporaneous interview or reputable archive; major fact-checking outlets have not verified that Trump said this exact wording in 1998. While Trump has made disparaging remarks about voters and media over the years, the specific phrasing about Republicans, Fox News, and lying appears to be misattributed or apocryphal.

claim: Georgia has had the nation’s busiest Court of Appeals for a decade or more.
rationale: Available information shows Georgia’s Court of Appeals has at times ranked among the busiest intermediate appellate courts, but I cannot confirm it has been the single busiest in the nation continuously for a decade or more. Appellate caseload rankings fluctuate yearly and depend on metrics (total filings, filings per judge), and other states’ courts have led in different years.

claim: "The state is set to recapture an additional $500 million in Robin Hood payments from taxpayers and not one penny of it will go to public education in Texas."
rationale: Texas 'Robin Hood' recapture takes excess local property tax revenue and is intended to support public education either by redistributing directly to other districts or through the state's school finance system. It is therefore incorrect to assert that an additional $500 million recaptured would result in 'not one penny' going to public education; recapture dollars are generally used for K–12 funding. The exact $500 million figure and timing are context-dependent and would require checking the specific legislative or budget action.

claim: "The CBO, the Congressional Budget Office has said that Obamacare will kill 800,000 jobs."
rationale: The CBO did not state categorically that the Affordable Care Act 'will kill 800,000 jobs.' CBO analyses projected a modest reduction in labor supply and fewer full‑time equivalent (FTE) workers in some scenarios and timeframes, but its estimates vary by year and measure (hours, participation, or FTEs) and it did not present a single definitive '800,000 jobs killed' finding. Claims quoting a round 800,000 figure typically misstate or oversimplify CBO's nuanced results.

claim: There is a Republican "plan to end Medicare."
rationale: There is no single, formal Republican Party plan explicitly labeled to 'end Medicare.' However, many Republican lawmakers and past GOP budget proposals have advocated converting traditional Medicare to a premium‑support/voucher model or privatizing parts of it, changes critics describe as effectively ending Medicare as currently structured. Thus the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: "That’s 5,615 projected coal-powered plants in just 8 countries. The USA has 15 - building 0 more."
rationale: The specific figure of 5,615 'projected coal-powered plants in just 8 countries' is not supported by widely reported datasets; global trackers (e.g., Global Energy Monitor, IEA) report far fewer planned/cooled coal plants or capacity and numbers vary by definition (units vs sites). The U.S. does have very few or no large new coal plants under construction in recent years, but saying the U.S. 'has 15' (without clarifying whether that means planned, operating, or retired) and 'building 0 more' mixes inconsistent categories and misstates the widely available data.

claim: Says Texas high school graduates must pass Algebra II to be eligible for automatic admission to state's public universities.
rationale: The claim is overstated. Automatic admission in Texas (commonly the "Top 10%" rule) is primarily based on class rank and completion of an approved college-preparatory curriculum, and while Algebra II is part of many recommended curricula, it is not an absolute, universal statewide checkbox that every graduate must pass to be eligible — specific course requirements and permissible alternatives or exemptions vary by law and institution.

claim: "There's going to be a slowdown and delays in flights" as a result of the sequester.
rationale: A sequester can reduce discretionary aviation funding and create the risk of FAA furloughs or reduced services that could cause delays, but it is not guaranteed that flights will slow or be delayed. In past U.S. sequesters lawmakers and agencies often took steps (reallocations, temporary fixes, or exemptions) that mitigated or prevented major nationwide delays. The claim presented as an absolute outcome is therefore misleading without timing and policy context.

claim: "Recent data showed Nevada ranks 50th in the money received from" the stimulus bill.
rationale: The claim is vague and cannot be confirmed as stated. Different stimulus laws (e.g., CARES Act, American Rescue Plan) and different metrics (total dollars, per-capita, or program-specific payments) produce different state rankings, and Nevada — with a mid-sized population — is not consistently ranked 50th in the commonly reported breakdowns. Without a specific bill and metric, the assertion that Nevada ranks 50th is unsupported.

claim: "Klein did not hold a single town hall meeting (on health care) where the general public was invited to ask questions or present their views."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement and is likely incorrect because during Ralph Klein’s tenure the government organized public consultations and forums on health care reforms; while critics complained about limited or managed engagement, there were publicly promoted meetings and consultations where members of the public could attend and express views. Without specifying which 'Klein' or which time period, the blanket denial that 'not a single town hall' occurred is not supported.

claim: Claims Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said "she prefers the South African Constitution over the United States Constitution."
rationale: Ruth Bader Ginsburg did publicly praise aspects of the South African Constitution—particularly its explicit equality and dignity provisions—but she did not state that she prefers the South African Constitution wholesale over the U.S. Constitution. The claim is a misleading summary of her comparative comments rather than an accurate direct quote.

claim: Says our national debt is greater than our gross domestic product.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous because it does not specify which country or which year is meant; debt-to-GDP ratios differ across countries and over time. Without a named nation and date the statement cannot be verified and thus cannot be treated as a factual general claim. (As an example, the United States' gross federal debt has exceeded annual GDP in recent years, but that depends on the exact measure and timing.)

claim: "While the initial increase in oil prices resulted in a near instantaneous increase in gas prices for consumers, the subsequent decrease in crude oil prices has failed to meaningfully provide relief for Georgia's families at the pump."
rationale: The claim is too general and time‑dependent to be verified as stated. While retail gasoline prices often rise quickly when crude oil spikes and can fall more slowly due to taxes, refining capacity, distribution costs and retailer margins, whether Georgia drivers have been denied 'meaningful' relief depends on the precise time period and local price data. Without a defined timeframe and supporting Georgia-specific price series, the absolute claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: "In 1992, the Democratic Party had in their platform provisions that said that illegal aliens were coming in this country, committing felonies, sent back and then they were right back across the border to do the same thing."
rationale: The quoted sentence is not a verbatim or accurate characterization of the 1992 Democratic Party platform. Party platforms are formal documents that generally use measured policy language about immigration enforcement and reform rather than accusing groups of repeatedly committing felonies and immediately returning; moreover, unauthorized border crossing is not uniformly a felony under U.S. law. There is no reliable record that the 1992 Democratic platform contained the specific allegation quoted.

claim: Says award-winning Milwaukee Public Schools teacher Megan Sampson was laid off because Gov. Scott Walker cut state aid to education.
rationale: There is no clear public evidence that award-winning Milwaukee teacher Megan Sampson was laid off solely because Gov. Scott Walker cut state aid. Although Walker-era policies reduced some state education funding and districts faced budget pressure, layoffs are typically decided by local school districts based on seniority, program changes, and local budget decisions; attributing a particular teacher’s layoff directly to the governor’s actions requires specific documentary evidence.

claim: "25,000 businesses have been created since (Scott) Walker took office."
rationale: There is no independently verified, widely accepted statistic confirming exactly '25,000 businesses' created since Walker took office; such figures typically came from campaign statements that counted certain business filings or registrations rather than net new employer firms and did not account for closures. Independent analysts and state data show different counts depending on definitions and timeframes, so the precise claim is not reliably supported.

claim: "Biden won’t allow Delta-variant COVID patients to get proven and effective monoclonal treatments even though there are 50,000-100,000 Americans infected by Delta EVERY DAY."
rationale: The claim is false: the federal government did not categorically "not allow" monoclonal antibody treatments for Delta patients. During the Delta wave the FDA had emergency authorizations for monoclonal therapies (for example casirivimab/imdevimab) and HHS distributed doses, although specific monoclonal products that lacked activity against particular variants were restricted or withdrawn. The stated daily infection figure (50,000–100,000) is a broad, time-dependent estimate and not a fixed fact applicable to all dates.

claim: "Surveys show that many of our citizens think we devote a full quarter or even a third of our federal budget to foreign aid."
rationale: Multiple reputable public-opinion surveys have consistently found that large shares of Americans substantially overestimate how much of the federal budget goes to foreign aid, with many respondents giving answers around 25% or even 33%. These survey results contrast with actual U.S. foreign assistance, which is a small fraction (around 1%) of the federal budget, indicating the claim about public belief is accurate.

claim: The Republican tax bill is "not being scored by the Congressional Budget Office, as it is traditionally."
rationale: Tax legislation is typically scored by the Congressional Joint Committee on Taxation for revenue effects, and the Congressional Budget Office routinely provides budgetary and macroeconomic cost estimates as well. In major Republican tax bills (for example the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act) JCT and CBO both produced official scores or estimates, so the blanket claim that the CBO is not scoring the bill “as it is traditionally” is inaccurate.

claim: "Half of all hospitalized seniors are suffering from malnutrition so severe that it either caused their illness or it prevents them from getting better."
rationale: This statement overstates the evidence. Studies report widely varying rates of malnutrition or risk of malnutrition in hospitalized older adults (commonly 20–50% depending on setting and assessment tool), but there is no robust, general finding that half of all hospitalized seniors have malnutrition so severe that it caused their illness or definitively prevents recovery.

claim: In the 2012 election, there were more votes cast than registered voters in St. Lucie County, and Palm Beach County had 141 percent turnout.
rationale: Official post‑election counts and contemporaneous fact checks show no evidence that St. Lucie County had more votes cast than registered voters or that Palm Beach County had 141% turnout in the 2012 election. The erroneous figures arose from comparing ballots to inappropriate subsets of the voter rolls or to outdated/incomplete registration lists, not from an actual turnout above 100%.

claim: "Medicaid expansion isn’t necessarily a very popular issue on the street."
rationale: The claim is vague but implies Medicaid expansion generally lacks public support. However, numerous national and state polls over recent years have shown majority support for Medicaid expansion in many states; while the issue’s salience (how prominently it features 'on the street') can vary, the policy itself tends to be broadly popular. Therefore the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: Says "I have been through the gauntlet, when we had riots in that Capitol."
rationale: The statement is presented without any attribution, context, or corroborating evidence, so it cannot be verified as an authentic quote. Without knowing who said it, when, and which "Capitol" and "riots" are referenced, the claim is unprovable and should be treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "When you look at the nearly 150 men and women who have served us on the Texas Supreme Court, more than half of them had zero prior judicial experience."
rationale: I cannot verify the claim and available biographical patterns of Texas Supreme Court justices show a mix of prior judicial and non-judicial backgrounds. Many justices historically served in lower courts or as judges earlier in their careers, so the assertion that more than half of nearly 150 had zero prior judicial experience is unlikely without a precise headcount. Absent a compiled biographical tally, the claim is not reliably supported.

claim: "While all COVID-19 news has been going on, the U.S. Government has been sneakily trying to remove end-to-end encryption" which means "the government will be able to see all of your messages and listen to all of your calls."
rationale: The claim mixes two things and overstates them. It is true that U.S. law enforcement and some lawmakers have publicly advocated limits or lawful‑access measures for end‑to‑end encryption (e.g., debates around the EARN IT Act and DOJ/FBI statements), but those efforts have been public, contested, and not a secret 'sneaky' removal. Equally, even if some legal or technical constraints were enacted, that would not automatically mean the government can instantly "see all messages and listen to all calls" — access would depend on specific technical changes, provider cooperation, and legal process, and introducing universal backdoors is technically and politically difficult.

claim: "I have given $30,000 of my unused travel expenses over the years to supplement the school system's general budget."
rationale: This is a first-person factual claim about past financial actions that cannot be independently verified from the statement alone. Without corroborating records (donation receipts, school accounting or tax documents) there is no reliable evidence to accept it as true, so it is treated as unverified/false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: Says Measure 3-386 will cost a fortune for elections while Measure 3-388 will cost less.
rationale: The claim asserts a comparative cost outcome for two ballot measures (3-386 and 3-388) but provides no jurisdiction or sourcing and I cannot find a verifiable, universal statement that one will 'cost a fortune' while the other 'will cost less.' Fiscal impacts of ballot measures vary by locale and depend on official fiscal notes and analyses, so the blanket claim is unsupported as presented.

claim: The city of Richmond "built the second richest team in the NFL a $14 million stadium."
rationale: There is no record of an NFL franchise being based in a city called Richmond and no NFL stadium was built for $14 million by a small city.
