Biden’s campaign climate plan on his website incorporated many policies and goals that overlap with the Green New Deal, but his campaign repeatedly said he did not endorse the Green New Deal resolution as written and he denied full support in debates. The website emphasized alignment with many goals rather than an explicit endorsement of the Green New Deal legislative text.

claim: "President Obama has declared disasters in 48 of 50 states this year."
rationale: There is no evidence that President Obama declared disasters in 48 of 50 states in a single year; FEMA’s public declaration records show far fewer state-level major disaster declarations in any one year and such an unprecedented action would have been widely reported. Similar claims often conflate county-level or multi-year declarations or misstate the timeframe.

claim: Says Central Texas river water sent to downstream rice farmers in 2011 equaled about three years’ worth of Austin’s water use.
rationale: I found no authoritative data supporting the claim that 2011 releases to downstream rice farmers equaled roughly three years of Austin’s water use. Typical figures put Austin’s annual treated-water use at tens of thousands of acre-feet, while reported reservoir releases to support downstream rice irrigation during the 2011 drought were substantially smaller than the hundreds of thousands of acre-feet that 'three years' of Austin would imply.

claim: "Joe, I keep hearing you every morning talking about the biggest tax increase in history, but you don't mention it's also the biggest tax cut in history.''
rationale: The statement asserts a single policy is simultaneously "the biggest tax increase in history" and "the biggest tax cut in history," which is self-contradictory and not supported by mainstream fiscal analyses. Major tax actions are measured by net revenue impact, affected group, and time horizon, and no credible analysis shows one law is both the largest historical increase and the largest historical cut under the same metric.

claim: "Colorado raked in $60 million in marijuana taxes and licensing fees in the past year."
rationale: Colorado’s annual marijuana tax and licensing revenue is much higher than $60 million; recent state reports show total annual sales and excise tax collections (plus fees) in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Therefore the claim that the state "raked in $60 million" in the past year significantly understates actual revenue.

claim: "The Chinese last year probably stole $360 billion in intellectual property from the United States."
rationale: There is no reliable, narrowly agreed figure showing that "the Chinese" stole $360 billion in U.S. intellectual property in a single recent year. Public estimates of annual losses from IP theft range widely (hundreds of billions) and are based on different methodologies; no authoritative source supports the specific $360 billion-for-last-year claim as a proven fact.

claim: Every former North Carolina governor opposes "constitutional amendments Raleigh lawmakers put on the ballot this fall."
rationale: It is very unlikely that every former North Carolina governor uniformly opposed those constitutional amendments; former governors come from different parties and have expressed varied views on ballot measures. Public reporting around such amendments typically shows mixed reactions rather than unanimous opposition, and the claim asserts unanimous opposition without evidence.

claim: "As we watch the news from Colorado with horror and sympathy for the families, we should remember that each day more than 80 Americans are killed by gunfire, unnecessary tragedies."
rationale: Recent U.S. mortality data show that total firearm deaths (including suicides and homicides) number well over 30,000–40,000 per year, which translates to well above 80 deaths per day on average. For example, CDC counts in recent years have averaged roughly 100–135 firearm deaths per day, so the statement that more than 80 Americans are killed by gunfire daily is accurate.

claim: "It costs nearly five times as much in California to build and maintain a mile of road as it does in the rest of the nation."
rationale: California does incur higher-than-average road construction and maintenance costs because of factors like higher labor and land costs, stringent environmental and permitting rules, and seismic standards, but independent studies and industry reporting do not support a consistent statewide cost that is nearly five times the national average. The fivefold figure appears to be an overgeneralization based on select high-cost projects or narrow comparisons rather than representative statewide data.

claim: A video shows an animal chip scanner detecting a microchip where a woman was vaccinated.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that COVID (or other) vaccines contain trackable microchips, and animal microchip readers are designed to detect specific pet RFID tags and can produce readings from external objects, metals, or staged tags. Viral videos typically show false positives, an external sticker/tag, or reader sensitivity rather than proof of an implanted vaccine microchip at the injection site.

claim: "Much more than 50 percent of parents out there are spankers."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: prevalence of parents who spank varies widely by country, culture, time period and how 'spank' is defined. Some surveys in particular places and times report rates above 50%, but many other surveys and countries report lower or declining rates, so a blanket statement that 'much more than 50 percent of parents' spank is not reliably true. Without a specified population and timeframe the claim cannot be established as factual.

claim: "Kids coming from an affluent background" are "taking advantage of all these student loan programs and grants" while many middle-class families with no connection to college are picking up the tab.
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. Need‑based grants (e.g., Pell Grants in the U.S.) are targeted to low‑income students rather than affluent ones, and while federal loans are widely available, the main beneficiaries of many higher‑education subsidies are students who attend college (who skew higher in income). There is no broad evidence that affluent kids are the primary users of need‑based grants nor that middle‑class non‑college families are uniquely bearing the costs as described.

claim: Says Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ted Cruz "opposes the DREAM Act, which is supported by 85% of Latinos."
rationale: As a 2012 Republican Senate candidate Ted Cruz publicly opposed the DREAM Act, and multiple contemporaneous polls of Hispanic/Latino respondents showed very high support (commonly reported in the 80–90% range). Therefore the two-part assertion (Cruz opposes the DREAM Act and ~85% of Latinos support it) is accurate in context.

claim: Scientists are "questioning the original idea that man-made global warming is what is causing the climate to change. … (It is) more and more being put into question."
rationale: Majority of climate scientists and major scientific organizations conclude that recent global warming is primarily caused by human activities; the scientific consensus has been reinforced by successive IPCC assessment reports rather than eroded. While research continues on details like climate sensitivity and regional impacts, the core attribution to anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions is well supported and not 'more and more' in question.

claim: "The U.S. is borrowing approximately $2.52 for every $1 of economic growth so far in 2012."
rationale: The statement is misleading and not verifiably supported by official 2012 data because it mixes ill-defined measures (borrowing vs. cumulative debt and which months/quarters of 2012) and depends entirely on choice of definitions and time window. Using standard measures (federal budget deficits and annual GDP growth) produces a different ratio and many fact-checks at the time flagged this as a selective or incorrect presentation of the numbers.

claim: Says "76 percent of all voters in the United States say they want Johnson-Weld, by name, in the presidential debates."
rationale: There is no reputable national poll showing that 76% of all U.S. voters, asked by name, said they wanted the Johnson–Weld ticket in the presidential debates. Historical national polls of third‑party candidates have shown far lower recognition and support, and the Commission on Presidential Debates uses objective thresholds (e.g., 15% in national polls) that Johnson/Weld typically did not meet.

claim: "When you pull up to the gas pump to fill up your car, get your cell phone and search for Bluetooth devices. If a sequence of letters and numbers show up don’t pay at the pump. One of the pumps has a credit card skimmer inside of it. All of these skimmers run on bluetooth."
rationale: This is inaccurate. Some gas‑pump card skimmers do use Bluetooth to transmit stolen data and can be detected that way, but many skimmers do not use Bluetooth (they store data locally or use other wireless methods), and Bluetooth scans often show legitimate nearby devices so are an unreliable indicator of a skimmer.

claim: "When unemployment goes down, inflation goes up."
rationale: The claim states an absolute relationship but is not universally true. While the short-run Phillips curve describes a tendency for lower unemployment to be associated with higher inflation, the relationship is unstable and can be broken by supply shocks, changing inflation expectations, and monetary policy; in the long run there is no guaranteed trade-off.

claim: In Afghanistan, "over 100 billion dollars spent on military contracts."
rationale: Multiple official audits and analyses (including DoD contracting data and SIGAR summaries) show that U.S. obligations for contracts and reconstruction in Afghanistan over the course of the war exceeded $100 billion. The figure commonly cited covers spending across years of operations, logistics, security, and reconstruction contracts rather than a single year or a different country.

claim: "Facts have now come out to show conclusively" that the 2020 presidential election wasn’t legitimate.
rationale: Multiple independent audits and recounts, state certifications, a Department of Justice review, and numerous court rulings found no evidence of widespread fraud that would overturn the 2020 result. Cybersecurity officials described the election as secure, and legal challenges were overwhelmingly dismissed, so the claim that facts have emerged proving the election was illegitimate is incorrect.

claim: Says Troy Nehls "called wearing masks 'un-American' and called those who do 'communists.'"
rationale: I cannot find a reliably sourced direct quote attributing both the phrases 'un-American' for wearing masks and calling people who wear them 'communists' to Rep. Troy Nehls. While some politicians criticized mask mandates and there are partisan attacks in media, the specific double attribution appears unverified and may be a misquote or conflation with other figures.

claim: California has instituted a "bacon ban."
rationale: There is no California state law that bans bacon or pork products statewide. Occasional local policies, institutional menu choices, or viral misinformation have sometimes been described as a "bacon ban," but these are not a legally enacted statewide prohibition.

claim: "Ivanka Trump charged with major crime."
rationale: As of my last knowledge update in June 2024, Ivanka Trump had not been criminally charged. She had been subpoenaed and referenced in civil and investigative reporting related to the Trump Organization, but there was no public record of a major criminal indictment against her.

claim: "Las Vegas shooting witnesses report multiple gunmen dressed as security guards."
rationale: While some witnesses initially reported hearing multiple shooters or seeing people in security-style clothing during the chaotic 2017 Las Vegas mass shooting, thorough investigations by the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department and the FBI found only a single shooter (Stephen Paddock) and no credible evidence of additional gunmen dressed as security guards. Eyewitness perceptions and early rumors in the immediate aftermath do not change the official investigative conclusions.

claim: "Human meat found in McDonald’s meat factory"
rationale: There are no credible reports, inspections, or verified investigations showing human meat was found in any McDonald’s processing facility; this allegation matches a long-running internet hoax repeatedly debunked by fact-checkers. McDonald’s suppliers operate under food-safety regulations and testing regimes that would detect and prompt public disclosure of such a contamination event.

claim: "Half the workforce in the country may have just been idled" by coronavirus.
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: no credible national-level data indicates that half of a country's entire workforce was universally 'idled' by coronavirus. While many countries experienced large job losses, furloughs, and reduced hours, national unemployment or furlough rates rarely approached 50% and varied greatly by country, sector, and date.

claim: "Actor Tom Hanks has passed away age 63."
rationale: This claim is false. Tom Hanks is alive; he was born July 9, 1956 (making him older than 63) and there have been no credible reports of his death. He continues to be publicly active in film and media.

claim: "Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton have changed their positions (on the Iraq war withdrawal) to follow Chris Dodd."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton specifically changed their Iraq withdrawal positions in order to follow Chris Dodd. Both candidates adjusted their stances over the 2007–2008 primary for a variety of reasons (public opinion, national security debates, and campaign dynamics), and Dodd was a low-polling contender without documented leadership on that issue. News coverage and public records attribute their shifts to broader political pressures rather than to copying Dodd.

claim: House Republicans required the use of Styrofoam cups in House cafeterias that are "part of Koch Industries."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: House cafeterias are not "part of Koch Industries" and there is no evidence House Republicans mandated use of Styrofoam cups tied to Koch. Procurement and cafeteria operations are handled by House administrative offices and independent vendors, and the trademark Styrofoam is associated with Dow, not Koch.

claim: "Florida’s high school graduation rate falls well below the national average."
rationale: Recent data show Florida’s adjusted cohort high school graduation rate has generally been at or above the national average, not well below it. Florida Department of Education reports and NCES national ACGR figures in recent years place Florida in the high-80s to low-90s percentage range while the national rate is in the mid-to-high 80s.

claim: "If we had been on 'Obamacare' and a bureaucrat was trying to tell me when I could get that CAT scan, that would have delayed my treatment."
rationale: The statement asserts that being covered under the Affordable Care Act would have put a federal bureaucrat in charge of authorizing a CAT scan and thereby delayed care. In reality the ACA primarily expanded private insurance and Medicaid coverage and did not create a single centralized federal gatekeeper that schedules individual imaging; prior-authorization rules that can delay imaging are practices used by many private and public insurers and predate the ACA. Claiming ACA uniquely would have caused that specific delay is therefore misleading and not factually supported.

claim: "New Jersey today has fewer employees in state government than it had when Christie Whitman left office in January of 2001, and I think that’s good. And we did it without any layoffs. We did it through attrition."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because 'today' is unspecified and official New Jersey state employment totals have fluctuated since January 2001; at various points headcount and FTE measures exceeded 2001 levels. Additionally, budget crises and managerial actions since 2001 have included layoffs, furloughs, and reorganizations in some years, so the blanket assertion of fewer employees achieved entirely without any layoffs is inaccurate.

claim: "Already this calendar year, since January 1, we have had more than 20,000 people come across the border, apprehended, unauthorized."
rationale: The claim lacks crucial context (which year, which border, and the exact reporting period) and cannot be independently verified as stated. Apprehension totals at U.S. borders frequently exceed 20,000 over multi-week or month-long periods, but whether they exceeded 20,000 'already this calendar year since January 1' depends on the specific year and dataset referenced. Without a clear date or source, the statement is not reliably provable.

claim: "In North Carolina, they used stimulus money to hire one new state worker. His job, apply for more stimulus funds from the taxpayers by the way of the federal government."
rationale: The specific assertion is unverified and implausible as stated: while states (including North Carolina) have used federal stimulus funds to cover administrative costs and to hire staff to manage programs and grants, I find no credible evidence of a case where stimulus money was used to hire exactly one new state worker whose sole job was to apply for additional federal stimulus funds. The claim is vague and appears to conflate normal grant-administration roles with a sensational single-hire allegation.

claim: Says taxpayer subsidy for the Oregon Convention Center hotel jumped $100 million in closed-door sessions
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable evidence that taxpayer subsidy for the Oregon Convention Center hotel suddenly 'jumped $100 million' specifically in closed‑door sessions. Reporting about the Portland/Multnomah County convention hotel has documented debates over public incentives and some private negotiations, but no authoritative source confirms a $100M increase occurred behind closed doors as the claim asserts.

claim: Says First Lady Melania Trump posted a photo of herself "yesterday" and Facebook took it down.
rationale: The claim is time-relative and lacks a specific date; there are no reliable contemporaneous reports or archived evidence confirming that First Lady Melania Trump posted a photo 'yesterday' that Facebook then removed. Without verifiable timestamps, screenshots, or reporting from credible sources, the assertion cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says Miami-Dade Mayor Carlos Gimenez "approved a 67% pay raise for himself and increased his own pension. He makes $250,000 a year, more than almost every big-city Mayor in the country. He also kept his taxpayer-funded Mercedes-Benz after slashing $400 million in government jobs and spending."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate, outdated, and unverified elements. Public records put the Miami‑Dade mayoral salary around $250,000 (so that number is plausible), but Giménez did not unilaterally approve a 67% pay raise for himself — pay changes are set by the county commission and reporting on any large raise is either incorrect or taken out of context. The assertions that he increased his own pension, kept a taxpayer‑funded Mercedes after cutting $400 million in jobs/spending, and that his pay is larger than 'almost every' big‑city mayor are either unsubstantiated or misleading.

claim: "All non-US citizens, illegal or not, will be provided with free health care services."
rationale: U.S. policy does not provide free health care to all non-citizens; eligibility depends on immigration status, program rules, and state policies. Undocumented immigrants are generally limited to emergency care under EMTALA and some local/state programs, while lawful permanent residents often face waiting periods or restricted eligibility for Medicaid and other benefits.

claim: "We became a net exporter of natural gas in 2017, and until recently, our exports have exceeded our imports."
rationale: Assuming 'we' refers to the United States, U.S. Energy Information Administration data show the U.S. became a net exporter of natural gas in 2017, and in the following years exports generally exceeded imports as LNG export capacity rose. There are monthly and regional fluctuations, but the overall annual trend since 2017 has been net exports until more recent variability.

claim: "Thirty-four of the last 44 (debt ceiling increases) have been for less than a year. So, this notion that short-term is somehow the exception, it's actually the rule."
rationale: The claim gives a precise count without a cited data source and appears to conflate different ways of counting debt-limit actions (temporary measures, short-term extensions, multi-year increases). Publicly available histories of U.S. debt-limit actions show many variations in length and form, and I cannot confirm an authoritative list in which exactly 34 of the last 44 increases were under one year. Because the statement is numerically specific but underspecified and unsupported, it is not reliable as presented.

claim: "If the FAA is worried about what the 5G deployment will do to the planes, what do you think it will do to our bodies?"
rationale: The statement implies that FAA concerns about 5G affecting aircraft mean 5G will harm human bodies. FAA’s documented worries were about potential radio-frequency interference with aircraft radar altimeters (avionics), not evidence of biological harm. International health agencies and regulators (WHO, ICNIRP, FCC) conclude that 5G’s non‑ionizing radiofrequency emissions at regulated exposure limits have not been shown to cause adverse health effects. Therefore the rhetorical leap from avionics interference to proven human harm is unsupported by current evidence.

claim: Says TikTok found Cassie Compton, who has been missing from Arkansas since 2014.
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable reporting or law enforcement confirmation that TikTok 'found' Cassie Compton, who was reported missing from Arkansas in 2014. The claim appears to be a social-media rumor; without confirmation from police or reputable news outlets it should be treated as false or unverified.

claim: Bill White "is discriminating. He's taking jobs from African Americans and giving them to his friends."
rationale: This is a specific allegation of racial discrimination and cronyism against 'Bill White' but there is no publicly available, credible evidence (such as investigative reports, lawsuits, or official findings) confirming that he systematically took jobs from African Americans to give to friends. Without named incidents, records, or legal determinations, the claim is unverified and treated as false.

claim: "In 2010, everybody said you can't dare let guns go into the national parks, and of course the rapes, murders, robberies and assaults are down about 85 percent since we did that."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that allowing firearms in national parks in or around 2010 produced an approximately 85% drop in rapes, murders, robberies, and assaults. National Park Service and law-enforcement crime data do not show a uniform, dramatic decline of that magnitude attributable to a single policy change; crime in parks is low and varies year to year and by reporting jurisdiction.

claim: "The (health reform) legislation which Washington passed last year has made it more difficult to hire" because it’s increased costs for employers.
rationale: The claim is a broad causal statement that the health reform passed last year made hiring more difficult by increasing employer costs; empirical evidence for such a large, economy-wide effect is weak. Analyses of similar reforms (notably the U.S. Affordable Care Act) found only modest or mixed impacts on employer hiring decisions, with many firms exempt or receiving credits and mandates phased in or delayed, so a blanket claim that it has made hiring more difficult is not supported.

claim: In President Barack Obama’s 2015 State of the Union address, "the words ‘al-Qaida’ were never used, the first time those words have not been used in a State of the Union address since February 2001."
rationale: The official transcript of President Obama’s 2015 State of the Union does not include the phrase “al-Qaida,” and contemporary fact-checking noted he referred to ISIL/ISIS and “terrorists” instead. Review of State of the Union transcripts shows that addresses from after February 2001 consistently referenced al-Qaida until the 2015 speech omitted the term.

claim: "The coronavirus has officially reached Milwaukee County."
rationale: The claim gives no date or source, so it is not verifiable as stated. Whether the coronavirus has 'officially reached' Milwaukee County depends on a specific confirmed case announcement from the Milwaukee County Health Department or state public health authorities; without a time reference or citation the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says when Rhode Island Lottery was proposed, "state residents were enticed to vote for it with the promise that the money would be used for education."
rationale: When Rhode Island's state lottery was proposed in the early 1970s, supporters explicitly promoted lottery proceeds as a source of revenue for public programs including education, and that messaging was used to persuade voters. Framing lottery approval as a way to fund schools was a common and documented selling point in Rhode Island and other states at that time.

claim: Says Stefani Carter "repeatedly used her campaign contributors’ donations to rent margarita machines for our state house office."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official ethics finding that Stefani Carter repeatedly spent campaign contributors’ donations to rent margarita machines for a state house office. While campaigns sometimes spend funds on hospitality for events, public campaign finance records and reporting do not substantiate a repeated pattern of misuse that this claim asserts.

claim: Rhode Island voters are moving away from the Democratic party to non-affiliation
rationale: While unaffiliated (no-party) registration has grown modestly in many states including Rhode Island, Democrats have remained the largest registered party in Rhode Island and there is no clear evidence of a large-scale exodus from the Democratic Party to non-affiliation. The claim overstates the trend without specifying a timeframe or magnitude.

claim: Says Jason Carter has "gotten David Axelrod to come down and be his campaign advisor."
rationale: There is no credible reporting that David Axelrod formally joined Jason Carter’s campaign as an advisor. While Axelrod has occasionally appeared at events or offered informal commentary for various Democrats, records of Carter’s 2014 campaign do not show Axelrod serving as a campaign advisor.

claim: Says Chris Dudley thinks Oregon’s minimum wage is too high.
rationale: I could not find verifiable evidence or a reliable sourced quotation showing Chris Dudley explicitly said Oregon’s minimum wage is 'too high.' Although Dudley has generally expressed fiscally conservative positions in past campaigns, that general stance is not a direct confirmation of this specific assertion.

claim: A U-Haul operated by antifa activists distributed "shields, weapons & black bloc" to protesters in Louisville, Ky., and is linked to "a George Soros-funded initiative."
rationale: Multiple independent fact-checks and statements from Louisville law enforcement found no verifiable evidence that a U-Haul was operated by 'antifa' activists or was part of a George Soros-funded initiative. While authorities reported finding makeshift shields and gear associated with protests in some vehicles, those findings do not substantiate the social-media claim of an organized antifa distribution linked to Soros.

claim: Ché Guevara "wrote extensively about the superiority of white Europeans over people of African descent."
rationale: Che Guevara did not produce a body of work arguing for the superiority of white Europeans over people of African descent. While historians have documented occasional racist or derogatory language in some private diaries, letters, or travel notes, his published political writings and revolutionary rhetoric emphasize anti‑imperialism and internationalist solidarity rather than a systematic white‑supremacist ideology.

claim: "Corporate entities are paying a lot less taxes this year than they have in the past. Part of that is from a loophole in a bill that was passed in 2015."
rationale: The claim is vague and appears inaccurate: the large, widely reported U.S. corporate tax cut occurred with the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, not a 2015 bill, and there is no well-known 2015 federal law loophole that suddenly caused corporations to pay far less “this year.” Corporate tax payments also vary by country and by economic conditions, so a blanket statement without specifying jurisdiction or year is unsupported.

claim: Says he holds the record for "most appearances on 'Meet the Press'."
rationale: The claim as written is unverifiable because it does not identify who "he" refers to or give a timeframe; without that context the statement cannot be confirmed. Records of appearances on Meet the Press exist and specific individuals (for example long-serving hosts or frequent guests) have known tallies, so a bare assertion that an unnamed man "holds the record" cannot be validated.

claim: "Under ‘Trumpcare,’" domestic violence and sexual assault "could be considered pre-existing conditions."
rationale: Proposed Republican replacements for the ACA (commonly called "Trumpcare") would have weakened federal protections against using past health status to set premiums or deny coverage. Although domestic violence and sexual assault are not medical diagnoses by themselves, the physical and mental health consequences (injuries, pregnancy, PTSD, STIs) could be treated as pre‑existing conditions by insurers under those plans or state waiver rules.

claim: The Democrats’ Green New Deal includes "working towards ending air travel."
rationale: The congressional Green New Deal resolution does not call for "working towards ending air travel." It proposes achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions and modernizing transportation (including investment in high-speed rail and clean technologies), but it does not prescribe banning or ending air travel.

claim: "Black and Latino people in NYC are arrested at TEN times the rate of white people for virtually the same rate of marijuana usage."
rationale: Analyses of NYC arrest data in recent years have shown that Black and Latino New Yorkers were arrested for marijuana possession at rates roughly in the 8–10× range compared with white New Yorkers, while population surveys indicate similar rates of marijuana use across racial groups. The claim matches documented racial disparities in arrests, though exact ratios vary by year and dataset.

claim: "Russ Feingold got a memo in 2009 that outlined veteran harm" at a Wisconsin VA facility "and nothing was done."
rationale: I find no reliable evidence that Sen. Russ Feingold received a specific 2009 memo alleging veteran harm at a Wisconsin VA facility and that no action was taken. Major reporting on Veterans Affairs problems (notably around 2014) documents investigations and congressional inquiries, and claims tying a 2009 memo to Feingold with a complete lack of response are not substantiated in available public records.

claim: Democrats "manufactured votes from low income voters to steal the battleground states."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Democrats manufactured votes from low-income voters to steal battleground states. Multiple audits, recounts, court rulings, and investigations by federal and state election officials found no widespread, coordinated fraud that would have altered outcomes.

claim: Says Amber Alerts are issued for white kids "but not Black kids in Milwaukee."
rationale: The claim alleges a formal practice of issuing AMBER Alerts for white children but not Black children in Milwaukee, but AMBER Alerts are issued based on neutral criteria (confirmed abduction, imminent danger, and sufficient descriptive information) rather than race. There is no credible evidence of an official Milwaukee policy that excludes Black children from AMBER Alerts. Although researchers and reporters have documented disparities in media attention and public visibility for missing children of different races nationally, that does not prove a systematic race-based policy by Milwaukee authorities.

claim: "Last year," Obama "administration officials released into our neighborhoods more than 36,000 criminal immigrants who had nearly 88,000 convictions. The crimes included hundreds of convictions for murder, rape and kidnapping and thousands of drug-related crimes."
rationale: The claim misstates and misattributes official data: fact-checkers and ICE reporting show that the headline numbers are misleading, rely on ambiguous timeframes and counting methods (multiple convictions per person), and omit context about why individuals were released. Independent analyses found the totals were either double-counted, included low-level offenses, or referred to releases from criminal custody rather than ICE proactively 'releasing into our neighborhoods.'

claim: "Crisis actor in Germany forgets he’s filming on TV."
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable evidence that a named "crisis actor" in Germany was caught on TV 'forgetting' he was filming; such allegations are common internet conspiracy-meme claims that have been repeatedly debunked. Without a specific, verifiable incident reported by reliable news or sourced footage, the claim is unsubstantiated and likely a misinterpretation or misinformation.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi diverted "$2.4 billion from Social Security to cover impeachment costs."
rationale: There is no evidence that Nancy Pelosi diverted $2.4 billion from Social Security for impeachment costs. Social Security benefits are financed by dedicated payroll taxes and held in trust funds; neither the Speaker nor Congress can lawfully redirect those funds outside of a statute changing benefits or financing. Impeachment-related expenses were paid through congressional appropriations and were not on the order of billions diverted from Social Security.

claim: Elderly people were "beat up by a BLM hate group" for being white.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a coordinated 'BLM hate group' systematically beat up elderly people for being white. While isolated incidents of violence have occurred at protests, reputable news outlets and fact-checkers have not substantiated claims of organized, race-targeted attacks by Black Lives Matter on elderly white people.

claim: "Last year, (Bill McCollum) spent more than $2.2 million dollars to produce and air campaign-style TV ads where you were featured in almost every frame."
rationale: The claim is vague and lacks corroboration: it names Bill McCollum, a known politician, but gives no verifiable attribution or timeframe and uses the ambiguous pronoun “you.” There are no widely reported or publicly available campaign finance records attributing a personal expenditure of more than $2.2 million by McCollum last year to produce and air ads centered on a specific individual, so the specific factual assertion cannot be supported.

claim: State Rep. Elena Parent "supported Governor Nathan Deal’s plan to slash the HOPE scholarship."
rationale: Available public record and contemporaneous reporting indicate Elena Parent, a Democratic member of Georgia’s legislature, opposed Governor Nathan Deal’s proposed reductions to the HOPE scholarship rather than supporting them. Democrats in the legislature publicly criticized those cuts, and Parent was not a proponent of Deal’s plan.

claim: Says there is proof Democrats hired actors to plan violence in Charlottesville.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Democrats hired actors to plan the violence in Charlottesville. Multiple reputable news investigations and independent fact-checkers have debunked claims about paid actors and attribute the rally and associated violence to white supremacist and extremist organizers.

claim: U.S. Rep. Phil Gingrey wants public schools to teach women to "stay in their place."
rationale: There is no reputable evidence that Rep. Phil Gingrey called for public schools to teach women to 'stay in their place.' Major news outlets and fact-checkers do not document such a statement, so the claim appears to be a misquotation or fabrication rather than a verified quote.

claim: "In her campaign for president, Hillary Clinton has received $100 million in contributions from Wall Street and hedge funds."
rationale: Public campaign finance records and analyses do not support a claim that Hillary Clinton's campaign directly received $100 million from Wall Street and hedge funds. While the finance sector and wealthy hedge-fund donors contributed substantially and independent groups backed by those interests spent large sums on her behalf, direct contributions to her campaign and joint committees from that industry were well below $100 million.

claim: "Our conservative Georgia values are under attack" ... (People) are "calling for the removal of George Washington and Thomas Jefferson statues."
rationale: The statement mixes a subjective political claim (“conservative Georgia values are under attack”) with an asserted factual claim that people are calling for removal of George Washington and Thomas Jefferson statues in Georgia. While nationwide debates have targeted some historical monuments, there is no clear evidence that organized calls in Georgia specifically demanded removal of Washington and Jefferson statues; the first part is an opinion rather than verifiable fact.

claim: "President Obama pledged to go through the budget 'line by line,' but on his watch, non-defense spending has spiraled out of control, increasing by 67 percent in the last year alone."
rationale: President Obama did pledge a "line-by-line" review of the budget early in his administration, but the claim that non-defense spending "increasing by 67 percent in the last year alone" is incorrect. Federal budget data from OMB/CBO do not show a single-year surge of 67% in total non-defense (or non-defense discretionary) spending; year-to-year changes were far smaller even during stimulus and recession-response years. The 67% figure appears to be a mischaracterization or taken out of context from a narrow program category rather than overall non-defense spending.

claim: "Here in Florida, despite 14 school shootings in eight years, we still have some of the weakest gun laws in the nation."
rationale: The statement mixes an unsupported numeric claim and a subjective ranking. Counts of 'school shootings' depend heavily on the definition and precise eight-year period, so the '14 in eight years' figure cannot be confirmed without a specified timeframe and source; similarly, whether Florida has 'some of the weakest gun laws' depends on which laws and which ranking are used and ignores reforms enacted after 2018. Because the claim lacks clear sourcing and context, it is not verifiable as stated.

claim: "Drug overdose deaths decreased in 2018 for the first time in 30 years."
rationale: The statement is misleading as written. National overdose death totals did not show a clear, definitive nationwide drop in 2018 that represented the first decline in 30 years — trends were driven by different substances (prescription opioids vs synthetic opioids) and provisional counts and later revisions complicate comparisons. Any narrow reports of small declines in some categories or locales do not support the broad claim as a definitive national first decrease in three decades.

claim: "The average cost of child care in this country is more than what it costs to send a child to college for one year."
rationale: The claim is untestable as written because it does not specify which country; cost relationships vary widely. In many countries, especially high-income ones, a single year of college (tuition and fees, often excluding room and board) typically costs as much as or more than average annual child care, though there are exceptions depending on public subsidies, in‑state tuition, and type of care. A blanket statement that child care costs more than one year of college for 'this country' is therefore not supported.

claim: Says the CBO said "it's not that people are getting pushed off a plan; it's that people will choose not to buy something they don't like or want."
rationale: I find no evidence that the Congressional Budget Office used that exact dismissive wording. The CBO typically issues measured analytic statements about coverage changes (not colloquial lines like ‘people will choose not to buy something they don't like or want’) and its published reports describe factors like cost, penalties, and eligibility affecting enrollment rather than framing it solely as consumer preference.

claim: Says U.S. Senate opponent Tommy Thompson "personally made over $3 million" from a federal contract granted to his healthcare company, but left  9/11 first responders "without the care they were promised."
rationale: I found no reliable evidence that former Wisconsin governor Tommy Thompson personally pocketed more than $3 million from a federal contract to a healthcare company he controlled, nor clear documentation that he directly left 9/11 first responders without promised care. The allegation appears to conflate possible corporate contract totals or association with outcomes for responders without producing verifiable contract, payment, or investigative reporting tying Thompson to those specific personal profits or deliberate denials of care.

claim: "Jurisdictions representing about 80% of WI residents have passed referendums or resolutions in favor of fair maps."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported by available public tallies. Numerous Wisconsin cities, towns and counties have passed nonbinding 'fair maps' resolutions or advisory referendums, but those actions have mostly been in smaller jurisdictions and reputable counts do not show they represent roughly 80% of the state population. Without a clear date and a precise methodology for how population was attributed, the 80% figure appears to overstate the population coverage.

claim: Says Donald Trump "spent the least amount of money of any of the competitive primary contenders that he beat so badly."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented because it fails to specify which primary contest, which opponents, and which spending measure (total campaign expenditures, advertising, or personal loans). Public campaign-finance records and reporting show Trump’s spending relative to opponents varied by cycle and by spending category, so he did not universally spend the least against every competitive rival he defeated. Without that context the blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: Says Matt Rosendale "consistently supported land use rules that would help developers like him and hurt farmers in Montana."
rationale: The claim is a broad, evaluative characterization that cannot be fully substantiated as stated. While Matt Rosendale is a businessman and has supported property‑rights and deregulatory measures that critics say favor developers, available records show a mixed set of votes and proposals rather than a clear, consistent pattern of supporting land‑use rules that demonstrably harmed Montana farmers statewide.

claim: "There are only about 10 people in the United States Senate who have any real business experience."
rationale: This claim is a substantial understatement. A large share of the 100 U.S. senators have prior careers as corporate executives, entrepreneurs, finance professionals, investors, or small‑business owners, so the number with 'real business experience' is well above about ten. While exact counts depend on how one defines 'real business experience,' it is not plausibly limited to only ~10 senators.

claim: "The government does not need a warrant to read your old emails."
rationale: The statement is overly broad and therefore false in most modern legal contexts. In the U.S., the Fourth Amendment plus statutes and court rulings mean the government generally needs a warrant or comparable court authorization to obtain the content of emails; while older provisions of the 1986 Electronic Communications Privacy Act allowed weaker process for long‑stored messages, subsequent court decisions and the 2018 CLOUD Act have changed and clarified those rules. Exceptions and different standards can apply in limited circumstances, but it is not correct to say the government categorically does not need a warrant.

claim: "The average student will be spending $1,700 to $1,800 more during the life of their loan because of this surcharge."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as given because it lacks critical context (which surcharge, what loan balance, interest rate, repayment plan, and which 'average student' cohort). The additional lifetime cost from any surcharge depends on loan principal, surcharge rate, capitalization rules, and repayment term, so a single $1,700–$1,800 figure is not generally supportable without the underlying assumptions and calculations.

claim: "We haven’t seen a single American megachurch offer anything to help Ukrainians."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: numerous large U.S. churches and faith-based organizations publicly organized fundraisers, donation drives, and partnered with relief groups to send aid, shelter refugees, and provide financial support for Ukrainians after the 2022 invasion. It is highly unlikely that not a single American megachurch offered any assistance.

claim: "No one questioned that she (Judge Sotomayor) was out of the mainstream."
rationale: The claim’s absolute phrasing — that “no one questioned” Sotomayor being out of the mainstream — is incorrect. During her confirmation and in commentary about her judicial record, some politicians, conservative commentators, and legal critics explicitly argued she was outside mainstream judicial norms, while others defended her as mainstream, so it is not true that nobody questioned it.

claim: Says Rep. Betty Sutton supports allowing "welfare fund withdrawals from strip clubs, casinos and liquor stores."
rationale: This claim misrepresents Sutton's position. Fact-checkers found she did not advocate permitting welfare benefits to be withdrawn specifically at strip clubs, casinos, or liquor stores; debates at the time concerned broader EBT/ATM access in retail settings and existing rules already bar using SNAP for alcohol or gambling. The attack conflated expanded cash-access proposals with authorization to use benefits at prohibited venues.

claim: Says Rob Portman "said the auto rescue was a lousy deal for Ohio."
rationale: I find no verifiable record that Rob Portman used the exact phrase 'the auto rescue was a lousy deal for Ohio.' While Portman has criticized auto-industry bailouts in various contexts, attributing this specific quote to him appears unverified and may be a paraphrase or misattribution. Without a reliable source showing he said those exact words, the claim is not supported.

claim: If Joe Biden can’t serve his full term, Kamala Harris "cannot by constitutional law become president."
rationale: The U.S. Constitution and federal law provide that the vice president becomes president if the president dies, resigns, or is removed, and may serve as acting president under the 25th Amendment if the president is incapacitated. The Presidential Succession Act and the 25th Amendment explicitly enable the vice president to assume the presidency, so Kamala Harris can become president by constitutional law if Joe Biden cannot finish his term.

claim: 110 people a day move to Austin.
rationale: The claim is presented as an unqualified current fact but provides no timeframe or whether it refers to the city proper or the metropolitan area and whether it means net gain or gross arrivals. Reported migration figures for Austin have varied year to year and while some past periods had roughly on the order of tens of thousands of net new residents annually (which could average near 100/day), the statement as written is not verifiable and is misleading without context.

claim: The federal government requires "COVID passports to visit the movies."
rationale: There is no general federal requirement that people present a COVID 'passport' to attend movies. In countries like the United States, proof-of-vaccination mandates for indoor entertainment were set by states, local governments, or individual businesses, while federal vaccine requirements were limited to specific contexts (federal employees/contractors or certain travel rules) rather than blanket rules for movie theaters.

claim: Says as a result of the national health care reform, "the Congressional Budget Office says we save $250 million over the first 10 years. Over the next 10 years, we save $1.2 trillion in savings in terms of health care."
rationale: The Congressional Budget Office did not report a $250 million savings in the first ten years followed by $1.2 trillion in the next ten for U.S. national health reform. CBO scores of the Affordable Care Act showed net federal deficit reductions on the order of hundreds of billions over the first decade and different multi-decade impacts depending on what was measured (deficit, Medicare savings, or total health spending); the claim's magnitudes, units (million vs billion), and timeframes do not match published CBO analyses.

claim: "As Ohio treasurer, Josh Mandel loaned your money to Chinese business interests, and Mandel opposed a bill holding Communist China accountable when they cheated and stole American jobs."
rationale: The claim conflates and overstates facts. As Ohio treasurer Mandel oversaw investments in broadly managed state funds that sometimes had indirect exposure to Chinese companies through mutual/index funds or foreign bonds, but there is no evidence he personally 'loaned your money' directly to Chinese business interests. Likewise, public records and reporting do not support a clear finding that he opposed legislation specifically intended to hold China accountable; in fact Mandel has publicly taken tough rhetoric on China at times. The statement is therefore misleading and inaccurate as presented.

claim: "Seventy percent of the people in the state of New Jersey want marriage equality."
rationale: The claim gives a specific percentage for New Jersey without citing a source or date, so it cannot be independently verified. Public opinion on marriage equality has varied over time and across polls and subpopulations (adults, registered voters, likely voters), so asserting a precise 70% figure for the whole state as a current fact is unsupported.

claim: A photo shows "the Lincoln Memorial. His head damaged and defaced."
rationale: There are no credible news reports or statements from the National Park Service documenting the Lincoln Memorial's head being physically damaged or defaced; such a conspicuous act would have generated wide coverage. Similar viral images have previously been shown to be digitally altered or miscaptioned, so the claim that a photo legitimately shows the statue's head damaged is not supported.

claim: "Eleven individuals who make over $30 million each got $22 million credit" from Wisconsin's manufacturing and agriculture tax credit.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that eleven individuals each making over $30 million received a $22 million credit from Wisconsin’s Manufacturing and Agriculture Tax Credit. The credit is a business/pass-through tax benefit allocated to owners or entities, and reporting/public tax data do not corroborate this specific, concentrated payment as stated.

claim: Six states "decided to stop counting" votes as Donald Trump was "headed for a win" on election night.
rationale: No credible evidence shows six states 'decided to stop counting' votes while Trump was 'headed for a win.' Election officials and state authorities reported that counting continued in all states per law; what circulated as 'stopping' refers at most to brief procedural pauses or the end of polling on election night, not a decision to cease tallying ballots. Countdowns and delays were due to legal deadlines for mail ballots, processing time, or equipment issues, not a coordinated halt to counting.

claim: Bath and Body Works products are not recommended during pregnancy because they are suspected of "damaging fertility or the unborn child."
rationale: There is no authoritative medical or regulatory guidance that broadly recommends avoiding Bath & Body Works products during pregnancy because the brand is suspected of damaging fertility or the unborn child. While some ingredients found in some personal-care products (e.g., certain phthalates or concentrated essential oils) have raised caution in pregnancy, Bath & Body Works as a whole is not officially flagged by health agencies as universally contraindicated and clear evidence of reproductive harm from typical use is lacking.

claim: A provision of the Senate immigration bill would require you to have government permission to get a second job.
rationale: No mainstream Senate immigration bill has a provision requiring the general public to obtain government permission to take a second job; immigration legislation typically governs noncitizens' work authorization rather than restricting citizens from holding multiple jobs. The confusion likely arises because certain nonimmigrant visa categories (for example H‑1B) already limit employment to authorized employers and would require authorization to take additional work.

claim: Under Mayor Angel Taveras "Providence’s bond rating was downgraded from A to BBB, two steps above junk-bond status."
rationale: The claim is not supported as stated. While Providence did face credit-pressure and at least one downgrade during Mayor Taveras’s tenure, public reporting shows agency-specific notch changes and does not clearly document a straight A → BBB downgrade labeled as "two steps above junk." The phrase conflates different agencies' notch systems and misstates investment-grade thresholds.

claim: Video shows Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer laughing at Novak Djokovic after he was stuck in an Australian airport.
rationale: There is no credible, verified footage showing Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer laughing at Novak Djokovic after his Australian visa/detention episode. Multiple fact-checks and news reports found the circulated clips were misattributed or edited and originate from unrelated times or show lookalikes; Nadal and Federer publicly expressed sympathy rather than mocking him.

claim: Jim Renacci "voted repeatedly to end Medicare."
rationale: Jim Renacci did not cast votes to literally abolish Medicare outright. While he supported Republican budgets and proposals that would have changed Medicare’s financing (for example backing efforts to move toward premium-support/privatization and repealing Affordable Care Act provisions), those are not the same as votes to 'end Medicare' entirely. Characterizing those votes as 'repeatedly voting to end Medicare' is misleading.

claim: "We know how to stop AIDS: persuade men not to have sex with men."
rationale: The claim is false because HIV/AIDS is transmitted through multiple routes (heterosexual sex, injection drug use, mother-to-child transmission, contaminated blood) and cannot be ended by targeting only sexual behavior among men who have sex with men. Evidence-based prevention (condoms, testing, antiretroviral treatment as prevention, pre-exposure prophylaxis, syringe programs, and structural interventions) is required, and stigmatizing or singular behavioral campaigns have historically failed or worsened outcomes.

claim: Says President Barack Obama "came into office very concerned about" wiretappings but "then he became president of the United States, he got all the briefings … (and) he decided … the balance is probably pretty appropriately struck."
rationale: The specific quoted phrasing cannot be reliably attributed to President Obama and I find no authoritative source confirming he said those exact words. While Obama publicly expressed privacy concerns early in his presidency and later authorized/accepted certain intelligence practices after briefings, the claim presents an unverified direct quote and attribution. Because the precise quotation and speaker are not corroborated, it should be treated as false until a reliable source is provided.

claim: The IRS is "going to be in charge of our health care."
rationale: The IRS is not responsible for running or delivering health care. Its involvement is limited to tax administration and enforcement (for example, handling premium tax credit reconciliations, ACA-related reporting, and past individual mandate penalty collection), while federal health programs and regulation are administered by HHS/CMS and state agencies.

claim: "68% error rate in Michigan Voting Machines. Should be, by law, a tiny percentage of one percent."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official audit showing a 68% error rate for Michigan voting machines; such extreme figures have been repeatedly debunked and typically arise from misread or out-of-context data. Certified voting equipment is federally and state tested and Michigan requires post-election audits and recount procedures; real-world tabulation discrepancies are generally a tiny fraction of a percent, not tens of percent.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "paid only 14 percent in taxes — probably less than you."
rationale: Romney’s publicly released returns showed an effective federal tax rate around 13–15% in certain years (often cited as about 14% for 2011), but the claim as stated is misleading because it omits the year, whether it refers to federal vs. total tax, and uses a speculative "probably less than you" comparison that depends on anyone’s individual income and deductions. Using a single-year effective rate without context misrepresents his overall tax picture.

claim: Under the Iran nuclear deal, "we give them $150 billion, we get nothing."
rationale: The claim is misleading: the U.S. did not directly give Iran $150 billion in cash under the 2015 JCPOA. The agreement provided sanctions relief and access to previously frozen Iranian assets held abroad (estimates of freely accessible funds vary, often cited roughly $100–150 billion), and in return Iran accepted legally binding limits on its nuclear program, inspections by the IAEA, and verification measures. It is therefore incorrect to say we simply 'give them $150 billion' and 'get nothing.'

claim: Foxconn hasn't hit job targets on its massive Wisconsin factory because "No. 1, you had a pandemic."
rationale: While Foxconn has indeed fallen far short of its originally advertised Wisconsin job targets and cited the COVID-19 pandemic as a factor, independent reporting and state audits show the shortfall also reflects deliberate scale‑backs, changes in planned production, and shifts in corporate strategy. The pandemic was a contributing factor but not the sole or primary documented cause of the missed targets.

claim: The average Georgia family makes $6,000 less than the average family did 10 years ago when inflation is factored in.
rationale: The statement is unsupported as written because it fails to specify which 10-year period, which definition of "average family" (mean vs median), or which inflation index was used. Public income series (e.g., U.S. Census/ACS and BEA) do not consistently show a uniform $6,000 real decline for Georgia families across recent decades; trends vary by period and measure. Without a clear timeframe and data source, the claim is unverified and likely false.

claim: "In two terms in the Missouri General Assembly, Jason Kander passed ZERO bills that were signed into law."
rationale: This claim is incorrect: contemporary legislative records and multiple fact-checks indicate Jason Kander had at least one bill that became law during his two terms in the Missouri House. The assertion that he passed zero bills ignores enacted legislation he sponsored or was the primary mover of while serving 2009–2013.

claim: A collection of photos shows animals caught in the Australia wildfires.
rationale: Numerous reputable news organizations, photographers and wildlife groups published photo galleries showing animals injured, killed, or fleeing during the 2019–2020 Australian bushfires. While a subset of individual images circulated online were later found to be misattributed, the general claim that collections of photos depict animals caught in the Australian wildfires is supported by wide documentation.

claim: "House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said this week that the Democrats have to pass their terrible health care bill so that the American people can actually find out what's in it."
rationale: This is a misquote and misleadingly framed. Pelosi did famously say in 2010 a variant—"We have to pass the bill so that you can find out what's in it"—but she did not call it a "terrible health care bill," nor is there evidence she made the exact quoted sentence "this week." The claim mixes editorial language and timing that are not supported by the public record.

claim: Rare is the president "who's passed more legislation, who's done more things than what we've done, between the executive orders and the job-killing regulations that have been terminated."
rationale: The statement is a vague, comparative boast that cannot be verified as written and is misleading: presidents do not 'pass' legislation (Congress does), and claims about being unusually productive require clear metrics and timeframes. Without specific counts of laws, executive orders, and regulatory actions and a defined comparison set, the claim is unsubstantiated and therefore false as a factual assertion.

claim: "I was filibustered."
rationale: The statement 'I was filibustered' is unverified because it lacks any identifying details (who, when, in which legislative body, or which measure). Being 'filibustered' is a specific procedural outcome that can be confirmed with legislative records, cloture votes, or contemporaneous reporting. Without those specifics or supporting evidence, the claim cannot be accepted as true.

claim: A monthly "police and fire protection fee" on all Wisconsin phone bills does nothing to support police and fire.
rationale: Wisconsin levies a statutorily authorized "police and fire protection" surcharge on phone bills that is collected and distributed to local governments to help fund public safety and emergency services. While there are periodic disputes and complaints about how much revenue reaches specific departments or how funds are allocated, it is inaccurate to say the fee "does nothing" to support police and fire.

claim: "Obama certificate a fake."
rationale: Extensive official documentation and independent verification show Barack Obama's birth certificate is genuine. The State of Hawaii released his long-form birth certificate in 2011 and Hawaiian officials, as well as multiple fact-checkers and courts, found no evidence of forgery. Claims that the certificate is fake have been repeatedly debunked.

claim: Obamacare "will provide insurance to all non-U.S. residents, even if they are here illegally."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act does not extend marketplace subsidies or Medicaid coverage to undocumented immigrants. Eligibility for ACA exchanges and premium tax credits is limited to U.S. citizens and lawfully present immigrants; undocumented persons are generally excluded, though emergency Medicaid and limited state programs may still apply.

claim: "Seventy of Ohio's 88 counties now have more than 25 percent of their residents eligible for emergency food."
rationale: I cannot find authoritative evidence that 70 of Ohio’s 88 counties have over 25% of residents eligible for emergency food; typical measures (food insecurity or SNAP eligibility/participation) for Ohio and most counties are well below 25% in many places and vary by county. The claim is specific and would require a named study or state data source, which is not provided, so it appears unlikely and unverified.

claim: The 2018 Academy Awards show was the "lowest rated Oscars in HISTORY."
rationale: While the 2018 Oscars drew unusually low ratings (about 26.5 million viewers) and was widely reported at the time as the lowest-rated ceremony up to that date, subsequent telecasts have had even lower viewership (for example the 2021 ceremony drew a much smaller audience). Therefore the absolute statement that the 2018 show was the lowest-rated in history is no longer true.

claim: Says with his guilty impeachment vote, Senator Mitt Romney "could be removed from office."
rationale: A senator cannot be removed from office simply for casting a 'guilty' vote in an impeachment trial of another official. The Constitution’s impeachment removal applies to officers who are impeached by the House and convicted by the Senate; members of Congress are removed by their own chamber through expulsion (two‑thirds) or by separate legal processes. Historical practice and constitutional text do not support removal of a senator as a consequence of how they voted in someone else’s impeachment trial.

claim: Says Joe Biden wants to "defund the police."
rationale: Joe Biden has repeatedly said he does not support the 'defund the police' slogan or cutting police funding; his campaign and administration have advocated policing reforms and investments in community policing and public safety rather than abolition or wholesale defunding. Public statements and policy proposals from Biden contrast with the 'defund' demand promoted by some activists.

claim: "We are currently using only around 20% of our testing capacity."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as written because it gives no jurisdiction, time period, or definition of 'testing capacity' (type of test, labs included, etc.). Testing utilization rates vary widely by country, region, and date, and authoritative health agencies or lab reports are needed to support a specific 20% figure.

claim: Emails show Democrats, Hillary Clinton and George Soros instigated and orchestrated racial protests in Charlottesville by trying to "control" and keep people "desperate."
rationale: There is no credible evidence in released emails or official investigations that Democrats, Hillary Clinton, or George Soros instigated or orchestrated the Charlottesville protests. The August 2017 'Unite the Right' rally was organized by white nationalist groups, and multiple fact-checks and law-enforcement reviews found no support for a conspiracy tying Clinton, Democrats, or Soros to orchestrating the events. Assertions rest on vague or misinterpreted references to unspecified 'emails' and have been widely debunked.

claim: "CDC confesses: Vaccines are failing, and the vaxxed can be superspreaders."
rationale: The CDC has not 'confessed' that vaccines are failing; COVID-19 vaccines remain effective at preventing severe illness, hospitalization, and death. The agency has acknowledged that vaccinated people can sometimes become infected (breakthrough infections) and transmit the virus—especially with highly transmissible variants— but that does not equate to vaccines failing or that the vaccinated are uniquely or primarily 'superspreaders.'

claim: "Since the passage of Proposition 47 by voters in 2014 and the signing of AB 109 in 2011, violent crime has been on the rise in California, up 12 percent in 2015 statewide according to the FBI."
rationale: The FBI's 2015 data did not report a 12% statewide increase in California violent crime; the national violent crime increase in 2015 was about 4% and California's change was smaller and uneven across jurisdictions. Moreover, the FBI UCR data do not attribute causation to specific laws, so linking the rise directly to AB 109 (2011) and Proposition 47 (2014) is unsupported.

claim: The "stand your ground" law caused the shooting death of Trayvon Martin.
rationale: The fatal shooting was carried out by George Zimmerman in 2012; although Florida had a "Stand Your Ground" statute and Zimmerman’s defense asserted self-defense, there is no definitive evidence that the law caused him to shoot. The statute may have affected charging decisions, investigation and legal defenses, but attributing direct causation of the act to the law is speculative and not established.

claim: "As of today, no one has the right to film or photograph Mr. Biden as he climbs the flight of stairs. New White House spokesman orders!!?"
rationale: There is no evidence of a new blanket White House order that gives 'no one' the right to photograph or film President Biden climbing stairs. While the Secret Service and White House can restrict access in secured areas and set press-pool rules, that is not the same as a universal prohibition on all photography or filming in every context.

claim: "Texas legislators have filed voucher proposals in every legislative session since 1995, but all of them have failed to become law."
rationale: While Texas lawmakers have repeatedly filed school voucher and school-choice proposals across many legislative sessions, the blanket statement that every such proposal since 1995 has failed is unlikely to be correct. Texas has enacted various school-choice and voucher-like measures and subsidies (including some targeted programs and tax-credit scholarship mechanisms) over the years, so not all proposals have uniformly failed. The claim overstates both the uniformity and the outcome of legislative activity.

claim: Georgia has some of the best maintained roads in America.
rationale: The claim is vague but objective national assessments and state DOT reports do not typically rank Georgia among the top states for overall road pavement condition or maintenance. Georgia has documented pavement and congestion problems and ongoing infrastructure needs in multiple reports, so claiming it has "some of the best maintained roads in America" is not supported by broad comparative evidence.

claim: Says when New Jersey adopted guaranteed coverage and cost provisions without a mandate individual health insurance market rates "doubled or tripled" and enrollment dropped from 180,000 people to 80,000 people.
rationale: This claim overstates and simplifies the New Jersey experience. New Jersey’s early-1990s move to guaranteed-issue and community-rating coincided with some premium increases and a drop in individual-market enrollment, but independent analyses show the magnitude and causes are disputed — premiums did not uniformly 'double or triple' and enrollment changes vary by data source and timeframe rather than matching the exact 180,000→80,000 drop solely attributable to those rules.

claim: "A black woman in New York City is 12 times more likely to die in childbirth than a white woman."
rationale: The claim states a blanket 12-fold difference but is not supported as a general, current fact. Public-health data consistently show Black women face substantially higher maternal mortality than white women, but typical reported ratios are around 3–4 times nationally and NYC estimates vary by year and by how deaths are counted; a 12x figure reflects specific small-sample years or particular definitions rather than a general rule.

claim: "Wisconsin is #1 in the Midwest for personal income growth over the year."
rationale: The statement gives no year or data source and is therefore unsupported; state personal income growth rankings change year to year. Official data (e.g., BEA) do not consistently list Wisconsin as the top Midwestern state for annual personal income growth, and other states have led in different years.

claim: "Biden’s banking nominee demands all ‘private bank accounts’ be eliminated"
rationale: This is a misleading overstatement. The nominee most commonly associated with such claims (Saule Omarova) proposed reforms including a 'public option' of central bank accounts and tighter regulation of bank activities in academic work and testimony, but she did not demand the elimination of all private bank accounts and explicitly denied proposals to abolish private banks during her confirmation process.

claim: Photo shows Joe Biden’s license plate says "THEBIGGUY."
rationale: The claim misattributes a vanity-plate photo to Joe Biden himself. The president travels in official, Secret Service-protected vehicles with government plates, and fact-checkers have reported that the pictured plate belonged to another nearby vehicle or supporter, not Biden’s personal or presidential car.

claim: "@BernieSanders receives strong support from the conservative & most rural part of Vermont."
rationale: Bernie Sanders is popular statewide in Vermont and performs well in many rural areas, but the state’s most consistently conservative, rural enclaves tend to lean Republican and are not reliably strong backers of a self-described democratic socialist. Sanders often wins broad rural support and independents, yet it is inaccurate to say he specifically receives strong support from the most conservative parts of the state.

claim: "I'm not taking any corporate PAC money."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable without naming the speaker and the time period; campaign finance claims require checking FEC and campaign filings. Also the phrase "corporate PAC money" is ambiguous—corporations cannot give directly but corporate-affiliated PACs, party committees, joint fundraising, and transfers can result in similar funding—so I cannot confirm the claim as stated.

claim: Hank Aaron’s death was caused by a COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hank Aaron’s death was caused by a COVID-19 vaccine. Public reporting and statements from family and fact‑checking organizations found only a temporal coincidence (he had received a first dose earlier in January 2021) and did not establish a causal link between vaccination and his death.

claim: "Over the last several years, 40 percent (of) the jobs created in Texas were created for illegal aliens."
rationale: There is no evidence that 40% of jobs created in Texas were for undocumented immigrants. Labor agencies do not track hires by immigration status, independent estimates put unauthorized workers as a small (single-digit) share of the workforce in Texas, and fact-checkers have rejected similar 40% claims as unsupported or misleading.

claim: Abigail Spanberger and other Democrats "voted to spend public funds on their political campaigns; up to $5 million..."
rationale: There is no evidence that Rep. Abigail Spanberger or other House Democrats voted to authorize direct public funding of their own political campaigns up to $5 million. U.S. law does not provide general public campaign funding for House or Senate campaigns (public financing is limited and largely obsolete for presidential races), and a vote creating a $5 million public-pay provision for members' campaigns would be widely documented but is not found. The claim appears to be a mischaracterization or exaggeration of some other vote or funding item.

claim: "59 people die as pastor gives them dettol to drink in church to prevent coronavirus."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting from major news outlets or fact-checking organizations verifying that 59 people died after a pastor told them to drink Dettol to prevent coronavirus. Viral posts with this claim appear to be unverified or conflated with other unrelated poisoning incidents; while ingestion of disinfectant is dangerous, the specific mass-fatality story is unsupported.

claim: "A rural hospital in Missouri closes every 8 months. The legislature’s failure to expand Medicaid has brought crisis to many of Missouri’s rural health care providers."
rationale: The specific numeric claim that “a rural hospital in Missouri closes every 8 months” is not supported by publicly available data and appears to be an oversimplification; Missouri has seen rural hospital closures but not at a reliably documented 8‑month cadence. It is true that before voters approved Medicaid expansion in 2020 the legislature had repeatedly declined expansion and that lack of Medicaid coverage contributed to financial strain on many rural providers, but closures result from multiple factors and cannot be attributed solely to the legislature’s stance.

claim: Says President Barack Obama told a room of students, "Children, every time I clap my hands together, a child in America dies from gun violence," and then a child told him he could solve the problem by not clapping any more.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or news record that President Obama said this; independent fact-checkers and news archives have traced the anecdote to satire and viral fabrication rather than an actual speech. The implausible, joke-like exchange matches patterns of invented anecdotes often attributed to public figures.

claim: "Barnes opposed the creation of the HOPE Scholarship and campaigned against Zell Miller on the issue."
rationale: The HOPE Scholarship was created in 1993 under Governor Zell Miller and had broad bipartisan support in Georgia; Roy Barnes (the Georgia politician) was not a documented opponent of its creation nor is he known to have run a campaign specifically against Miller over HOPE. Barnes later served as governor and focused on education policy, but historical records do not show him opposing the establishment of HOPE.

claim: "They eliminated the funding for community policing."
rationale: The statement is framed as a universal, decontextualized claim with no actor, place, or time specified. While some jurisdictions have reduced or reallocated community-policing funds, there is no broad, verifiable fact that 'they' (unspecified) eliminated funding everywhere or as a general rule.

claim: "Bill White used D.C. connections from his job in the Clinton administration to form a company that did business in the Middle East and defaulted on a $60 million loan."
rationale: There is no credible, documented evidence that the Bill White commonly referenced in U.S. politics (the former Houston mayor and gubernatorial candidate) used Clinton‑era D.C. connections to form a company that did business in the Middle East and defaulted on a $60 million loan. Contemporary news reporting and public biographies of Bill White detail his government and private‑sector roles but do not substantiate a $60 million loan default or the specific scheme described.

claim: Quotes Andy Borowitz as saying "stopping Hillary is a short-term solution. The long-term solution — and it will be more difficult — is fixing the educational system that has created so many people ignorant enough to vote for Hillary."
rationale: There is no reliable record or reputable attribution of Andy Borowitz saying this; the phrasing is inflammatory and reads like a fabricated or misattributed political insult rather than a documented Borowitz line. Borowitz is a satirist whose pieces are usually clearly labeled as satire, and this specific quote does not appear in his known columns or verified social posts.

claim: Says 2010 was the "worst year ever for America's doctors" reimbursed by Medicare.
