FEMA and federal grant programs assess and approve requests case-by-case, and historically not every state request is automatically granted or fully funded. Without a specific time period or list of requests, the blanket claim that every Texas request was fulfilled is implausible and unverifiable.

claim: Video shows a child who tested positive for COVID-19 "being separated from their parents."
rationale: There is insufficient evidence to confirm that the unnamed video actually shows a child who tested positive for COVID-19 being separated from their parents. Short online videos are frequently miscaptioned, edited, or shown out of context, and this claim lacks provenance, date, location, or corroboration from reliable authorities. Without independent verification (metadata, news reporting, or official statements) the assertion cannot be treated as fact.

claim: "Crime has been getting worse since Jerry Brown was elected governor."
rationale: The claim is an overly broad generalization that is not supported by available data: crime trends since Jerry Brown’s most recent election (2010) vary by year, crime type, and locality. Some categories and jurisdictions saw increases in certain years while others saw declines, so it is incorrect to say crime has uniformly been getting worse since he was elected.

claim: "(Ronald Reagan) raised taxes a billion dollars in his first year as governor of California."
rationale: While Ronald Reagan did approve tax increases during his time as California governor, the precise claim that he raised taxes by exactly one billion dollars in his first year is not supported by clear historical records and is misleading. Contemporary accounts and later fact-checking show he signed tax measures during his governorship but the timing and amounts do not cleanly match the asserted $1 billion in that first year.

claim: "Chris Christie has led New Jersey to a record-breaking 9 credit downgrades."
rationale: While New Jersey experienced multiple credit downgrades during Chris Christie’s time as governor, authoritative records do not support the specific claim that he led the state to a "record-breaking 9" state-level downgrades. Major rating agencies (S&P, Moody’s, Fitch) downgraded New Jersey’s general obligation or other credits on several occasions, but the number of distinct state GO downgrades attributed to his tenure is far fewer and the "9" figure appears to double-count different agencies, instruments, or interim actions. The statement is therefore misleading and unsupported as stated.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to get rid of the federal minimum wage."
rationale: Donald Trump has on multiple recorded occasions said he would like to do away with the federal minimum wage and let individual states set wages. His public comments (especially during the 2016 campaign) explicitly expressed this preference, though he has also made inconsistent remarks about modest federal increases at other times.

claim: "Bill Gates talked about using vaccines to control population growth" in an "unedited 2010 TED Talk video"
rationale: In his 2010 TED Talk Bill Gates said that improving child health (including vaccines) helps reduce population growth because fewer children die and families choose to have fewer children; that line appears in the unedited talk in its proper context. He framed vaccines as part of health interventions that lower child mortality and thereby slow population growth, not as a coercive population-control scheme.

claim: Says Joe Biden’s presidential campaign donated $20 million to bail out protesters.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or campaign finance record showing Joe Biden’s presidential campaign donated $20 million to bail out protesters. Fact-checks and news reports have found this claim conflates independent donors and outside groups that supported bail funds with the official Biden campaign or DNC, which did not make such a payment.

claim: "Ten retired nuns were barred from voting in the 2008 Indiana Democratic primary."
rationale: There are no reliable contemporary news reports or official records documenting that ten retired nuns were barred from voting in the 2008 Indiana Democratic primary. An incident of that size and nature would likely have attracted local or national media coverage; the widely documented 2008 Indiana voting issues do not include this claim, so it appears unsubstantiated.

claim: "Wind powers nearly 13 million homes across the country."
rationale: If the claim is referring to the United States, it understates wind’s contribution: recent U.S. wind generation (roughly 350–450 TWh/year in recent years) divided by average household consumption (~10,000–11,000 kWh/year) implies wind could theoretically power on the order of 30–40 million homes, not nearly 13 million. The precise number varies by year and by the household consumption figure used, but 13 million is substantially lower than current estimates for U.S. wind generation.

claim: Says he would be first CPA to serve as Texas comptroller.
rationale: The assertion that he would be the first Certified Public Accountant to serve as Texas comptroller is unlikely and not supported by public historical records; past comptrollers have included individuals with accounting or financial credentials, so the "first CPA" claim appears incorrect. This statement requires checking official biographical records of prior comptrollers to confirm, but available summary histories do not clearly support the uniqueness of a CPA caller.

claim: "Barack Hussein Obama will ... force local authorities to allow Occupy protesters to live in parks."
rationale: The President does not have unilateral authority to compel state or local governments to permit encampments in municipal parks, and there is no record that the Obama administration issued an order forcing local authorities to allow Occupy protesters to live in parks. Federal power is limited to federal lands and narrow civil-rights enforcement, not blanket control over local land-use or policing decisions.

claim: Says a study indicates up to $8.5 billion in lost GDP and up to 185,000 lost jobs if Texas lawmakers approve a measure limiting transgender bathroom choices.
rationale: I cannot find a clearly attributable, reputable study that specifically concludes Texas would lose up to $8.5 billion in GDP and up to 185,000 jobs solely from approving a measure limiting transgender bathroom choices. Similar economic impact estimates have been produced for other states’ "bathroom bills" (notably North Carolina) or for broader anti-LGBT policies, so these figures may be conflated or taken out of context from a different study, timeframe, or metric.

claim: The Southern strategy is a "myth" that "never happened."
rationale: The claim is false: historians and primary sources document a deliberate Republican effort in the 1960s–70s to attract white Southern voters through appeals to race-coded themes (e.g., states' rights, law-and-order) as Democrats supported civil rights. Archival evidence (campaign memos, Nixon-era tapes), contemporary political strategy accounts, and electoral data showing a durable white Southern shift to the GOP support that the 'Southern strategy' occurred. While scholars debate emphasis and motives and note the strategy used coded rather than always overt racial language, the overall phenomenon is well-documented.

claim: Under the GOP tax law, "if you live in Hinsdale, Illinois … you are now being double-taxed to the tune of $35,000."
rationale: This statement is misleading. The 2017 GOP tax law capped the state-and-local-tax (SALT) deduction at $10,000, which can raise federal tax liability for some high‑tax-area taxpayers, but it does not create a universal or uniform “double‑tax” of $35,000 for Hinsdale residents; actual federal tax increases depend on income, deductions, and marginal rates and are typically much smaller than $35,000 for most households.

claim: Says U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson wants to put 100,000 troops, including 25,000 Americans, "into the area where ISIS is."
rationale: There is no reliable record that Sen. Ron Johnson publicly advocated deploying 100,000 troops with 25,000 U.S. servicemembers into areas where ISIS operates. Johnson has occasionally supported arming local forces and limited U.S. involvement against ISIS, but proposing a 25,000-person U.S. ground contingent within a 100,000-troop force would be a notable and widely reported position that lacks corroborating sources.

claim: "For the first time in history, Wisconsin has more government jobs than manufacturing jobs."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Wisconsin has, for the first time in its history, shifted to more government jobs than manufacturing jobs. Manufacturing has been a historically large employer in Wisconsin and, while manufacturing employment has declined in recent years, claims of a historic crossover require specific year-by-year state labor data that are not supported here.

claim: "The State of Texas is funding … women’s health services at historically high levels; they just increased their level another $50 million for the next two years."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and I cannot verify that Texas is funding women's health “at historically high levels” nor confirm a recent, specific $50 million increase for the next two years. Texas budgets and program names (e.g., Healthy Texas Women, family-planning programs) have seen funding changes, but the assertion’s exact dollar amount and characterization lack clear, corroborating budget documents or authoritative announcements.

claim: "The labor participation rate is at an all-time low."
rationale: The claim is presented without a country or date and therefore cannot be taken as a factual universal statement. For the United States — the most common reference for this metric — the labor force participation rate fell sharply during the 2020 COVID shock but is not at an all-time historic low (mid-20th-century levels were lower and recent values have recovered from the deepest pandemic troughs).

claim: Says there’s an 800 number you can call to track the status of your stimulus check.
rationale: There was no official dedicated 800-number issued for checking the status of COVID stimulus (Economic Impact) payments; the IRS provided an online 'Get My Payment' tool and limited general phone assistance for taxpayers but not a single call-in status line. Many scammers advertised 800 numbers claiming to track payments, and the IRS warned against calling or giving personal information to such numbers.

claim: "Since 1970, the Clean Air Act has reduced toxic and health-threatening air pollution by 60 percent while our economy has grown more than 200 percent."
rationale: EPA and other government analyses report that aggregate emissions of key air pollutants (commonly the six criteria pollutants) have fallen by roughly 60% or more since 1970, while U.S. economic output (real GDP) has increased by over 200% in the same period. The reductions are widely attributed to the Clean Air Act and its implementing regulations.

claim: "At the Democratic convention, the Pledge of Allegiance was read with the words 'under God' removed."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported as a blanket fact. While individual attendees or speakers at various Democratic events have at times omitted the words "under God" when reciting the Pledge, there is no verified, single Democratic national convention action formally removing those words from the Pledge. Fact-checkers have described such viral claims as misleading without specifying a particular official removal.

claim: "Not even (House Intelligence Chairman Adam) Schiff’s Republican colleagues were allowed into the SCIF" during the House impeachment investigation.
rationale: Republican members of the House Intelligence Committee were generally given access to the secure SCIF and participated in many closed-door depositions during the impeachment inquiry; complaints about exclusion referred to non-committee Republicans or to specific limited moments, not a blanket ban on committee Republicans. Major GOP committee members (e.g., the ranking member and other Republicans) attended and took part in interviews and hearings.

claim: "Fifty percent of the Ottawa police force have all turned in their resignation."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official statements indicating that half of the Ottawa Police Service has turned in resignations. A resignation event on that scale would be widely reported by mainstream media and contradicted by public staffing records and union or departmental communications. The claim likely misinterprets other staffing actions (temporary leaves, retirements, or a small number of resignations).
cited_knowledge: General awareness of reporting norms and the absence of mainstream or official confirmation of mass resignations from the Ottawa Police Service.
safety_notes: The claim lacks a date and context; it could be conflating resignations with temporary absences, retirements, or actions within a specific unit. Check official Ottawa Police Service statements or reputable local news for current staffing information.

claim: Obama "said (the individual mandate) wasn't a tax."
rationale: President Obama publicly stated that the individual mandate in the Affordable Care Act was not a tax, characterizing it as a penalty/insurance requirement in speeches and press statements during the ACA debate. That factual claim about his words is supported by multiple public remarks, though courts later treated the mandate as within Congress's taxing power.

claim: "Arizona audit" shows 86,391 voters "don’t appear to exist."
rationale: The widely circulated claim misstates what the Arizona audit data showed. The audit flagged 86,391 records as not matching the specific voter file extract the auditors used, but that was a result of poor data matching, different name formats, and incomplete data supplied to auditors — not proof those people do not exist or did not legitimately vote. County and independent reviewers found many of the apparent mismatches were explainable or resolvable.

claim: When it comes to income taxes, Wisconsin is "one of the best places in the country to be poor" but "top 4 or 5 worst" for middle-income earners.
rationale: The claim presents a definitive ranking that depends heavily on the year, data source, and methodology; while Wisconsin does offer credits (like refundable credits) that can reduce tax burdens for low-income households, rankings vary and Wisconsin is not consistently identified as unequivocally “one of the best” for the poor nor always in the top 4–5 worst for middle-income earners. Different analyses (state/local combined tax share, percent of income, or absolute dollars) produce divergent results, so the blanket statement is not reliably supported.

claim: "Missouri, in general, has more crime, percentage-wise, than the rest of the country. So, we are seeing overall crime throughout the country is going down but not here in Missouri."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While Missouri’s statewide violent‑crime rate has often exceeded the national average (driven by high rates in cities like St. Louis and Kansas City), that is not uniformly true for all offense categories or every year, and national crime levels have fluctuated recently rather than steadily 'going down.' Whether Missouri is rising or falling compared with the nation depends on the specific crime type and timeframe.

claim: The Trans-Pacific Partnership "knocks out 18,000 tariffs that other countries place on American products and goods."
rationale: This is a broadly accurate restatement of claims made by TPP proponents and the U.S. Trade Representative that the TPP would eliminate tariffs on roughly 18,000 tariff lines affecting U.S. exports to partner countries. The headline number counts individual tariff lines across all partner markets; many eliminations were phased in over several years and some lines already had low or zero tariffs.

claim: Says Georgia ranks "near the bottom in per capita transportation spending."
rationale: The statement is vague and lacks a year or definition of “transportation spending” (state-only vs. total state+federal+local). Rankings fluctuate by dataset and year, and available historical data generally place Georgia in the lower-middle range rather than consistently “near the bottom.” Without a specific dataset/time period the broad claim is not supportable.

claim: As state Commerce secretary, Mary Burke drafted, sponsored and promoted "budgets that raised taxes by billions, created high structural deficits and raided funds to finance huge spending hikes."
rationale: The claim misattributes budgetary authority to Mary Burke. As Wisconsin’s Commerce Secretary she was an appointed cabinet official and not the official who drafts or sponsors state budgets—those actions are undertaken by the governor’s office and the legislature. Specific assertions about billions in tax increases, creating structural deficits, or 'raiding funds' are not supported as actions uniquely undertaken by her in that role.

claim: "At his father's bank, Alexi made tens of millions in risky loans to convicted mobsters. Then, the bank collapsed."
rationale: This claim mixes true elements with exaggeration and unproven causal links. Alexi Giannoulias worked at his family's Broadway Bank and the bank failed in 2010 after losses on risky commercial real-estate and other loans during the financial crisis; political opponents also highlighted some controversial loans to borrowers who later faced criminal charges. However, characterization that he personally made "tens of millions" in loans specifically to "convicted mobsters" and that those loans alone caused the collapse is not supported by clear evidence and overstates the facts.

claim: "Vice President Kamala Harris laughs at the plight of Ukraine; at idea of America offering assistance"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Vice President Harris 'laughs at the plight of Ukraine' or at the idea of American assistance; the Biden administration and Harris have repeatedly expressed support for Ukraine, announced aid packages, and she has met with Ukrainian-Americans and allies. Viral clips claiming she laughed are either taken out of context or misreported and do not show her mocking Ukraine’s suffering or U.S. assistance policy.

claim: The Buffalo protester pushed to the ground "had been previously arrested 300 times. 82 times for incitement. Riots is what he does for a living."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Buffalo protester (Martin Gugino) had been arrested 300 times or 82 times for incitement. Multiple news organizations and fact-checkers reviewed public arrest and court records and found no record supporting those numbers; the claim circulated on social media as a smear.

claim: "The average age of the minimum wage worker is 35 years old."
rationale: The claim is misleading: U.S. labor statistics and multiple fact-checks show that workers earning the minimum wage skew younger, with typical median or modal ages in the 20s rather than a universal average of 35. Average age estimates vary by country, year, and whether mean or median is used, so the blanket statement that the average minimum-wage worker is 35 is not generally supported.

claim: Says she "called for addressing risks of derivatives, cracking down on subprime mortgages and improving financial oversight" early on in the financial crisis.
rationale: The claim as written lacks a named subject and any sourcing, so it cannot be verified that a particular 'she' made those specific statements early in the crisis. While many public figures did call for tighter oversight, limits on derivatives and crackdowns on subprime lending during the 2007–2009 financial crisis, this assertion is unverified without a clear attribution and evidence. Therefore I judge the statement false as stated.

claim: Says Tim Tebow wrote, "The government might be preparing us for a cashless society, but it was predicted by the Bible."
rationale: There is no credible record of Tim Tebow — in verified social media posts, interviews, or reputable reporting — saying or writing this line. The wording matches a common internet meme tying 'cashless society' claims to biblical prophecy that is frequently misattributed to public figures.

claim: "New Jersey's governor cut $1.6 billion from public education while handing out $2.1 billion in corporate tax breaks, more than the entire previous decade."
rationale: The claim bundles several specific numeric assertions without identifying a timeframe or named governor and I cannot confirm those exact totals. While New Jersey governors have reduced state school aid in some years and the state has awarded multi‑billion dollar business tax incentives, public budget and tax records do not clearly support the precise claim that one governor simultaneously cut $1.6 billion from public education while granting $2.1 billion in corporate tax breaks 'more than the entire previous decade.' The statement appears to conflate different programs and periods and is therefore not reliably true as stated.

claim: Schools are putting litter boxes in bathrooms to accommodate kids who identify as furries.
rationale: Multiple independent fact-checks and statements from school districts found no verified instances of schools installing litter boxes for students who identify as furries; viral images and social posts were hoaxes, misattributions, or misinterpretations. No credible evidence supports the widespread claim.

claim: Hillary Clinton in 2005 co-sponsored legislation that would jail flag burners.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Hillary Clinton specifically co‑sponsored a 2005 bill that would jail people for burning the flag. She did support and vote for measures in the mid‑2000s aimed at allowing restrictions on flag desecration (including support for a constitutional amendment to permit prohibitions), but that is not the same as co‑sponsoring a 2005 criminalization statute explicitly authorizing jailing flag burners.

claim: When Honduran children came into this country, "Secretary Clinton said send them back."
rationale: There is no credible record or contemporaneous transcript showing that Secretary (Hillary) Clinton said the phrase "send them back" about Honduran children. Public statements and fact-checkers have not found evidence she issued such a directive; her comments on migration were more nuanced and did not use that formulation.

claim: "Whether you like to admit it or not, half our general revenue goes to education."
rationale: The statement as a blanket claim is incorrect because the share of 'general revenue' spent on education varies widely by jurisdiction and is not universally 50%. At the federal level in the U.S. education comprises a small single-digit share of revenues; at the state/local level education is a large part of general funds but typically falls below half in many states (though a few places may approach or exceed 50%). Without a specific government or definition of 'general revenue,' the universal claim is false.

claim: Says fewer than 30 percent of Texas college students graduate in four years and only 58 percent graduate within six years.
rationale: The statement is imprecise and inconsistent with commonly reported higher-education statistics: for first-time, full-time bachelor's-seeking students at Texas public four-year institutions the four‑year graduation rate is typically above 30% and six‑year rates are often at or above ~60%. Aggregated statewide rates depend heavily on cohort definitions (full- vs part-time, inclusion of community colleges and transfers), which the claim does not specify.

claim: The Postal Service’s financial losses result from "a 2006 law that drains $5 billion a year from post office revenue, while the Postal Service is forced to overpay billions more into federal accounts."
rationale: The 2006 Postal Accountability and Enhancement Act imposed a prefunding mandate for retiree health benefits that required USPS to make roughly $5–5.5 billion annual payments for several years, and those charges are widely acknowledged as a major driver of reported losses. That said, the Postal Service’s deficits also reflect declining mail volume and other cost/revenue pressures, and the phrase about "overpaying billions more into federal accounts" is imprecise.

claim: In 2013, under a Democratic Senate, "a majority of the Senate voted in favor of" gun-related legislation sponsored by Republican Sens. Chuck Grassley and Ted Cruz, "but the Democrats filibustered it."
rationale: The prominent 2013 gun vote was the Manchin–Toomey background‑check amendment (sponsored by Democrat Joe Manchin and Republican Pat Toomey), not by Grassley and Cruz. That amendment received a simple majority of 54 yes votes but failed to invoke cloture because 60 votes were required, and the Republican minority (not Democrats) provided the opposition that blocked it. Democrats, who held the Senate majority in 2013, were not the filibustering party in that high‑profile vote.

claim: If you ask Amazon’s Alexa about the origin of the coronavirus pandemic, it says "the government planned" it.
rationale: There is no evidence that Alexa reliably or officially responds with the statement "the government planned" when asked about the coronavirus origin. Isolated social-media clips showed voice assistants repeating conspiracy phrasing pulled from web or media sources, but that is not a consistent, endorsed Alexa answer.

claim: "There's one (study) that came out of Pew in 2008 that showed 14 percent of people who voted were noncitizens."
rationale: Pew did not show that 14% of all people who voted in 2008 were noncitizens. The ‘14%’ figure that has been circulated refers to a small subset of self‑identified noncitizen respondents in a survey who reported having voted; Pew and later analysts treated that result as likely survey/misreporting error rather than evidence that 14% of voters were noncitizens.

claim: The debt limit deal "allows President Obama to borrow unlimited amounts of money."
rationale: That claim is false. Debt-limit legislation may raise or temporarily suspend the statutory ceiling, but it does not give the president unlimited borrowing authority; borrowing remains constrained by Congress’s appropriations, the terms of the suspension or new cap, and legal and fiscal limits on Treasury issuance.

claim: Newt Gingrich "has suggested" building "a mirror system in space" could improve the Earth’s habitability.
rationale: Newt Gingrich has publicly advocated researching geoengineering ideas including large space-based mirrors or sunshades to reflect sunlight as a way to counteract warming and make Earth more habitable. He made such proposals in interviews and public remarks discussing unconventional technological responses to climate change.

claim: Says the KKK marched in Mebane, N.C., after Trump’s victory
rationale: Social media posts claiming the KKK marched in Mebane after the 2016 election were investigated and found to be misattributed or unsubstantiated. Local news and independent fact-checkers found no credible evidence of an organized KKK march in Mebane tied to Trump's victory, and circulated photos were from other times or contexts.

claim: "In the last several months, the Biden administration has released over 7,000 illegal aliens who were COVID positive just in one Texas city." Biden's border policies are "endangering not just the people of Texas, but people all across the country."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Biden administration released over 7,000 COVID‑positive migrants in a single Texas city in the recent months referenced. Public health and local officials, as well as press fact‑checks, have not documented such a large, concentrated release; reported cases of COVID among migrants have been far smaller and often involve different timeframes or cumulative figures. The broader claim that border policies are endangering the entire country is an assertion not directly supported by the specific numeric allegation.

claim: President Trump has signed more bills into law "than any president previously before at this stage in the game."
rationale: The claim is misleading and not supported by historical records. Fact-checks and congressional law-count data show that several recent presidents (for example, Obama, Clinton, Reagan and others) had signed more public laws than Trump had at comparable points early in their terms. Without a specific time marker the statement is too vague and the available comparisons contradict the assertion.

claim: "Only Reuters" reported that the doctor who detected the omicron variant said its symptoms are "very mild."
rationale: The claim of exclusivity is false: numerous major news organizations besides Reuters reported that the South African doctor who first flagged Omicron described the cases as mild or "very mild." Contemporaneous coverage by outlets such as the BBC, AP, Guardian and others repeated her comments, so Reuters was not the only reporter.

claim: Says his plan to end the toll on Ga. 400 fulfills his campaign promise to commuters.
rationale: The claim is unverified as written because it does not identify who “he” is or provide evidence that the plan would actually remove the GA‑400 toll and directly fulfil a specific campaign promise to commuters. Confirming this requires matching a named official’s campaign pledge to the specific policy details and timeline; without that information the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: "27 U.S. Air Force pilots resign over COVID-19 vaccination mandate."
rationale: There is no credible, corroborated evidence that exactly 27 U.S. Air Force pilots resigned specifically over the COVID-19 vaccine mandate. Official Department of Defense statements and major fact-checks reported only a small number of separations or administrative actions related to vaccination refusals, and claims of '27 pilots resigned' have not been substantiated.

claim: The GOP’s health bill will protect people with pre-existing conditions "every bit as well as Obamacare did."
rationale: Major GOP health bill proposals (e.g., AHCA/BCRA-era plans) included state waiver authority, allowed variations in community rating and essential benefits, and promoted alternatives like high-risk pools and short-term plans; these changes would weaken or leave gaps in the guaranteed-issue and non‑discrimination protections that the ACA provided. Nonpartisan analyses (CBO and health-policy experts) concluded those proposals would not protect people with pre-existing conditions as comprehensively as the Affordable Care Act did.

claim: Says Austin trains are "full" at rush hour and "packed" for special events.
rationale: Public transit systems, including Austin’s commuter rail and event-oriented services, routinely see higher ridership during weekday rush hours and significantly increased loads for major events; contemporary reporting and rider accounts describe trains being full at peak commute times and packed during UT games and large festivals. The claim is a general observation consistent with typical service patterns and documented event-time crowding in Austin.

claim: "Barack Obama had 150 days in the U.S. Senate where he was able to vote quite often 'present.' "
rationale: This claim is incorrect. Senate roll-call records and contemporary fact-checking show Barack Obama cast only a small number of "present" votes during his Senate tenure, not anywhere near 150 days where he repeatedly voted "present." The figure appears to be a misunderstanding or miscount of voting days or missed votes rather than an accurate count of "present" votes.

claim: When Joe Biden’s son Hunter was serving as "a director to Ukraine’s largest private gas producer," the elder Biden "threatened to withhold $1 BILLION in U.S. aid to Ukraine if they didn’t fire a prosecutor looking into" the gas company.
rationale: While Hunter Biden did serve on the board of Burisma (a large private Ukrainian gas firm), and Joe Biden as vice president did threaten to withhold about $1 billion in U.S. loan guarantees to press for the removal of Ukrainian Prosecutor General Viktor Shokin, contemporaneous records and multiple fact-checks show Shokin was widely criticized for failing to pursue corruption cases and was not actively investigating Burisma at that time. The claim that Biden withheld aid specifically to protect his son by stopping a probe into the company is therefore misleading and not supported by the evidence.

claim: "The price tag amounted to nearly $4,200 for every man, woman and child in the state."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as presented because it omits which state, what expenditure ('price tag'), and the time period; without a stated total cost and the state's population at the relevant time you cannot confirm a $4,200 per-person figure. While such a per-capita number could be true for a specific program or state if the math and data match, this sentence alone is unsupported.

claim: "6,400 Ohioans ... lost manufacturing jobs in the month of September."
rationale: The claim omits which year and source are being referenced, so it cannot be verified as stated. Monthly manufacturing employment figures for Ohio are reported by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and state labor agencies and fluctuate by year and month; without a specified September (year) and data source the statement is unverified and therefore treated as false.

claim: Promotes a chart saying that Barack Obama has "increased the debt" by 16 percent, compared to George W. Bush, who increased it by 115 percent.
rationale: The "16% vs 115%" claim is misleading and depends on cherry-picked definitions and dates of federal debt. Different measures (total debt, debt held by the public, or including intragovernmental holdings) and choice of start/end points for each president produce very different percent changes, and fact-checkers have found that the cited chart uses an inconsistent or selective metric to make that contrast.

claim: "Cities in notoriously ‘tough on crime’ states like Texas and Florida saw a more significant increase in violent crime than cities in NYS."
rationale: The claim is too general and lacks a specified timeframe or list of cities; violent-crime trends differ by year and locality. Available national and local crime data show mixed patterns—some cities in Texas and Florida had larger increases in certain years while others did not, and many New York State cities also experienced increases—so the blanket comparative statement cannot be supported as presented.

claim: After Fahrenheit 9/11 came out, "Bush's approval rating never was better, it only got worse."
rationale: Fahrenheit 9/11 was released in late June 2004, but President Bush's approval did not only decline afterwards. Polling showed fluctuations with at least one clear uptick after his November 2004 re‑election (a typical post‑election bounce) before later declines, so it is incorrect to say it 'never was better' after the film's release.

claim: Kohl’s Department Stores in 2012 "announced the creation of 3,000 new jobs."
rationale: I am not aware of a verified Kohl's announcement in 2012 claiming creation of exactly 3,000 new jobs; major retailer hiring announcements that year typically referenced different (often larger) seasonal hiring numbers or specific local distribution-center openings. Given the absence of a clear, widely reported Kohl's press release matching this claim, it appears inaccurate or at best a mischaracterization of a different hiring announcement.

claim: Abortion services are "well over 90 percent of what Planned Parenthood does."
rationale: Abortions constitute only a small, single-digit percentage of Planned Parenthood’s total services, not over 90%. The organization’s reported service mix is dominated by contraception, STI testing and treatment, cancer screenings, and other preventive care.

claim: "Most of these killers tend to be 18, 19 years old."
rationale: The statement is vague and unsupported: homicide and violent-offender data show a broad age distribution rather than a majority concentrated at ages 18–19. Some specific subsets (for example certain juvenile offenders or particular incidents) may include people in that age range, but there is no general evidence that most killers are specifically 18 or 19 years old.

claim: A bill to eliminate Delta Air Lines’ jet fuel tax breaks "violates federal law and puts the state at risk of losing critical funding from the Federal Aviation Administration."
rationale: The claim overstates the legal consequence. States generally have broad authority to change tax policy, and eliminating a state tax break does not automatically violate federal law or trigger loss of FAA grants. FAA grant assurances prohibit discriminatory treatment in airport grants and operations, so only a targeted, airport‑specific action that breached those assurances could create a real risk to FAA funding — a general repeal of a tax break for one airline would not necessarily do so.

claim: Says "Dan McCready took money from Ilhan Omar"
rationale: There is no well-documented evidence or major press reporting that Rep. Ilhan Omar personally gave campaign contributions to Dan McCready. Public campaign finance records (FEC) and news coverage of McCready’s campaigns list donors and endorsements, and Omar is not shown as a contributor. The claim appears to conflate endorsement or public support with a direct monetary contribution.

claim: Says "Ruth Bader Ginsburg was nominated and confirmed 43 days before an election."
rationale: Ruth Bader Ginsburg was nominated by President Bill Clinton in June 1993 and confirmed by the Senate in August 1993. Those dates do not fall 43 days before any U.S. general election, so the statement that she was nominated and confirmed 43 days before an election is incorrect.

claim: "Right now we’re the highest taxed country in the world."
rationale: The statement is vague and unlikely to be true as written — there is no single country that is universally “the highest taxed” at all times. International comparisons (tax revenue as a share of GDP) typically show countries like Denmark, France, and Sweden near the top, while many others (including the U.S.) are well below them.

claim: Blue Cross headquarters has "a $30,000 granite table."
rationale: The claim is unverified and ambiguous: “Blue Cross” can refer to many independent Blue Cross/Blue Shield organizations, and there is no clear, reliable reporting or public procurement record confirming a $30,000 granite table at any specific Blue Cross headquarters. Without a named entity, date, or supporting source, the assertion cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says "56 percent of (the U.S.-Mexico) border is not under our control."
rationale: There is no authoritative, publicly available source showing that exactly 56% of the U.S.–Mexico border is “not under our control.” Agencies like U.S. Customs and Border Protection use terms such as “operational control” and report varying metrics (fence miles, sensor coverage, patrol presence), but those measures do not support a single 56% figure and the claim appears to conflate different concepts. Without a clear definition of “control” the numeric claim is unsupported.

claim: Says Oregon’s highest income tax bracket included anyone making more than $250,000 in 2012 before the state expanded its upper bracket to include "anyone making more than $125,000."
rationale: This statement misstates Oregon’s brackets and ignores filing-status differences. In 2012 the top marginal rate threshold differed by filing status (roughly $125,000 for single filers and about $250,000 for joint filers), so it is incorrect to say the highest bracket was only >$250,000 before being expanded to >$125,000. Later changes adjusted rates and thresholds, but the claim simplifies and reverses the actual configuration.

claim: The minimum wage "in real terms right now is below where it was when Harry Truman was in office."
rationale: The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 since 2009; when adjusted for inflation, that nominal level is generally lower than the inflation‑adjusted minimum wage in the late 1940s/early 1950s (the latter part of Truman’s presidency), which converts to roughly $8–$9 in today’s dollars. Historical federal minimums and CPI inflation series show Truman‑era statutory rates (after late‑1940s increases) exceed $7.25 in real terms.

claim: Says Russian President Vladimir Putin "calls me brilliant."
rationale: There is no publicly verifiable record that Vladimir Putin has told others or said publicly that he 'calls' the unnamed claimant 'brilliant.' Such statements are typically self-reported by the person claiming the praise and have not been independently confirmed in official transcripts or major press accounts.

claim: "West Virginia is near last in the U.S." rankings of education, clean drinking water, and child mortality.
rationale: West Virginia does rank near the bottom on many education indicators and has among the highest infant/child mortality rates in the U.S., but it is not uniformly 'near last' on clean drinking water across all national rankings. Water-quality rankings vary by metric, timeframe, and regulatory measure—while the state has notable contamination incidents and infrastructure challenges, it is an overbroad claim to say it is near last on all three measures.

claim: The streetcar project planned by Mayor Tom Barrett would be a "1900s style trolley."
rationale: The streetcar project advanced by Milwaukee Mayor Tom Barrett called for a modern, low-floor streetcar system with contemporary vehicles and accessibility features, not a restored or replica early-1900s trolley. The vehicles procured and the project specifications described modern streetcars rather than vintage turn-of-the-century trolleys.

claim: "These are radical Islamic terrorists, and (Hillary Clinton) won't even mention the word."
rationale: The claim bundles two assertions: that unspecified attackers are "radical Islamic terrorists" and that Hillary Clinton "won't even mention the word." The first part depends on which actors are meant and is a contextual judgment; the second part is inaccurate as an absolute statement because Clinton has both criticized blanket labeling and at times used terms like "radical Islam/Islamist extremists" in public statements. Saying she "won't even mention the word" overgeneralizes her recorded remarks.

claim: Says "Scott Walker says he would ban stem cell research"
rationale: There is no clear record of Scott Walker explicitly saying he would ban all stem cell research. He has opposed embryonic stem cell research using taxpayer funds and expressed pro-life positions, but that is different from a stated pledge to ban all stem cell research outright.

claim: California Republican gubernatorial hopeful Meg Whitman "contributed to, and campaigned, for" Democratic Sen. Barbara Boxer.
rationale: While Meg Whitman has a documented history of making political donations to candidates from both parties in the past, there is no clear evidence that she actively campaigned for Democratic Senator Barbara Boxer. News coverage of Whitman’s gubernatorial run highlighted prior contributions to some Democrats but did not substantiate claims that she campaigned on Boxer’s behalf.

claim: When President Donald Trump walked across Lafayette Square to a church, he held the Bible upside down.
rationale: Photographs taken as Trump walked across Lafayette Square to St. John’s Church show the cover of the book he held with the text oriented upside down in at least one widely circulated image. Multiple news organizations and fact-checkers reviewed the photos and concluded the Bible was held inverted, even though some angles later published made the orientation less clear. Intent cannot be determined from the images alone.

claim: Biden was responsible for "ending genocide in Bosnia."
rationale: Joe Biden was not the primary actor who "ended" the genocide in Bosnia. The 1995 end of large-scale violence is widely attributed to the Dayton Peace Accords brokered by U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke and the Clinton administration, supported by NATO air power and multilateral diplomacy; Biden, then a senator, was not the central decision-maker responsible for ending the conflict.

claim: Sen. Kamala Harris "may have broken laws" when she visited a voting site in Ohio
rationale: There is no public evidence, official complaint, or criminal charge showing Sen. Kamala Harris violated Ohio law during a visit to a voting site. Whether a visit could violate law depends on specific actions (e.g., campaigning within a restricted zone), and no credible reports documented such prohibited conduct in her case.

claim: Says he has supported "George Bush more than I have Barack Obama."
rationale: The claim as presented is unverifiable: it gives no named speaker, source, date, or context for the quote and there is no independent evidence provided that someone actually said this. Because key identifying information is missing, I cannot confirm the statement and therefore treat it as false for lack of evidence.

claim: "One hundred and ninety-four countries signed the Paris Agreement to control greenhouse gases. Our own voluntary agreement to accomplish the same goal — the Under2  MOU — has 165 signatories, representing a billion people."
rationale: The Paris Agreement figure is off — commonly reported counts list about 195 countries signing the agreement (and signature/ratification totals have varied by date), so '194 countries signed' is inaccurate. The Under2 MOU figure is broadly plausible: the subnational memorandum has had roughly 160–170 signatory jurisdictions representing on the order of one billion people, so that part is approximately correct.

claim: Says Rick Scott’s "hospital company stole millions, defrauding the military’s health care program."
rationale: Rick Scott was CEO of Columbia/HCA, a hospital company that faced federal investigations and paid large settlements in the late 1990s/2000s over Medicare and Medicaid billing practices, but Scott himself was never charged with stealing and there is no clear, established finding that his company specifically 'stole millions' from the military’s health care program. The company’s legal trouble involved broad federal healthcare fraud allegations, not a proven personal conviction tied to defrauding the military.

claim: HR 1 will allow members of Congress to draw a second salary "worth an estimated $600,000 per year!"
rationale: HR1 (the For the People Act) is legislation about voting rights, campaign finance, and ethics reforms and does not contain any provision authorizing members of Congress to collect a separate $600,000-per-year salary. The $600,000 claim appears to be a viral misrepresentation with no basis in the bill's text or official summaries. There is no mechanism in HR1 that would create such an additional congressional payout.

claim: There are 86 languages spoken at Miami Dade College.
rationale: The exact figure '86 languages' is not a stable, independently verifiable fact; Miami Dade College commonly advertises that students speak 'more than 80' or a similar approximate number, and reported counts vary over time. Without a current official source confirming exactly 86, the precise claim is unreliable.

claim: "Sixty percent of Americans now support legalizing marijuana."
rationale: Multiple recent national polls have found majority support for legalizing marijuana in the U.S., typically in the roughly 60–70% range. Therefore the claim that about 60% of Americans now support legalization is consistent with current polling evidence.

claim: Photo shows "all the men who have killed police officers this year (2020)."
rationale: The claim that a single photo shows 'all the men who have killed police officers this year (2020)' is implausible and unverifiable. It asserts a complete, nationwide (or global) accounting with no specified jurisdiction and social media image collages are frequently incomplete or inaccurate; many cases are ongoing, involve unknown suspects, or include perpetrators of different genders.

claim: Says Edward Snowden "could have gotten all of the protections of being a whistleblower."
rationale: Snowden did not follow designated classified-information whistleblower channels and was a private contractor in the intelligence community, so he would not have automatically received the full legal protections afforded to statutory whistleblowers. U.S. law protects certain disclosures made through authorized internal channels or to Inspectors General/Congress, but unauthorized public disclosure of classified material can trigger criminal prosecution under the Espionage Act and other laws.

claim: "I've either balanced every budget or we turned back a surplus."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement about an unspecified speaker and time period and therefore is not verifiable as presented. Balancing every budget or always returning a surplus is historically uncommon for governments; confirming it would require specific fiscal records for the named officeholder and years. Without that context or documentation the blanket assertion should be treated as false.

claim: After attacking Emma Gonzalez, U.S. Rep. Steve King is "facing arrest."
rationale: There are no credible news reports or official records showing Representative Steve King was arrested or formally 'facing arrest' after his public criticism of Emma Gonzalez; the assertion appears to be a viral rumor. Major media coverage of the exchange did not document any charges, warrants, or law enforcement actions against King.

claim: Say North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper was arrested for driving while intoxicated in Stanly County.
rationale: There are no credible news reports, official statements, or public records indicating North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper was arrested for driving while intoxicated in Stanly County. An arrest of a sitting governor would be widely covered by state and national media, and no such coverage or arrest record exists.

claim: In nine Democratic debates, "We've not had one question about a woman's right to make her own decisions about reproductive health care, not one question."
rationale: The claim that there were zero questions about a woman's right to make reproductive health decisions across nine Democratic debates is incorrect. At least some Democratic primary debates included direct questions about abortion and reproductive rights, especially after high-profile state actions and legislation, so it is not true that there were none.

claim: "I became a Republican sooner in my life than" Ronald Reagan did in his.
rationale: The claim compares an unspecified person's age-of-conversion to Ronald Reagan’s, but no information is given about who “I” is or when they became a Republican. Ronald Reagan, born in 1911, is generally recorded as switching his party affiliation to Republican in the early 1960s (around 1962), at roughly age 51. Without the speaker’s birthdate and the date they became Republican the statement cannot be verified.

claim: Says House Democrats’ impeachment inquiry of President Donald Trump "doesn’t feature the opposition party, it doesn’t feature cross-examination."
rationale: The claim is misleading: while some televised public hearings were dominated by Democratic questioning, Republicans and their counsel were not entirely excluded from the House impeachment inquiry. Minority members and party counsel participated in closed-door depositions and had opportunities to submit questions and question witnesses at various stages, so the process did include the opposition and instances of cross-examination.

claim: Photo shows Barack Obama and George Clooney in a compromising situation with a child.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that such a photo exists; an image showing Barack Obama and George Clooney in a compromising situation with a child would have been widely investigated and reported by reputable news and fact‑checking organizations. Circulating images tied to this claim have been unverified and are consistent with manipulated or misattributed content.

claim: The United States has a "record number of abortions year after year after year."
rationale: U.S. abortion totals have not been setting new records every year. National counts peaked in the early 1990s and overall trended downward for decades; while there have been recent fluctuations and some year-to-year increases in specific years or states, there is no sustained pattern of record-setting increases "year after year after year."

claim: President Barack Obama is "ending Medicare as we know it."
rationale: The statement is political rhetoric and not factually accurate. President Obama did not terminate Medicare; the Affordable Care Act preserved Medicare benefits and expanded preventive coverage while implementing payment and cost-control changes that reduced certain provider and Medicare Advantage payments but did not end the program or convert it to a voucher system.

claim: "95 percent of teachers and principals are not implicated in the [Atlanta Public Schools cheating scandal] report at all."
rationale: The specific 95% figure is not supported by the official Atlanta Public Schools investigation and subsequent legal actions. The scandal and reports named and investigated dozens of educators and school leaders, and the reports did not state a blanket ‘‘95 percent not implicated’’ clearance for teachers and principals; therefore the precise claim is misleading.

claim: Says she "wiped out" the state Agriculture Department’s inspections of eggs at retail sites like grocery stores.
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as presented: no speaker is named, no date or source is given, and there is no readily available public record showing a specific official both saying she 'wiped out' and actually abolishing state Agriculture Department egg inspections at retail sites. Eliminating routine retail egg inspections would require formal rulemaking or public notice and would likely appear in government records or news coverage; absent that corroboration the assertion cannot be verified.

claim: To abide by Environmental Protection Agency rules when mining or drilling you have "to take caution not to disturb bodies of water barely bigger than a puddle."
rationale: The statement overstates EPA authority. The Clean Water Act regulates “waters of the United States” and can cover some small streams and wetlands, but it does not categorically prohibit disturbing every tiny isolated puddle; jurisdiction depends on connectivity, size, and legal definitions refined by court rulings and agency rules. Whether a permit is required for mining or drilling impacts therefore varies by the specific water feature and location.

claim: "Pfizer and Moderna could share their design with dozens of other pharma companies who stand ready to produce their vaccines and end the pandemic."
rationale: While the mRNA sequence could in principle be shared, producing Pfizer/BioNTech or Moderna vaccines requires proprietary lipid nanoparticle formulations, specialized manufacturing equipment, skilled know‑how, quality control systems, raw material supply and regulatory approvals. Several manufacturers have taken part in organized tech transfers, but simply handing over a 'design' to dozens of companies would not immediately enable widespread production sufficient to 'end the pandemic.'

claim: "In 1986, President Ronald Reagan" cut the business tax rate to 34 percent and "it worked -- our economy boomed, the middle class thrived and median family income increased."
rationale: It is true the 1986 Tax Reform Act lowered the top corporate tax rate to 34%, but the broader claim is misleading. Although the economy recovered and grew after the early-1980s recession, gains were uneven: median family/household income showed little real improvement through much of the 1980s and income gains were concentrated among higher earners rather than indicating a broadly 'thriving' middle class.

claim: "President Obama took more money from Wall Street in the 2008 campaign than anybody ever had."
rationale: Though Barack Obama's 2008 campaign raised large sums and did receive notable contributions from the financial sector, independent analyses and campaign finance records do not show he received more Wall Street money than every prior candidate. The claim is sweeping and ignores earlier large finance-sector giving and differences in how 'Wall Street' donors are counted.

claim: "Today, it is more difficult to enlist in the U.S. military than it is to enroll in college."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and cannot be universally true because enlistment and college enrollment have different, variable standards. Military enlistment requires age, citizenship/immigration status, medical/fitness, security and criminal-history screens, and minimum education or waivers, while college admissions range from open-enrollment community colleges to highly selective universities with rigorous admissions; many people can enroll in college even if they cannot meet military medical or legal standards, and vice versa. Because difficulty depends on which branch, which college, and individual circumstances, the blanket statement is false.

claim: Says "Nicolás Maduro is carrying out a genocide on his people."
rationale: While numerous credible reports and investigations document serious human rights abuses, extrajudicial killings, torture and crimes against humanity by Venezuelan state actors under Nicolás Maduro, there is no widely accepted legal finding that these acts meet the specific legal definition of genocide (intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a protected national, ethnic, racial or religious group). International bodies have described crimes against humanity and opened examinations, but have not concluded a genocide determination.

claim: Says James Clapper "and virtually everyone else" said "there is no collusion" in the Russia investigation findings.
rationale: While James Clapper at times said he saw no evidence of a criminal conspiracy, it is incorrect to say he and "virtually everyone else" uniformly said "there is no collusion." The Mueller report stated investigators did not establish conspiracy/coordination but did not fully exonerate the president, and other officials and congressional reports documented numerous contacts and Russian interference—views were mixed and carefully worded rather than a universal "no collusion" declaration.

claim: "Taxes for every New Yorker are lower today than when I started"
rationale: The claim is absolute — that taxes for every New Yorker are lower — but taxes vary by type (income, property, sales, local levies), by individual circumstances, and by locality. Over any multi-year period some residents experience higher property or local taxes, changes in taxable income, or the imposition of new fees, so it is extremely unlikely all New Yorkers pay less now than at an unspecified start date.

claim: "Records suggest more than 100 batches of absentee ballots in Fulton County could be missing."
rationale: While some election records and reporting forms in Fulton County showed inconsistencies or counting/reporting errors, multiple official reviews and fact-checkers found no evidence that more than 100 batches of absentee ballots were actually missing. Discrepancies were explained by duplicate entries, mislabeling, batch-size variation and clerical/reporting mistakes rather than lost ballots.

claim: "At my first ‘Let’s Get to Work Day’ … we sold out;" more than 240 dozen doughnuts by 8:30 a.m.
rationale: I cannot verify the specific numeric claim from my training data and there is no independent corroboration that more than 240 dozen (2,880) doughnuts were sold out by 8:30 a.m. at a particular 'Let’s Get to Work Day.' The statement is a specific, easily checkable quantitative claim but lacks supporting evidence here, so I treat it as unverified and therefore report it as false per guidance to favor false when uncertain.

claim: "If you look at what we’ve done over the last several years, the crime rate has actually gone down in [Providence] and . . . the number of shootings has been going down."
rationale: The statement asserts a clear multi-year decline in overall crime and shootings in Providence, but official city/state crime statistics and local reporting show year-to-year fluctuations rather than a sustained steady decline. Shootings in particular rose in some recent years and trends depend heavily on the specific timeframe and crime categories chosen.

claim: "We have the highest corporate tax rate in the world. It’s 35 percent."
rationale: While the U.S. federal corporate tax rate was 35% prior to the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, that did not make it the highest in the world; several countries have had higher statutory or combined (national plus subnational) corporate rates. Additionally the U.S. rate was cut to 21% in 2018, so the claim is time-dependent and factually inaccurate as a general statement.

claim: Says Gov. Scott Walker "has caused Wisconsin to lose more jobs than any other state in the country."
rationale: Authoritative employment data do not show Wisconsin losing more jobs than any other state under Governor Walker, and independent analysts have not attributed such a uniquely large loss to him. The stronger claim that Walker 'has caused' statewide job losses is also unsupported because employment outcomes reflect national trends and many factors beyond a single governor's policies.

claim: "A Cornell University research study concludes that ethanol generates a 29 percent energy loss, meaning it takes more than a gallon of gasoline to produce a gallon of ethanol."
rationale: A Cornell researcher (David Pimentel) published analyses concluding that corn ethanol exhibits about a 29% net energy loss, meaning more fossil-fuel energy is used in its production than is contained in the ethanol. That specific Cornell-based conclusion is accurate, though it is contested by many other lifecycle analyses that find a small net energy gain depending on methodology.

claim: "Drone technology now allows an individual to be recorded in their homes by drones as small as birds and immediately uploaded to the internet."
rationale: Miniature drones comparable in size to birds exist and can carry high-quality cameras and wireless transmitters; such devices are capable of entering buildings or flying near windows and streaming video in real time to the internet. Practical limits (flight time, obstacle navigation, connectivity and legal constraints) affect how easily this can be done, but the underlying technology to record individuals inside homes and immediately upload the footage is available.

claim: "In 1935, more than 50% of the elderly population lived in poverty. Today that poverty rate stands officially at 9.4%."
rationale: The claim mixes a broadly accurate historical fact with a specific modern statistic that is ambiguous. It is true that in the mid-1930s a majority of Americans aged 65 and over lived at or below the poverty threshold before Social Security was enacted, but the statement that the rate today is "officially 9.4%" depends on the year and which poverty measure is used; recent official (Census Bureau) elderly poverty rates have been around 8–10%, not precisely 9.4% for every recent year. Because the exact modern figure is presented without a year or measure, the composite claim is not reliably provable as stated.

claim: Before "our last three presidents, you have to go back to the 1800s, early 1800s to find three presidents in a row being consecutively re-elected."
rationale: The three most recent consecutive presidents who each won re-election were Bill Clinton (re-elected 1996), George W. Bush (re-elected 2004), and Barack Obama (re-elected 2012). Before that run, the previous instance of three successive presidents each winning re-election was in the early 1800s: Thomas Jefferson (re-elected 1804), James Madison (re-elected 1812), and James Monroe (re-elected 1820).

claim: "In the 2020 election, President Trump voted from behind the desk in the White House in Florida."
rationale: The claim is internally inconsistent and incorrect: the White House is in Washington, D.C., not in Florida. By 2020 Trump was a Florida resident and cast his ballot as a Florida voter (not from the White House), so he did not 'vote from behind the desk in the White House in Florida.'

claim: "There's no such thing as a lone wolf. ... That was a phrase invented by the last administration to make Americans stupid."
rationale: The term 'lone wolf' is a longstanding concept in criminology and counterterrorism used to describe individuals who act without direct organizational support and predates any recent U.S. administration. Numerous documented cases have been characterized as lone-actor attacks, and there is no credible evidence that a prior U.S. administration invented the phrase as propaganda to 'make Americans stupid.'

claim: Says a video shows a "gay party in Italy few weeks before COVID-19."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false: no authoritative sourcing or metadata is provided to confirm the video’s time, location, or participants, and independent fact-checks of similar viral clips have repeatedly found misattributed dates and countries. Videos alleging a 'gay party in Italy few weeks before COVID-19' have been shown in other cases to originate elsewhere or at different times, so the specific attribution to Italy just before the outbreak is unsupported.

claim: Paul Ryan’s budget "keeps the Obamacare taxes and spending cuts that paid for Obamacare, but then cuts all of the benefits."
rationale: That characterization is misleading. Paul Ryan’s budgets repeatedly proposed repealing large parts of the Affordable Care Act (including many of its taxes and mandates) while also proposing major changes to entitlement programs; they did not simply keep ACA’s dedicated taxes and spending cuts intact while eliminating only the law’s benefits. Whether specific revenue or Medicare payment changes were retained varied by proposal, so the blanket claim that his budget 'keeps the Obamacare taxes and spending cuts that paid for Obamacare, but then cuts all of the benefits' is not an accurate summary.

claim: "Now, 50% of all of America, more than any other country, is fully vaccinated."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and incorrect: if 'America' means the United States, many other countries have had higher fully vaccinated percentages than 50% at various times; if it means the entire continents of the Americas, the combined fully vaccinated share varies and is not described accurately as '50% of all of America' being fully vaccinated and 'more than any other country' (which conflates countries and continents). Global vaccination data show numerous countries exceeding 50% fully vaccinated, so the assertion that 50% of 'America' is fully vaccinated and that this is more than any other country is false.

claim: Says Luke Messer and Todd Rokita "voted to fast-track Obama’s trade deals."
rationale: The statement that both Luke Messer and Todd Rokita "voted to fast-track Obama’s trade deals" is inaccurate as a blanket claim. Public House roll-call votes on Trade Promotion Authority/"fast track" in 2015 show differing votes among members of the Indiana delegation, so it is not correct to assert that both specifically voted to fast-track without citing the exact roll call. The claim overgeneralizes without supporting roll-call evidence.

claim: More than one-quarter of America’s young adults are too fat to serve in the U.S. military
rationale: Multiple government and research reports have found that roughly a quarter to a third of Americans in the prime enlistment ages (commonly cited 17–24) exceed military weight/fitness standards and are therefore ineligible to serve. The commonly reported figure around 25–30% supports the statement that more than one-quarter are too heavy to qualify under current DoD medical/fitness rules.

claim: Quotes show Joseph Stalin and Joe Biden expressed similar views about counting votes.
rationale: The infamous line commonly attributed to Joseph Stalin (“It’s not the people who vote who count...”) is a historical quote; Joe Biden has not voiced a comparable sentiment and publicly urged that all lawful ballots be counted. Social media posts that present matching quotes are based on misattribution or out-of-context snippets rather than documented statements by Biden expressing that voting should be subverted by those who count ballots.

claim: "In Ohio, more than half the providers of safe and legal abortion have had to shut down" since Gov. John Kasich took office in 2011.
rationale: Public reporting shows Ohio experienced a substantial decline in abortion clinics after 2011, but available counts and definitions vary and do not clearly support a definitive "more than half" shutdown attributable solely to Kasich’s term. Media and advocacy groups have reported large percentage declines, but figures differ depending on whether one counts clinics, individual providers, or facilities and on the exact baseline year. Because the claim is precise and the underlying numbers are disputed and ambiguous, it cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: Al Sharpton went to Ferguson, Mo., and is "declaring as a matter of fact that ... Michael Brown didn't use any deadly force or posed no deadly threat to the officer."
rationale: Al Sharpton traveled to Ferguson in 2014 after Michael Brown’s shooting and publicly argued that Brown was unarmed and did not pose a deadly threat to the officer, presenting that position as fact in speeches and interviews. Multiple contemporary news reports and Sharpton’s own statements conveyed that stance while he led protests and called for justice.

claim: Georgia spends fewer tourism advertising dollars than any other state in the South.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Georgia spends the least on tourism advertising of any Southern state; Georgia runs a substantial tourism promotion program and hosts major destinations (Atlanta, Savannah) that typically justify significant ad budgets. The claim is unsubstantiated without specific, recent comparative budget data and a defined timeframe.

claim: Says each of the past three years "has been the hottest on record."
rationale: The statement is too general and depends entirely on which specific three years and which temperature dataset are meant. While there have been stretches of three consecutive record-warm years (for example 2014–2016 in major global surface-temperature records), that is not universally true for every recent three-year span and rankings differ by dataset and methodology, so the blanket claim cannot be verified as true.

claim: "To give a sense of how families are struggling, a record four out of every 10 school kids in Ohio now qualifies for subsidized lunch."
rationale: The claim states a "record" 4 in 10 Ohio students now qualify for subsidized lunch, but publicly reported school meal eligibility figures use free and reduced-price counts and have varied over time; available state and federal data indicate the share has been at or above 40% in some prior years and the phrasing is ambiguous about timeframe and definition. Without a clear date and definition of "subsidized lunch," the assertion that 40% is a new record is misleading or incorrect.

claim: In Ohio, "each year an estimated 1,000 children become victims of human trafficking, and over 3,000 more are at risk."
rationale: I could not confirm a reliable, authoritative source that exactly 1,000 children in Ohio become trafficking victims each year with an additional 3,000 at risk. Official counts from hotlines and law-enforcement are much lower while modeled estimates vary widely depending on methodology, so the precise figures in the claim appear unverified and likely stem from an unclear or outdated estimate.

claim: "The unemployment rate for Wisconsin workers has reached historic lows. It’s never been this low before, ever, ever, ever."
rationale: The claim asserts an absolute all-time low but gives no date or measure. Historical labor data for Wisconsin show prior periods with similarly low unemployment rates (for example in the late 1990s/early 2000s and in the 2018–2019 period), and different series (seasonally adjusted vs not, U-3 vs other measures) can produce different lows. Because historical series record comparable or lower rates, the blanket statement “never been this low before, ever” is incorrect.

claim: Says former NBA player Rick Fox was also on board with Kobe Bryant
rationale: Contemporary news reports and the official passenger list for the January 26, 2020 helicopter crash that killed Kobe Bryant do not include former NBA player Rick Fox. The confirmed passengers were Bryant, his daughter Gianna, and several others; Rick Fox was not on that flight.

claim: "The very first Republican convention after the Civil War was held in Virginia in a Black church."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated. The first Republican National Convention after the Civil War met in 1868 in Chicago, not Virginia; although Reconstruction-era Republican meetings and state conventions in the South often met in Black churches, there is no basis to assert the "very first" postwar Republican convention occurred in a Virginia Black church.

claim: "The  firefighters, the policemen and others who supported (Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker) in his election bid ... don't have to worry about their collective bargaining rights."
rationale: Wisconsin’s 2011 Budget Repair Bill (Act 10) curtailed collective bargaining for many public employees but largely exempted public safety personnel (police and firefighters), so any retained rights were a matter of job classification and statute rather than whether those workers supported Walker. The claim implying supporters specifically would be protected is misleading—legal protections (or losses) apply to categories of employees, not to individuals based on political support.

claim: Says state budget deal between Texas House and Senate leaders "funds nursing homes, our public schools and universities and provides financial aid for college students."
rationale: The statement is too broad and cannot be confirmed without the specific budget text or a clear timeframe. While Texas biennial budgets routinely appropriate formula funding for K–12 schools and public universities, funding for nursing homes is generally handled through Medicaid/provider rate actions and may not have been specifically increased in the deal, and direct financial aid for college students requires separate appropriations. Because the claim asserts all three outcomes categorically without citation, it is unsupported as stated.

claim: Says Ken Cuccinelli "attacked churches for helping the poor."
rationale: There is no clear, widely reported instance showing Ken Cuccinelli explicitly launched an effort to 'attack churches for helping the poor.' Cuccinelli has taken conservative legal and policy positions (on abortion regulation, Medicaid/Obamacare, etc.) that critics sometimes said negatively affected nonprofits, but the blanket claim is unsupported without a specific cited incident.

claim: In-N-Out cups say "Let’s go Brandon."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that In-N-Out Restaurants prints the political slogan "Let’s go Brandon" on its official cups; the company has historically avoided partisan messaging. Images claiming this are likely doctored, from third‑party custom products, or isolated pranks rather than standard corporate practice.

claim: Says President Trump "has ended up attracting larger numbers of people coming to the United States presenting themselves for asylum status at our border than we’ve ever seen."
rationale: The claim asserts Trump ‘attracted’ historically larger numbers presenting for asylum than ever, which conflates causation with a disputed empirical record. Border encounter and asylum statistics vary by year and metric (apprehensions, family units, asylum applications), and while there were major spikes (notably 2019), other periods and later years have comparable or higher totals; experts attribute flows to multiple factors beyond a single president’s rhetoric or policies.

claim: Insurance companies have seen their profits soar by more than 400 percent since 2001.
rationale: The statement is too broad and unsupported: there is no single, widely accepted statistic showing that "insurance companies" as a whole have increased profits by more than 400% since 2001. Profit performance varies widely by country, line of business, and individual firms, and industry-wide profit totals have fluctuated (including major downturns) over that period. Some firms or sectors may have seen very large gains, but the blanket claim lacks necessary scope and supporting data.

claim: "Throughout his time in elected office, Barack Obama has taken multiple positions on banning handguns and the D.C. handgun ban."
rationale: Over his elected career Obama made multiple, evolving statements and votes on handgun restrictions: as an Illinois state senator he supported stricter local gun-control measures and later, during the 2008 campaign and as a U.S. senator/candidate, he criticized the Supreme Court’s D.C. handgun decision (Heller) while also clarifying he did not advocate a wholesale national handgun ban. The record shows nuance and shifts in emphasis that constitute multiple positions on handgun bans and the D.C. ban.

claim: "I’m running the second-largest county district attorney’s office … at 1985 staffing levels."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated and likely false because it provides no named office or staffing figures; major county DA offices have generally changed size since 1985 due to population, caseload, and budget changes. Verifying such a claim would require specific historical and current payroll/personnel records and a clear definition of “staffing levels” (attorneys vs total staff), which are not provided.

claim: Says a gun bill before the Senate "is proposing the universal registration of all firearms and their owners."
rationale: Without citation to a specific bill, there is no evidence that a Senate proposal universally mandates registration of every firearm and owner. Most recent federal proposals have focused on expanded background checks, safe-storage measures, or targeted registration for certain categories, so a claim of blanket universal registration is unverified and likely inaccurate absent explicit bill language.

claim: "On the pace that we're on with job creation in the last four months ... we will have created more jobs in this year than in the entire Bush Presidency."
rationale: The statement is misleading and cannot be confirmed as stated because it depends on how “jobs created” and the reference period for the Bush presidency are defined. By standard BLS net nonfarm payroll measures, the U.S. saw essentially flat to slightly negative net job change over George W. Bush’s term (early-2001 to Jan‑2009) so a short-term extrapolation could be framed to look superior, but using common, transparent metrics the speaker’s broad claim is deceptive.
