Published estimates for fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) are on the order of 0.2–1.5 cases per 1,000 births and broader fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) prevalence estimates are typically in the 1–5% range in some populations—both far below 300,000 annual births in a typical high-birth country. The statement also conflates terms ("deformed", "alcoholics") and implies a simple one-to-one causal attribution that public health research does not support.

claim: "The Parole Board operates with Mark Herring’s advice and consent."
rationale: ‘Advice and consent’ is a legislative confirmation power, not something an attorney general exercises. Mark Herring, as attorney general, may give legal opinions but does not provide formal advice-and-consent authority over Parole Board appointments, which are handled through gubernatorial appointment and legislative confirmation in Virginia.

claim: Says COVID-19 has killed more North Carolinians in a year than the flu has in 10 years.
rationale: The claim is too imprecise to verify and likely false as stated because it provides no specific year for the COVID-19 deaths or the 10-year span for influenza. COVID-19 caused thousands of deaths in North Carolina during pandemic years, but cumulative influenza deaths over a 10-year period can also total several thousand and results depend on which years are compared. Without specifying exact years and using official state counts the comparison cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Black Lives Matter, who are attacking law enforcement officers" -- Barack Obama "had them to the White House."
rationale: The claim conflates two things and misrepresents them: the Obama White House and administration did meet with and host some Black Lives Matter activists and community members to discuss policing and reforms, but the movement is decentralized and cannot be accurately labeled as 'who are attacking law enforcement.' Additionally, many engagements were with White House officials or convenings rather than a singular presidential reception of the entire movement.

claim: "If you’re a single mom, and you’ve two kids in the city of Richmond, you can almost make $50,000 a year on the public dole."
rationale: The claim is vague and misleading: direct cash welfare (TANF) for a single parent with two children is typically only a few hundred dollars per month, far below $50,000/year. While the combined value of in-kind benefits (housing vouchers, Medicaid, SNAP) plus tax credits (EITC, child tax credits) can materially help a household, for most single mothers in Richmond those benefits rarely sum to nearly $50,000 annually. Benefit levels also vary by which Richmond is meant, family circumstances, and program eligibility.

claim: "More Americans receive food aid than work in (the) private sector."
rationale: The private sector workforce in the U.S. numbers well over 100 million people, while major food assistance programs serve far fewer individuals (SNAP around ~40 million, WIC and school meal programs add millions but with overlap). Even aggregating common food-aid program participation does not approach the size of the private‑sector workforce.

claim: The Democratic health care bill in the House would "create 53 new government bureaucracies."
rationale: Fact-checks of the House Democratic health-care bill found the claim that it would “create 53 new government bureaucracies” is misleading and inaccurate. The legislation did create or expand some offices, boards, and programs, but opponents inflated the count by including existing agencies, state entities, and advisory panels and by using a broad, inconsistent definition of “bureaucracy.”

claim: "Here in Pennsylvania, the annual cost for infant childcare is over $10,000 per child, which is more than most families pay in rent and almost the same cost as in-state college tuition."
rationale: While infant center-based childcare in Pennsylvania commonly runs around or just above $10,000 per year, the claim's comparisons are misleading. Median rents in many parts of Pennsylvania are similar to or higher than $10,000 annually, so it is not clearly true that childcare costs are 'more than most families pay in rent.' Likewise, in‑state college tuition varies widely by institution and level, so it is inaccurate to state it is 'almost the same' without specification.

claim: "In Italy, they have thrown their money on the streets. A clear message to the whole world that money is not enough when health is in danger."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or widespread reporting that Italians 'threw their money on the streets' as a mass action; the phrase appears to be figurative rather than a factual description of events. Coverage of Italy during health crises (e.g., COVID-19) documents public displays of support like balcony applause and donations, not mass dumping of cash in the streets.

claim: "Over 60 percent of the provisional ballots cast in [the 2012] election were disqualified because those folks were not duly registered as voters."
rationale: Nationwide data from federal and nonpartisan analyses of the 2012 U.S. general election do not support a claim that over 60% of provisional ballots were disqualified for lack of registration. Provisional ballots are handled and adjudicated by states for a variety of reasons and the overall rejection rate nationwide was far lower, with only a minority of provisional ballots left uncounted and multiple distinct reasons for rejection. While some localities had high rejection rates, the blanket figure of over 60% for the entire 2012 election is incorrect.

claim: "As compared to last year, Texas has about 15% more power generation capacity."
rationale: A ~15% year‑over‑year increase in Texas generation capacity would mean adding on the order of 10–15+ GW in one year, which is much larger than typical annual additions. Historical additions to Texas/ ERCOT capacity from wind and solar have generally been a few gigawatts per year, so a 15% jump is unlikely without extraordinary, documented construction.

claim: "A miscarriage is considered an abortion."
rationale: The claim is misleading: in medical terminology a miscarriage is often called a 'spontaneous abortion,' but in everyday, legal, and political usage the word 'abortion' normally refers to an induced termination of pregnancy. Thus a blanket statement that a miscarriage is considered an abortion is context-dependent and inaccurate without qualification.

claim: "North Carolina spends $855 less per student than it did before the Great Recession, and we have one of the lowest per pupil spending levels in the nation."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and cannot be verified as presented: per‑pupil comparisons depend on which year is used as the pre‑Recession baseline and whether numbers are adjusted for inflation. North Carolina did reduce education funding after the Great Recession and has trailed the national average at times, but different datasets and years produce different dollar changes and rankings, so the specific claim of '$855 less' and 'one of the lowest' is not reliably supported without more context.

claim: "Last year we spent more than $40 billion on highways. And Lord knows we need that. But that's more than we spent on Amtrak in its entire 40-year history."
rationale: Federal and total spending on Amtrak over its first ~40 years is roughly on the order of tens of billions of dollars and by most estimates equals or exceeds $40 billion, so a single year of highway spending being "more than we spent on Amtrak in its entire 40-year history" is incorrect. While annual federal highway outlays are indeed around $40+ billion in many recent years, Amtrak’s cumulative federal subsidies and capital grants since 1971 are generally reported to be about the same magnitude or higher, so the comparison as stated is misleading.

claim: "Most of the people that work in finance make $70,000, $80,000 a year."
rationale: The finance sector includes a wide range of roles and pay levels; many entry-level and support positions earn well under $70,000 while senior, technical, or investment roles often earn well above $80,000. There is no reliable evidence that a majority of finance workers fall narrowly into a $70k–$80k salary band.

claim: "Nationally, the unemployment rate for veterans is far greater than the national unemployment rate," and Wisconsin is "one of those rare examples where unemployment is actually lower for veterans than it is for the population as a whole and certainly lower than it is nationally."
rationale: BLS data over the past decade show veteran unemployment rates have generally tracked the overall national rate and in many recent years have been similar to or lower than the civilian rate, so it is inaccurate to say veterans’ unemployment is 'far greater' nationally. While Wisconsin has at times reported veteran unemployment lower than its overall state rate and lower than the national average for some years, that pattern is year-dependent and not so uniformly rare as the claim implies.

claim: "John Cornyn has voted to increase the debt, raise taxes, bail out Wall Street banks and fund Obamacare."
rationale: The claim bundles several different votes into a single assertion that is misleading. John Cornyn, a conservative Republican senator, has generally opposed the Affordable Care Act and major tax increases and has voted repeatedly to roll back or block funding for Obamacare; he has not broadly supported tax hikes. While he has supported some debt-increasing budget or continuing-resolution measures (and like many senators voted on occasional financial rescue or stabilization measures), the blanket statement that he voted to increase the debt, raise taxes, bail out Wall Street banks and fund Obamacare is inaccurate without specific roll-call references.

claim: "They were going to build the wall a while ago, not so long ago, like in '06. And they couldn't get environmental impact statements."
rationale: The statement is misleading. There were plans and congressional authorization for border barriers in 2006 (Secure Fence Act) and construction began in some areas, but the claim that 'they couldn't get environmental impact statements' is inaccurate — federal agencies were required to perform environmental reviews, and in many cases did environmental assessments or analyses; delays and lawsuits occurred and in later years Congress or the executive branch used legal waivers to limit or bypass some environmental reviews.

claim: "More people now die in Wisconsin from drug overdoses than car crashes."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous without a specified year and current official data vary by year. While drug overdose deaths have risen sharply nationwide and in Wisconsin, official state vital statistics through recent years show motor vehicle fatalities and overdose deaths can be close and year-to-year, and I cannot confirm a persistent and current crossover without a specific timeframe. Given the uncertainty, the claim as stated cannot be verified as a present fact.

claim: Says Barack Obama was silent on Iran "when the students took to the streets in Tehran and the people there protested, (and) the Green Revolution occurred."
rationale: President Obama was not silent during the 2009 Iranian Green Movement; he and his administration issued public statements condemning violence, calling for a transparent investigation of the election, urging restraint, and expressing support for protesters' rights. Although he stopped short of calling for regime change or direct intervention, he repeatedly voiced concern about the conduct of the Iranian authorities.

claim: A letter from BP to the Minerals Management Service "actually recommends improvements and specific recommendations around safety regulations should they choose to change them."
rationale: There is no specific, verifiable source provided for the quoted statement and I cannot confirm that a particular BP letter to the Minerals Management Service contained those exact recommendations. While BP has exchanged correspondence with MMS, the claim cites no dated letter or text and the assertion cannot be verified from general public records alone. Without the original document, the statement should not be treated as a confirmed fact.

claim: "About 95 percent of America’s production of ethylene is produced on the Gulf Coast in Texas and Louisiana."
rationale: While a large majority of U.S. ethylene production capacity is concentrated on the Gulf Coast in Texas and Louisiana, the figure of about 95% is an overstatement. Industry data and analyses typically show a substantial Gulf Coast share but well below 95%, and the exact percentage varies by year and whether one counts nameplate capacity, actual output, or export-oriented capacity.

claim: A Marine painted his house red, white and blue after he "was told by his neighbors that he could not fly the American flag in his yard all year long."
rationale: I cannot confirm this specific anecdote from reliable news or fact‑checking sources; the story appears to circulate as an unverified viral item and lacks corroboration from mainstream reporting. Without independent verification (names, location, or news coverage), the claim remains unsupported and likely apocryphal.

claim: Ted Cruz "helps run two national organizations that have been leading the push to give amnesty to illegal immigrants."
rationale: Ted Cruz has publicly and legislatively opposed granting blanket 'amnesty' to undocumented immigrants and is not documented as helping run national organizations that lead a pro-amnesty push. Public records, his voting record, and his speeches show opposition to amnesty rather than leadership of pro-amnesty groups, and no credible sources attribute such organizational roles to him.

claim: "Governor Evers' budget would increase property taxes by the largest amount in a decade"
rationale: The claim is not substantiated as stated: Wisconsin governor budget proposals can affect local spending pressures but do not directly set local property tax levies, and available summaries of Evers’ budgets do not conclusively show they would produce the single largest property tax increase in a decade. Whether property taxes rise depends on local school and municipal levies, state aid changes, and specific year-to-year comparisons, so the blanket statement is unsupported without a precise metric and timeframe.

claim: "A lot of the move to free the slaves ... did not come from the federal government. It came from a growing movement among the people, particularly people of faith."
rationale: Abolition in many places was driven substantially by grassroots movements and religious activists (e.g., Quakers, evangelicals, and wider moral campaigns during the British and American abolition movements) who pressured governments to act. While federal or parliamentary measures ultimately abolished slavery legally, those measures often followed sustained popular and faith-based campaigning rather than originating solely from government initiative.

claim: "Covid-19 means ‘certificate of identification of vaccination with artificial intelligence.’"
rationale: COVID-19 is an abbreviation for 'coronavirus disease 2019' (CO = corona, VI = virus, D = disease, 19 = 2019). The proposed expansion 'certificate of identification of vaccination with artificial intelligence' is fabricated and not supported by WHO or scientific naming conventions.

claim: A video shows Joe Biden speaking slowly and slurring on the Fourth of July.
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim that a video exists showing Joe Biden speaking slowly and slurring on 'the Fourth of July' because the date is unspecified and my knowledge only goes through June 2024. Viral clips are often taken out of context, edited, or misattributed to different dates or events. Without a verifiable source or timestamp, the claim is not proven.

claim: "We know that every 85 visitors create one Florida job."
rationale: The claim is presented without a source, timeframe, or definition of ‘visitor’ or how a job is ‘created,’ and there is no established, constant ratio that every 85 visitors create one Florida job. Tourism job-per-visitor ratios vary by year, methodology, and whether jobs are measured as full-time equivalents, temporary, or supported indirectly, so the blanket statement is not verifiable as a general fact.

claim: "Gas prices were WAY higher in 2008, under REPUBLICAN president George W. Bush."
rationale: U.S. national average retail gasoline prices peaked in mid-2008 at about $4.00–4.10 per gallon, the highest on record at that time, and that peak occurred while George W. Bush was president (he served through January 2009). Saying prices were “way higher in 2008 under Republican president George W. Bush” is accurate in the sense that 2008 saw unusually high prices relative to many other years.

claim: "Thousands of Westerners and Americans" are fighting with extremists in eastern Syria and Iraq.
rationale: While several thousand foreign fighters from Western countries traveled to Syria and Iraq at the height of the conflict, the number of US citizens who joined extremist groups is far smaller (generally estimated in the low hundreds). Moreover many foreign fighters have been killed, detained, or returned, so current active fighters from Western countries and the U.S. are not 'thousands' on the ground in eastern Syria and Iraq today.

claim: The Milwaukee County Board’s staff grew from four workers to 38 over four decades and now costs taxpayers "a lot more," while the total county workforce was more than cut in half in the same period.
rationale: I cannot verify the specific numeric claims with available information: the statement bundles precise staffing levels, a four-decade timeframe, and a dramatic countywide workforce decline without citing sources. Such claims are often misleading because they omit context (e.g., role reclassifications, inflation, transferred services, or changes in which employees are counted). Without contemporaneous county payroll and budget records to confirm both the board staff change and the claim that the total county workforce was cut by more than half, the assertion should be treated as unsubstantiated.

claim: "Fauci admits Covid vax doesn't work"
rationale: Dr. Anthony Fauci has not admitted that COVID-19 vaccines “don't work.” Public statements and scientific data he has cited acknowledge reduced effectiveness against infection for some variants and waning immunity over time, but consistently affirm that vaccines significantly reduce severe disease, hospitalization, and death. Saying he admitted they “don't work” misrepresents his nuanced comments about changing effectiveness against infection.

claim: Says critics who say he cut Medicaid are wrong; his budget added $1.2 billion to the program
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify and therefore likely misleading: it does not identify who 'he' is, which budget or year is meant, or whether the $1.2 billion is gross funding, net state spending, or includes federal matching funds. Without that context, an apparent numeric increase can coexist with policy changes that reduce eligibility or shift costs, so asserting critics are 'wrong' based solely on the cited figure is unsupported.

claim: Dollar General "added 2,500 stores and 20,000 jobs" during his four-year tenure as CEO.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about which CEO and which four-year window and I find no authoritative source that exactly matches “2,500 stores and 20,000 jobs” added within a single four-year CEO tenure. Dollar General’s store counts and employee headcount have grown over time, but public filings and company reports show different totals depending on the years chosen and do not corroborate that exact pair of figures for one four-year span.

claim: "About 80 percent of (the manufacturing and agriculture) tax credit goes to claimants who are making $1 million or more."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unsupported: there is no widely established evidence that a generic “manufacturing and agriculture” tax credit directs about 80% of benefits to claimants earning $1 million or more. Distribution of tax-credit benefits varies greatly by specific program and jurisdiction, and while some business tax benefits can be concentrated among larger, higher‑income firms, a precise 80% figure requires a cited study or official data. Without specifying the credit, year, or country, the statement cannot be verified and is likely misleading.

claim: "One would have to go back more than a century to find a scenario where a president’s nominee for the Supreme Court was confirmed by the opposition party in the Senate when the vacancy occurred during an election year."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. Historical records of Supreme Court nominations and Senate party control show instances within the 20th century where a president’s nominee was confirmed by a Senate controlled by the opposing party even though the vacancy occurred in an election year. The statement’s sweeping “more than a century” phrasing therefore overstates the rarity of such occurrences.

claim: Says Joe Biden talked about eating wooden corn dog sticks.
rationale: There is no well-sourced record or reputable reporting that President Joe Biden said he ate wooden corn dog sticks; the claim appears to be a vague or viral mischaracterization rather than a verifiable quote. Without a specific time, place, or reliable source, the statement cannot be substantiated and is likely a distortion or joke taken out of context.

claim: Sherrod Brown "has been running for public office since Richard Nixon was president."
rationale: Sherrod Brown's first campaign for public office was in 1974 when he ran for the Ohio House of Representatives at age 22. That campaign began during Richard Nixon's presidency (Nixon left office in August 1974), so it is accurate to say his runs for public office started while Nixon was president.

claim: The increase in the current state budget was greater than the inflation rate and the rate of population growth in Georgia.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it omits the jurisdiction (U.S. state vs country) and the time period for the “current” budget. Whether a budget increase exceeds both inflation and population growth requires specific, same-period percentage figures for the budget change, the consumer price/inflation rate, and population change; those vary by place and year. Without those numbers the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: Stay-at-home orders "actually are the law of these states."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and misleading. Stay‑at‑home orders were typically issued as executive emergency orders and could be enforceable in many states, but they are not identical to statutes passed by legislatures and their legal status and enforceability varied by state and over time, with some orders facing legal challenges or limits.

claim: Ninety-five percent of the money used for union-operated worker training centers comes from employers.
rationale: There is no general evidence that 95% of funding for union-operated worker training centers comes from employers. Funding mixes vary widely—many centers receive employer contributions but also substantial federal/state grants, union dues, and other sources—so a blanket 95% figure is unsupported.

claim: "Seventy four percent of Californians are absolutely against sanctuary state" policies.
rationale: No reputable statewide poll substantiates the precise claim that 74% of Californians are 'absolutely against' sanctuary state policies. Public-opinion surveys on sanctuary/immigration issues in California show mixed results and vary substantially with question wording and timing; opposition levels are generally lower and context-dependent.

claim: Says up to a quarter of African Americans don’t have government photo ID.
rationale: Multiple reputable analyses (notably research cited by the Brennan Center and similar studies) have estimated that about one quarter of African‑American voting‑age adults lack a government‑issued photo ID. While exact figures vary by survey method, definition of ID, state, and year, saying 'up to a quarter' aligns with published estimates of racial disparities in ID ownership.

claim: "My mask will keep someone else safe and their mask will keep me safe."
rationale: Masks substantially reduce the risk of spreading and inhaling infectious respiratory particles, but they do not guarantee complete protection. Source control (your mask protecting others) is generally stronger than wearer protection, and how much a mask protects you depends on mask type, fit, and proper use, so the absolute statement 'will keep ... safe' is incorrect.

claim: "We have an increase in murder within our cities, the biggest in 45 years."
rationale: The claim is vague (no country, cities, or time period) and therefore unsupported as stated. In the United States, homicides did rise notably in 2020–2021 in many cities, but national homicide levels were not the highest in 45 years — homicide rates peaked in the late 1980s–early 1990s and earlier decades saw higher counts. Without a specified jurisdiction and timeframe the assertion that murders increased the most in 45 years is not supported.

claim: "Since I was elected, crime rates have been at their lowest in over a decade."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify and therefore cannot be accepted as true: it omits the jurisdiction, the speaker’s election date, the specific crime categories, and the data source. Crime trends vary by location and offense and must be confirmed with official, time‑series statistics or independent analyses to support a decade‑long low claim.

claim: Says that in 41 states, government workers "are better paid than the taxpayers who support them."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and misleading: comparisons of government-worker pay to "the taxpayers who support them" depend on what is being compared (average vs median, wages only vs total compensation, full-time vs all workers). Fact-checkers and economic analyses have shown that once you specify measures and control for factors (occupation, education, hours, benefits), the blanket statement that in 41 states government workers are paid more than the taxpayers who fund them does not hold up.

claim: Says "over 1 million signatures" were submitted in attempt to recall Gov. Scott Walker.
rationale: In the 2012 recall effort against Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker activists collected roughly a million petition signatures, but the state certified about 931,000 valid signatures — below one million. Statements claiming 'over 1 million signatures were submitted' conflate collected totals with the number certified by state officials and are therefore inaccurate.

claim: Says "the Kardashians donate whopping sum to Las Vegas mass shooting victims"
rationale: There is no reliable reporting that members of the Kardashian family made a widely publicized, large donation specifically to victims of the Las Vegas mass shooting. Major news outlets documented many celebrity donations after the 2017 Route 91 Harvest shooting, but coverage does not support a claim that “the Kardashians” gave a notable lump-sum gift. The statement appears to be an unverified or viral claim lacking corroboration.

claim: Says Joe Biden said, "This country is doomed, not just because of African Americans, but because by 2040 this country is going to be minority white European."
rationale: There is no credible record or reputable reporting showing Joe Biden ever uttered that exact racist statement; it appears to be a fabricated or heavily distorted quote. Biden has discussed demographic change in the U.S. in more neutral terms, but not with language saying the country is 'doomed' or singling out 'African Americans' in that way.

claim: The U.S. has "over $62 trillion in unfunded liabilities."
rationale: There is no single, official, universally accepted figure of “over $62 trillion” in U.S. unfunded liabilities; that number typically comes from specific aggregations and present-value assumptions that are not standard. Official budget agencies (CBO, OMB) and actuarial reports show very large long-term shortfalls for programs like Social Security and Medicare under certain assumptions, but totals vary widely with discount rates, time horizons, and which obligations are included, so presenting $62 trillion as a definitive fact is misleading.

claim: U.S. military uniforms are manufactured in China.
rationale: U.S. military uniforms are generally produced under procurement rules (notably the Berry Amendment) that require clothing and textile items be sourced and manufactured domestically. Although isolated cases or components have been traced to overseas suppliers, including China, it is incorrect to state as a general fact that U.S. military uniforms are manufactured in China.

claim: COVID-19 vaccinations are "a violation of the Nuremberg code."
rationale: The Nuremberg Code governs unethical human experimentation and requires voluntary informed consent for research subjects. COVID-19 vaccines were developed through clinical trials with informed consent and underwent regulatory review or emergency authorization before public use; routine vaccination programs are public health interventions, not illicit human experiments. While some dispute mandates or policies as coercive, that does not make the vaccines themselves a violation of the Nuremberg Code.

claim: Says the late Lady Bird Johnson sicced the CIA on actress and singer Eartha Kitt after Kitt spoke out against the Vietnam War during a White House luncheon in January 1968.
rationale: Eartha Kitt did publicly denounce the Vietnam War at a White House luncheon in January 1968 and suffered career repercussions and government surveillance afterward, but there is no credible evidence that Lady Bird Johnson "sicced the CIA" on her. Declassified records and contemporaneous reporting document FBI interest and monitoring, not a direct CIA operation ordered by the First Lady. The CIA’s mandate and legal restrictions also make it an unlikely agency for domestic targeting.

claim: Says Patrick Henry said, "The Constitution is not a document for the government to restrain the people: it is an instrument for the people to restrain the government."
rationale: No reliable primary-source evidence shows Patrick Henry uttered this exact wording; the line does not appear in his recorded speeches or papers and is treated by quotation researchers as a later paraphrase or misattribution. While the sentiment echoes Henry’s distrust of centralized power, the specific phrasing originates from later writers rather than Henry himself.

claim: A man was arrested "for wearing a T-shirt that says ‘We The People’ and has a picture of the ‘Statue of Liberty.’"
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that someone was arrested solely for wearing a T-shirt reading 'We The People' with a Statue of Liberty image. In the U.S., pure political apparel is generally protected by the First Amendment and arrests normally require another legal violation (e.g., trespass, disturbance, or refusal to comply with lawful orders). Claims of arrests for political shirts are frequently missing context or conflate separate conduct with the clothing itself.

claim: Says Dick Cheney "supported gay marriage sooner" than Hillary Clinton.
rationale: Publicly, Hillary Clinton did not endorse same‑sex marriage until 2013, while Dick Cheney’s own public acknowledgements of support are ambiguous and mostly reported later or described as private views. Because the claim hinges on who 'supported' it first and whether private views count, there isn’t clear evidence Cheney publicly supported marriage equality earlier than Clinton.

claim: Huckabee "was one of the highest taxing governors that we had in this country and rivaling Bill Clinton in terms of the Cato ratings."
rationale: While Mike Huckabee did sign some tax increases as Arkansas governor, Cato Institute’s fiscal ratings do not clearly place him among the very highest‑taxing governors nationwide, and directly “rivaling Bill Clinton” is misleading because Clinton’s governorship predated the Cato report series and is not directly comparable in those ratings. Numerous governors in the same period scored worse on Cato’s fiscal report cards than Huckabee did.

claim: "Nothing was done. I mean, $25 million was spent, but we don’t have that (gun ownership) database."
rationale: The statement is vague and unverified as written: there is no documented, universal fact that exactly $25 million was spent and yet no gun-ownership database exists. In the U.S. federal law and practice, a comprehensive national gun-owner registry is generally prohibited and instead funds have gone to background-check systems (like NICS) and various state-level databases — some states do maintain registries. Without a clear attribution (which program, agency, time period), the specific dollar figure and conclusion cannot be confirmed.

claim: "The average American is working through the month of May just to pay off the government."
rationale: This is an overgeneralization. The standard measure for this idea is "Tax Freedom Day," the date when the average American has earned enough to pay the year's tax burden, and that date varies by year and state; in most recent years it has fallen in April, not through the entire month of May. Saying the average American is "working through the month of May just to pay off the government" is therefore inaccurate without a specific year, state, or methodology.

claim: "There's not a major bill I know with Hillary's name on it."
rationale: There is no widely recognized major federal law formally named for Hillary Clinton. Although she sponsored and advocated for many measures during her career as First Lady, U.S. Senator, and Secretary of State, none of the major enacted bills are commonly known to bear her name.

claim: "All evidence points to the fact that our kids are 17 times more likely to have ill effects from the seasonal flu than they are from the coronavirus."
rationale: There is no consistent, robust evidence that children are 17 times more likely to have ill effects from seasonal flu than from COVID-19; in many periods and locations pediatric COVID-19 hospitalization and serious outcome rates equaled or exceeded influenza and COVID-19 can cause unique complications like MIS-C and long COVID. The specific 17x figure appears unsupported and the blanket phrasing "all evidence points" is misleading because risks vary by time, variant, vaccination status, and age.

claim: Democratic Party candidates for the state Assembly "actually received 200,000 more votes statewide" than their Republican counterparts in the 2012 election
rationale: The statement as given cannot be confirmed and is inaccurate as a general claim. Official certified statewide vote totals for 2012 assembly races (which vary by state) do not uniformly support the blanket claim that Democratic candidates 'actually received 200,000 more votes' than Republicans; reported margins differ and the claim omits which state's assembly is meant. Because the claim is imprecise and the specific certified returns do not match this asserted figure, it is false as stated.

claim: "Senator Cryin’ Chuck Schumer fought hard against the Bad Iran Deal, even going at it with President Obama, & then Voted AGAINST it! Now he says I should not have terminated the deal"
rationale: Senator Chuck Schumer publicly opposed the 2015 Iran nuclear agreement, confronted the Obama administration over it, and announced he would vote to disapprove the deal under the congressional review process. After President Trump withdrew from the JCPOA in 2018, Schumer criticized that withdrawal and said abandoning the deal was a mistake.

claim: Says the U.S. Constitution provides for just compensation when land is taken under eminent domain.
rationale: The Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause states that private property shall not be taken for public use without just compensation, which establishes a constitutional requirement for compensation when land is taken under eminent domain. This principle has been consistently recognized and applied by U.S. courts.

claim: Says that in Curry County, "if you make a 911 call you’re likely to wait for an hour for a response."
rationale: The claim is a broad, absolute statement presented without supporting evidence. Emergency services generally prioritize life‑threatening 911 calls and aim for much shorter response times; while rural counties can have longer waits, saying callers are "likely" to wait an hour is an unsubstantiated exaggeration. Without specific data for a named Curry County, the claim cannot be treated as factual.

claim: "Overdoses in Virginia (are) up 35%."
rationale: The claim lacks a specified time period and data source; overdose counts and rates in Virginia did rise in some recent periods (for example during the COVID era), but reported increases vary by year and metric and are not universally 35%. Without a clear timeframe or whether this refers to deaths, ER visits, or calls, the flat statement that overdoses in Virginia are up 35% is unsupported.

claim: A CNN chyron said, "Antifa has just taken responsibility for storming Capital Hill."
rationale: This claim is false. Multiple contemporaneous fact-checks and CNN itself confirmed no chyron saying 'Antifa has just taken responsibility for storming Capital Hill' was ever broadcast; images circulating online showing that text were doctored or misattributed.

claim: "We have over a million (legal immigrants) a year, more than at any time in the history of this country. We have the largest percentage of immigrants, almost tied now with the historical high as a percentage of immigrants living in this country."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate and inaccurate elements. Recent years have not consistently seen over one million new legal immigrants annually and historical admissions in some periods were comparable or higher, so the blanket statement that we now admit more than at any time is incorrect. The second half — that the foreign‑born share of the U.S. population is near its historical high — is broadly correct (foreign‑born share is near levels last seen in the late 19th/early 20th century).

claim: "White supremacist who killed protester is a Democrat and visited (President Barack) Obama in Oval Office."
rationale: The widely reported attacker in the Charlottesville incident (James Alex Fields Jr.) was identified with white supremacist beliefs and extremist online activity; there is no credible evidence he was a Democrat or that he ever visited President Obama in the Oval Office. Major news organizations and fact-checkers investigated viral claims tying the attacker to Obama and found them unsupported or fabricated.

claim: "If we ban the practice of earmarks, we could save the American taxpayer anywhere between $15 (billion) to $20 billion dollars a year in pork-barrel spending."
rationale: The precise claim that banning earmarks would save $15–$20 billion per year is not reliably supported by authoritative data. Estimates of earmark or 'pork' spending vary widely depending on definitions and time period, and watchdog groups’ figures differ from official accounting; furthermore, banning earmarks does not guarantee equivalent reductions because Congress can reauthorize or relabel projects through other budget mechanisms.

claim: "Wages adjusted for inflation haven’t risen since the turn of the last century."
rationale: The claim is false as a general statement: in most advanced economies real (inflation-adjusted) wages are much higher today than around the turn of the last century (circa 1900) due to large productivity and living‑standards gains. Even over shorter periods, results depend on the country, measure (mean vs median), and time window; some measures have been stagnant for decades but not universally since 1900.

claim: The oil industry has "9,000 permits to drill now. They could be drilling right now, yesterday, last week, last year."
rationale: The assertion that the oil industry currently holds 9,000 permits that would allow immediate drilling is misleading. Counts cited in public debate often conflate different categories (applications vs approved permits, federal vs state/private permits), include permits that are outdated, incomplete, or subject to additional approvals or land-access and infrastructure constraints, and omit the commercial decisions (rigs, crews, economics) that determine whether companies actually drill immediately.

claim: Judge Jeff Davis "spent years defending a convicted cop killer" and "tried to get him off the hook."
rationale: I can find no reliable, corroborated reporting or public record showing that a judge named Jeff Davis ‘‘spent years defending a convicted cop killer’’ or repeatedly sought to have such a person cleared. Public biographies and news coverage of judges named Jeff Davis do not substantiate a long-term defense role for a convicted police killer as described in the claim. Without specific case names, dates, or jurisdiction the allegation appears unverified.

claim: "Joe Biden tells voters he's 'going to beat Joe Biden.'"
rationale: There is no credible record of President Joe Biden telling voters he will “beat Joe Biden.” Biden’s public remarks about elections refer to defeating political opponents (notably Donald Trump), so this phrasing appears to be a misquote, joke, or transcription error rather than a factual statement he made. If a specific clip is cited, it likely reflects a slip-of-tongue or satirical framing rather than an intentional claim.

claim: Says a WHO proposal "portrays milk and dairy products as an obstacle to a healthy start in life."
rationale: No widely circulated WHO proposal characterizes milk and dairy broadly as an "obstacle to a healthy start in life." WHO policy consistently promotes exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months and provides targeted guidance cautioning against inappropriate marketing or early use of breast‑milk substitutes and certain processed foods for infants, but it does not categorically portray dairy products generally as an obstacle to healthy starts.

claim: Metro Atlantans spend "over an hour every day" or "five hours a week" commuting, for a total of "260 hours a year."
rationale: Typical data (e.g., U.S. Census/ACS and regional surveys) show Metro Atlanta one-way commute times around 30–33 minutes, which implies a round-trip of just over an hour per workday. Assuming a five-day workweek that is about five hours per week, and multiplying by 52 weeks gives roughly 260 hours per year.

claim: "Moderna chief medical officer admits: mRNA alters DNA."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Moderna’s chief medical officer explicitly 'admitted' that mRNA vaccines alter DNA. Reports that quote him are mischaracterizations or taken out of context; mainstream scientific consensus and Moderna's statements indicate mRNA does not integrate into the human genome under normal conditions.

claim: "The American economy is continuing its longest monthly streak of job growth in history, with 3.9 million jobs added since President Trump was elected."
rationale: The United States did experience a multi-year run of consecutive monthly job gains that became record-setting, but the specific claim that 3.9 million jobs were added 'since President Trump was elected' is misleading without a cutoff date and does not match official Bureau of Labor Statistics payroll totals for most common reference dates. Official BLS monthly nonfarm payroll figures and the White House’s own rolling tallies give different cumulative totals depending on the end month, so presenting 3.9 million as a timeless fact is inaccurate.

claim: Each Georgia taxpayer would have to send $5,000 to the treasury to cover the state’s debt.
rationale: The claim is misleading because it treats a single precise per-taxpayer figure as if it were an established fact, but the result depends entirely on which debts are included (state-only, tax-supported, pension liabilities, or state+local) and which population is counted as "taxpayers." Using rough, publicly available figures (roughly 4–5 million Georgia individual tax filers and typical state tax-supported debt well below $25 billion) a simple division does not consistently yield $5,000 per taxpayer. Without a clear year and definitions the $5,000 number cannot be verified as accurate.

claim: Says Judge Gonzalo Curiel "is a member of a club or society, very strongly pro-Mexican."
rationale: This is a paraphrase of remarks made by Donald Trump in 2016 about Judge Gonzalo Curiel, in which he suggested Curiel was biased because of his heritage and said he was a member of a club or group that was "very pro-Mexican." Multiple news organizations quoted or summarized Trump using wording very close to this when criticizing Curiel over the Trump University litigation.

claim: "Together we added more jobs than any other area" while I was Dane County executive.
rationale: The statement is unverified and ambiguous: it does not name the timeframe or the comparator (‘any other area’). I have no specific employment data showing Dane County added more jobs than every other comparable area during the speaker’s tenure, so the claim cannot be substantiated as stated.

claim: "Marjorie Taylor Greene just scrubbed her Twitter feed of all things Gaetz."
rationale: I cannot confirm the claim: there are no reliable reports or archived records in my training to verify that Marjorie Taylor Greene 'just scrubbed' her Twitter feed of all mentions of Matt Gaetz. Social media accounts are often edited or posts removed, so without a timestamped archive or credible news sourcing this specific assertion is unverified. Given the time-sensitive wording ('just'), the claim cannot be treated as established fact based on available information.

claim: "I personally am pro-choice. I always have been. And I made no qualms about that when I was elected governor."
rationale: The statement is first-person and provides no information about who is speaking, so there is no way to confirm the person's long-standing pro-choice stance or whether they stated it when elected governor. Because the claim lacks identifiable context or supporting evidence, it cannot be verified and is treated as false under the instruction to prefer FALSE when uncertain.

claim: When he was Milwaukee County executive, "eight years in a row we pushed through budgets that did not increase the tax levy from the previous year."
rationale: Contemporary fact-checks and local reporting found this claim misleading: while the county levy was held largely flat for several years under the county executive, accounting moves, use of one-time revenue and shifting expenses were used to avoid nominal levy increases and in at least one year the levy did not strictly decline. Also property owners still sometimes saw higher bills because of changing assessments rather than levy increases. The claim as stated — eight straight years with no increase in the tax levy from the previous year — is not fully supported.

claim: "There aren't too many people outside protesting" his speech at the Phoenix Convention Center.
rationale: The claim lacks any specific time, date, or named speaker, so it cannot be verified as stated. Determining whether there were "too many" protesters requires contemporaneous evidence (news reports, police or organizer estimates, photos/videos), which is not provided.

claim: Opposition to having a fully elected Chicago Board of Education is in the "super minority."
rationale: There is no clear, credible evidence that opposition to a fully elected Chicago Board of Education is confined to a 'super minority.' Public opinion and political positions on elected versus appointed school boards in Chicago have been mixed and have shifted over time, with organized groups and elected officials both supporting and opposing full elections. Without a specific, recent poll or defined population, the claim overstates the size of opposition.

claim: "There is already a mosque four blocks away."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific local fact but provides no location or time, so it cannot be verified as stated. Without geographic context or evidence (e.g., address, map, or local knowledge), I cannot confirm that a mosque exists exactly four blocks away.

claim: "Six people in Florida die as a result of (not expanding Medicaid) every day."
rationale: The precise statement that 'six people in Florida die every day as a result of not expanding Medicaid' is not an established factual count but rather the sort of estimate produced by modeling studies with strong counterfactual assumptions. Different analyses produce varying results and there is no single, independently verified daily death toll directly attributable to Florida's non-expansion of Medicaid.

claim: "It takes almost a year for a refugee to be processed in the United States."
rationale: The time to process a refugee case in the U.S. is highly variable and commonly exceeds a year rather than taking "almost a year." US refugee resettlement involves multiple stages—referral, interviews, security and biometric checks, medical screening, and travel processing—many of which can add months and create backlogs, so the overall timeline often stretches to 18 months or longer for many applicants.

claim: Says President Barack Obama said that if he doesn’t turn the economy around after three years in office, he’ll be a one-term president.
rationale: President Obama publicly acknowledged early in his term that if the economy had not improved within a few years he would not deserve re-election, effectively conceding he could be a one-term president if he failed to turn the economy around in about three years. This sentiment was widely reported in contemporaneous press coverage and reflected in his own remarks about a multi-year timeframe for economic recovery and electoral accountability.

claim: Republican candidate for Georgia governor "dabbled" in birther conspiracy theories.
rationale: The claim as stated is unsubstantiated because it does not name a specific candidate or timeframe and I can find no clear, widely reported evidence that a Republican Georgia gubernatorial candidate publicly promoted birther conspiracy theories. 'Dabbled' is vague and without a precise reference this assertion cannot be verified. Given the lack of documented instances tying a named Georgia GOP governor candidate to birther claims, the claim is not supported.

claim: The omicron variant’s name is evidence the coronavirus pandemic is a hoax.
rationale: The label 'omicron' is a WHO-assigned name using the Greek alphabet to provide a simple, non-stigmatizing label for the B.1.1.529 SARS-CoV-2 variant and does not imply the pandemic is fabricated. Independent scientific evidence—genomic sequencing that identified the variant, case counts, and epidemiological data—confirms the variant's existence and ongoing pandemic activity. Using the naming choice as 'evidence' of a hoax is unfounded.

claim: Says former North Carolina elections board chairman "tried to drag a cancer-stricken woman out of her hospital bed to testify at her son’s hearing on the first day of early voting over a bogus complaint that the board hadn’t even fully investigated."
rationale: I cannot find reliable, corroborated reporting or official documentation that a former North Carolina elections board chairman physically tried to drag a cancer-stricken woman out of her hospital bed to testify at her son’s hearing. The allegation is highly specific and sensational but appears uncorroborated in major local and national news coverage of North Carolina election-board controversies. Without verifiable sourcing, the claim should be treated as unproven and likely false.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi "made millions in coronavirus insider trading."
rationale: Independent fact-checks and news reporting found no evidence that Nancy Pelosi personally engaged in coronavirus-related insider trading or that she 'made millions' from such activity. The trades cited in accusations were executed by her husband and investigators and reporters have not substantiated claims of illegal insider trading tied to her.

claim: "No Republicans voted for" recent hikes in the income tax, payroll tax, capital gains tax, dividend tax and estate tax. "These taxes were all passed under … Obamacare."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act did create two new taxes that affect high earners — a 0.9% Medicare payroll surtax and a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax on investment income (including capital gains and dividends) — and Republicans opposed the ACA. However, the ACA did not raise ordinary income tax rates broadly nor create a new estate tax, and describing all recent hikes in income, payroll, capital gains, dividend and estate taxes as having been passed under Obamacare is misleading and inaccurate.

claim: "The governor’s cuts would kick over 8,000 people out of their homes."
rationale: The claim is missing crucial context (which governor, which specific cuts, what timeframe and which programs), so it cannot be verified as stated. Such a precise numerical impact would require a named policy and underlying analysis; without that information the statement is unsupported and may be a speculative or contested projection.

claim: "North Korea is telling its people that their men’s national team is in the World Cup final."
rationale: There are no credible reports that North Korean authorities are telling citizens their men’s team is in a World Cup final, and historically North Korea’s men’s team has never reached a World Cup final (best known performances were 1966 quarterfinals and participation in 2010). While DPRK state media sometimes exaggerates or censors sports news, the specific claim is not supported by known facts.

claim: "Only a few months ago the FBI arrested three Broward County Commissioners for accepting millions of dollars in trade for illegal favors."
rationale: There are no credible national or local reports showing that the FBI recently arrested three Broward County commissioners for accepting millions in exchange for illegal favors. An action of that scale would have been widely reported; available records and major news outlets do not corroborate this claim. It may conflate or exaggerate unrelated past investigations or arrests of different officials.

claim: "Last year it was discovered that Rhode Island's public employees ranked 4th in average pay, while the private sector ranked 23rd."
rationale: I could not find a reliably documented, widely reported finding that “last year” Rhode Island public employees ranked 4th in average pay while the private sector ranked 23rd. Rankings of state public vs private pay differ substantially depending on the data source, year, and whether the metric is average wage, median wage, or total compensation, so the claim is likely a misstatement or lacks crucial context. Without a clear source or definition of the metric, the specific ranks cannot be confirmed.

claim: Louisiana is turning down $100 million "that would require us to change our unemployment law, that would have actually raised taxes on Louisiana businesses."
rationale: I cannot verify a specific, documented instance where Louisiana declined exactly $100 million on the grounds that accepting it would force a change to state unemployment law and directly raise taxes on Louisiana businesses. While federal or private funds sometimes come with conditions that require state law changes, the claim bundles multiple specific assertions (amount, legal requirement, and tax increase) without corroborating evidence and is therefore unsubstantiated as stated.

claim: "Under Operation Warp Speed, we’ve pioneered groundbreaking therapies, reducing the fatality rate 85% since April."
rationale: Operation Warp Speed did accelerate development and deployment of COVID-19 vaccines and some therapeutics, but there is no substantiated, attributable figure showing a single 85% reduction in the fatality rate 'since April.' The claim conflates program activities with a precise mortality decline without specifying timeframe, population, or which fatality metric, and official data do not support that exact 85% attribution solely to OWS.

claim: Ed Gillespie’s "firm even lobbied for five foreign governments, including a dictator now awaiting trial for war crimes."
rationale: I found no reliable, verifiable evidence that Ed Gillespie’s firm formally lobbied for five foreign governments including a dictator currently awaiting trial for war crimes. Public summaries of his career and mainstream reporting list U.S. political and private-sector clients and do not support that specific claim about multiple foreign governments and a war-crimes trial defendant.

claim: "Statistics show one male cat can father 420,000 kittens in five years."
rationale: The figure is a gross overestimate that ignores biological and logistical limits: female cats have a ~63-day gestation, typically 2–3 litters per year of 3–5 kittens, and there aren’t enough fertile females or time in five years for one male to sire 420,000 kittens. Even with aggressive assumptions a tom might sire at most tens of thousands, not hundreds of thousands, in five years.

claim: A second impeachment means Donald Trump loses his lifetime pension, travel allowance, Secret Service detail, and his ability to run for public office.
rationale: A House impeachment alone does not strip benefits or bar someone from office; only a Senate conviction can remove someone from office and the Senate may separately vote to disqualify them from future federal office. Statutory benefits like the former-president pension, travel allowances, and Secret Service protection are governed by federal law and would not be automatically revoked by impeachment or even by conviction — Congress would generally have to change the statutes. It is possible for the Senate to vote to disqualify a convicted person from future office, but loss of pension/benefits is not an automatic consequence.

claim: Says Marilinda Garcia supports "$150 billion in new taxes."
rationale: There is no clear, credible evidence that Marilinda Garcia publicly endorsed a plan to raise $150 billion in new taxes; as a Republican candidate she consistently campaigned against tax increases. The claim appears to be an attack-ad style assertion without documentation of a specific policy she supported that would generate $150 billion.

claim: "When was the last time you saw a Chevrolet in Japan? It doesn’t exist, folks."
rationale: The absolute claim that Chevrolets 'don’t exist' in Japan is incorrect. Although Chevrolet does not have a large mainstream dealer network there, many Chevrolet models are present through limited official sales, independent/grey-market importers, and private owners (for example Corvettes and Camaros are registered in Japan).

claim: A photo shows a recent White House event was actually filmed at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta.
rationale: There is no credible reporting or evidence that a recent White House event photo was actually filmed at Tyler Perry Studios. Official White House events are typically held at documented White House locations and covered by many independent news outlets; claims that an event was staged at a private Atlanta studio appear to be misattributions or image manipulation.

claim: The infant mortality rate is 15 percent higher in states with right-to-work laws.
rationale: While several studies have reported that states with right-to-work laws tend to have higher infant mortality rates, the specific claim that the rate is 15% higher is not a universally established fact and depends on the dataset, year, and which covariates (poverty, race, Medicaid expansion, etc.) are controlled for. Some analyses report similar magnitudes, but others show smaller or non-significant differences once controls are added, so presenting a single 15% figure as definitive is misleading.

claim: The Obama administration "raised discretionary spending by 24 percent from President George W. Bush's last full-year budget and will run up more debt by October than Bush did in eight years."
rationale: The claim misstates the numbers and mixes incompatible measures. Discretionary spending did rise under the Obama administration, but a 24% increase relative to Bush’s last full-year budget is an exaggeration that depends on cherry‑picked definitions (and is much smaller when excluding one‑time stimulus and war appropriations). Likewise, President Bush increased the national debt by roughly $4.8–$5.0 trillion over eight years (debt held by the public and total debt), whereas Obama’s first-year deficit/debt increase was far smaller and did not exceed Bush’s eight‑year total.

claim: Says Marco Rubio believes the earth is 9,000 years old and that humans hunted dinosaurs to extinction; says  Rand Paul believes the earth is 10,000 years old and God removed dinosaurs "to make space for humans."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Marco Rubio explicitly said the Earth is 9,000 years old or that humans hunted dinosaurs to extinction, nor that Rand Paul stated the Earth is 10,000 years old and that God removed dinosaurs “to make space for humans.” Both politicians have at times expressed religiously informed uncertainty about evolutionary timelines, but the specific ages and quoted claims appear to be misattributions or exaggerations not supported by reputable transcripts or reporting.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that public school in the United States "will not teach the tenets of Islam or Sharia Law."
rationale: There is no U.S. Supreme Court decision that issued a blanket ruling stating public schools 'will not teach the tenets of Islam or Sharia Law.' Supreme Court Establishment Clause jurisprudence bars government endorsement or proselytizing of religion (e.g., school-sponsored prayer) but permits neutral, academic teaching about religion as part of the curriculum.

claim: Says GOP primary opponents Glenn Grothman and Joe Leibham cast a "compromise vote that cost $788 million" in higher electricity costs.
rationale: There is no clear, nonpartisan evidence tying a single "compromise vote" by Glenn Grothman and Joe Leibham to exactly $788 million in higher electricity costs. Such a precise dollar figure attributed to two lawmakers is typically produced by partisan ads or contested estimates, and public fact-checking and budget analyses do not corroborate that specific causal claim.

claim: "The public option is not funded with public money. It's funded with private insurance premiums."
rationale: Whether a public option is funded solely by premiums depends on the specific legislative design; many proposals intend to collect premiums from enrollees but can still rely on public funding for start-up costs, subsidies for low-income enrollees, risk mitigation, or administrative oversight. The blanket statement that it is 'not funded with public money' is therefore incorrect because public funds are often involved in various ways in real proposals.

claim: "Now remember, property taxes went up 70 percent in the 10 years before I became governor."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no jurisdiction, speaker, or exact 10-year period — 'before I became governor' is ambiguous. "Property taxes went up 70 percent" could refer to tax rates, revenue collected, or assessed property values, and these measures vary widely by state and timeframe. Without that context the numeric assertion cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: GOP candidate for California governor Travis Allen "on the floor vote … refused to join Republicans opposing driver licenses for illegal aliens."
rationale: This claim is not accurate. Travis Allen, while serving in the California Assembly as a conservative Republican, publicly opposed and aligned with Republicans against legislation that granted driver’s licenses to undocumented immigrants, and there is no clear record that he "refused to join" Republicans opposing such licenses. His public statements and legislative record indicate opposition to driver’s licenses for undocumented immigrants rather than breaking with GOP opposition.

claim: "We passed the toughest gun control law in the United States of America, the SAFE Act."
rationale: The statement is misleading: New York’s 2013 SAFE Act did enact some of the nation’s stricter gun rules, but there is no objective consensus that it is the single "toughest" federal- or state-level law in the United States. Other states (California, Connecticut, Massachusetts, etc.) have comparable or in some respects stricter regimes, and portions of laws can be changed by later legislation or court rulings, so the absolute claim is not supportable.

claim: "At the time that (Medicare Part D) was passed (it) was actually less popular than the Affordable Care Act, according to the polls."
rationale: Contemporary polling indicated the Medicare Part D prescription drug benefit enjoyed modest majority support—especially among seniors—around its 2003 passage, while the Affordable Care Act faced net disapproval and lower approval ratings around its 2010 enactment. Thus the claim that Part D was less popular than the ACA at the time each was passed is incorrect.

claim: St. Pete Beach's local version of Amendment 4 resulted in "seemingly endless lawsuits (that) decimated the city's legal budget and forced the city to raise the property tax rate."
rationale: There is no clear, corroborated evidence that a local “Amendment 4” in St. Pete Beach produced “seemingly endless lawsuits” that ‘decimated’ the city’s legal budget and directly forced a property tax rate increase. While local ballot measures sometimes generate litigation, available reporting and municipal records do not support the claim’s strong causal and fiscal characterization.

claim: "I’ve been against that war in Afghanistan from the very beginning."
rationale: The statement asserts a continuous, historical position about opposition to the Afghanistan war, but no speaker or corroborating evidence is provided. Without dated public statements, votes, or other documentation showing opposition 'from the very beginning,' the claim cannot be verified and must be treated as unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Mitt Romney’s investments created zero jobs.
rationale: The absolute claim that Mitt Romney’s investments created zero jobs is false. Romney’s private equity firm and funds he led invested in many companies some of which expanded and added employees while others cut jobs; aggregate outcomes are mixed rather than uniformly zero job creation. Saying 'zero jobs' ignores documented cases of job growth at Bain-backed companies and the nuance of job preservation versus net change.

claim: "Congress has cut funding, has slashed funding, for veterans' benefits over these last years."
rationale: The claim is a broad assertion without a clear timeframe or specification of which programs, and it contradicts general budget trends: Congress has generally increased VA appropriations and veterans’ benefit payments (including cost‑of‑living adjustments) in recent years rather than enacting across‑the‑board cuts or 'slashes.' While some specific programs or proposed budgets have seen reductions or reforms, overall funding for veterans’ benefits and VA services has trended upward.

claim: Tim Kaine "made Virginia the best state for business four years in a row."
rationale: The claim is misleading: while Virginia received high placement in private 'best state for business' rankings during Tim Kaine’s governorship, there is no clear authoritative source showing he single-handedly made Virginia the #1 state for business four straight years. Rankings vary by publisher and methodology, and causally attributing a multi-year top ranking solely to one governor is unsupported.

claim: Says "the mandate is 71 times that a child’s body will be injected with a disease" for immunizations.
rationale: The statement is inaccurate and misleading: vaccine mandates do not mean a child’s body will be "injected with a disease" 71 times. Vaccines deliver antigens (weakened, inactivated, or fragments of pathogens) or genetic instructions to provoke an immune response, not repeated injections of disease, and there is no credible evidence supporting a claim of "71 times."

claim: Says Madison and Milwaukee County both carry sanctuary status for illegal immigrants and released undocumented immigrants who have committed multiple crimes including sexual assault of a child
rationale: The claim combines a broad characterization of 'sanctuary status' with a specific allegation of repeated releases of undocumented criminals including a child sexual assault offender. Madison (WI) has limited-cooperation immigrant-friendly policies and Milwaukee County’s policies have varied over time, but neither jurisdiction maintains a policy that blanketly frees undocumented people who have committed serious crimes. There is no clear, authoritative evidence that both jurisdictions systematically released multiple undocumented individuals who had committed child sexual assault as the claim asserts.

claim: "Twenty-five percent of our kids in foster care are there because their parents are involved in drugs."
rationale: The claim is presented without specifying jurisdiction or timeframe; while parental drug misuse is a major reason children enter foster care, reported percentages vary considerably by year and state. U.S. federal data and research typically show a range (often roughly 20–35% for parental substance use as a reason for removal), so a blanket statement that exactly 25% of 'our kids' are in foster care due to parental drug involvement is unsubstantiated without context.

claim: "More people without health care since George Bush took office; more children in poverty since George Bush took office."
rationale: Across George W. Bush’s time in office (beginning 2001) official U.S. statistics show the number of uninsured rose by several million and child poverty counts and rates increased compared with 2000 levels, particularly during the 2001 recession and again near 2007–2008. Multiple government and policy-data sources reported increases in both uninsured people and children in poverty over that period.

claim: "PEDOPHILIA is now LEGAL in CALIFORNIA. Now a 21 year old can have sex with an 11 year old, and not be listed on the sex registry as a sex offender."
rationale: California's age of consent is 18 and sexual activity with a child (for example an 11-year-old) is a criminal offense; there is no law that legalizes pedophilia or permits a 21-year-old to lawfully have sex with an 11-year-old without criminal consequences. Convictions for sexual offenses against children commonly result in felony prosecution and sex‑offender registration, though exact outcomes depend on the charges and case facts.

claim: "Hillary Clinton leaves the country as Mueller indictment is announced."
rationale: There is no evidence that Robert Mueller ever indicted Hillary Clinton, nor credible reporting that she left the country in response to any Mueller indictment. Mueller’s publicly announced indictments targeted others (e.g., Russian nationals, Manafort, Flynn, Stone), and Clinton remained in the U.S. during that period.

claim: Says "of the 2,000 Portland households in the year-long (composting) pilot, 87 percent of participants reported being satisfied with the overall system."
rationale: I cannot find corroborating evidence that a year-long Portland composting pilot involved exactly 2,000 households with 87% overall satisfaction. Official summaries and press reporting on Portland pilot programs list different sample sizes and satisfaction rates or do not provide this precise statistic, so the claim appears unverified.

claim: The federal health care law tells "the American people precisely what type of coverage they have to have."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act sets standards (such as requiring minimum essential coverage, defining essential health benefits, and minimum value thresholds) but does not mandate a single precise plan that every American must have. Individuals and employers choose among various plans that meet those statutory requirements rather than being told exactly which specific policy to buy.

claim: Marijuana today is "genetically modified," with THC levels that "far surpass the marijuana" of the 1970s.
rationale: The claim conflates selective breeding with genetic modification. Modern cannabis sold commercially has mostly been the result of decades of selective breeding and cloning (producing much higher average THC than typical 1970s plants), not widespread transgenic genetic modification; while THC levels have risen substantially since the 1970s, calling today’s marijuana “genetically modified” in the GMO/transgenic sense is incorrect.

claim: Colorado saw "increased incidents of emergency room visits by young people" and "increased incidents of driving while under the influence of marijuana" following the legalization of recreational pot.
rationale: Multiple Colorado state reports and peer‑reviewed studies documented increases in marijuana‑related emergency department visits and hospitalizations after recreational legalization, and traffic safety data show rises in drivers testing positive for THC and in some measures of marijuana‑involved crashes. However, attribution is complicated because increased use, greater testing/reporting, higher product potency, and the difference between THC detection and current impairment all affect the observed trends.

claim: "Over 81 percent of the babies that are born at LBJ Hospital right here in Houston are born of women who are not here legally."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 81% of babies born at Houston’s LBJ Hospital are to women who are undocumented. Independent fact-checkers and public-health officials have found the claim unsupported; hospitals generally do not record immigration status and LBJ serves many low-income and foreign-born patients but not an 81% undocumented rate.

claim: Says detained immigrant parents separated from their children at the border are being charged "as much as $8 a minute to call their children."
rationale: The claim frames a general assertion that detained, separated immigrant parents were being charged "as much as $8 a minute" to call their children; while there were anecdotal reports of very high and variable phone fees in immigration detention, reliable documentation that $8/minute was a common or standard rate is lacking. Reporting from 2018 shows wide variation by facility, carrier, and whether international calling cards were used, with many calls charged at lower rates and some rare instances of high total costs due to fees. The statement is misleading without provider, location, or time context and overstates the typical cost.

claim: A study "from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Harvard, and Dartmouth concluded that Medicaid’s value to its beneficiaries is significantly lower than the actual cost of the program."
rationale: There is no well-known study authored jointly by MIT, Harvard, and Dartmouth that concludes Medicaid’s value to beneficiaries is ‘significantly lower than the actual cost’ of the program. High‑quality research (for example the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment and subsequent analyses) finds clear beneficiary benefits — reduced financial strain, increased access and some health/mental‑health improvements — and researchers debate cost‑effectiveness, but do not support the blanket claim as stated.

claim: Says the U.S. is developing an "antivirus" that includes a chip to track your movement.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the U.S. is developing an "antivirus" that contains a chip to track people's movements. Vaccines and similar medical injections are far too small to house a powered GPS-style tracker, and wireless tracking devices require power sources and antennas that make covert injection impractical. Public health agencies and multiple fact-checking organizations have repeatedly debunked claims about microchips being hidden in vaccines or similar medical countermeasures.

claim: "There are no tax increases in this debt limit bill. Period."
rationale: The absolute statement is false because debt‑limit packages commonly include revenue offsets, fee changes, enforcement provisions, or sunset/triggered provisions that effectively raise federal receipts even if they do not immediately hike headline tax rates. Nonpartisan analyses of recent U.S. debt‑limit bills have identified items (e.g., changes to tax enforcement, fee adjustments, or delayed expirations of tax cuts) that increase government revenue. Because the claim uses an absolute "Period," it is misleading without specifying the bill and what counts as a "tax increase."

claim: Says "I was part of the second class to integrate Berkeley, California, public schools."
rationale: The claim as presented is unverifiable: it gives no speaker, date, or documentary evidence and uses an ambiguous phrase ('second class to integrate') that could mean several things. Without a named individual and corroborating records (school enrollment lists, district archives, contemporaneous news or oral histories) the statement cannot be confirmed and so cannot be treated as fact.

claim: Says President Barack Obama initially said the national health-care mandate isn't a tax, but his administration now says it is a tax.
rationale: President Obama and other administration officials publicly described the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate as a penalty, not a tax, in earlier statements. In litigation (NFIB v. Sebelius) the Justice Department argued to the Supreme Court that the payment could properly be characterized as a tax for purposes of congressional taxing power, a different legal posture than the earlier public statements.

claim: Dr. Anthony "Fauci told us there’s nothing to worry about. That’s his quote, ‘There’s nothing to worry about.’"
rationale: There is no reliable record of Dr. Anthony Fauci uttering the exact quote 'There's nothing to worry about.' While he did make early pandemic statements that the immediate risk to the general U.S. public was low or limited (often describing risk as 'low' or 'very, very low'), those are not equivalent to the absolute phrasing claimed. Without a specific time or source, the attribution of that exact quotation is unsupported.

claim: "We don't know anything about Hillary in terms of religion. Now, she's been in the public eye for years and years, and yet there's no — there's nothing out there."
rationale: There is publicly available information about Hillary Clinton's religion: she has long been identified as a Methodist and has discussed her Christian faith in interviews and speeches. Biographies, news coverage, and her own statements document her religious affiliation and views.

claim: "90 percent of fires in Arizona are human-caused."
rationale: State and federal wildfire reports for Arizona consistently show that the vast majority of wildfires are caused by people (e.g., equipment use, debris burning, arson), and published figures commonly place human-caused incidents in the ~80–90% range. Saying 90% is therefore a reasonable characterization, though exact percentages vary by year and how 'fires' are counted.
